items.stem: A 27-year-old woman with recurrent oral aphthous ulcers has Hb 115 g/L, low iron, mildly raised AST and ALT, and strongly raised IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies. She has occasional abdominal discomfort only. Which test is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
items.why: Raised anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA with iron deficiency anaemia, aphthous ulcers and raised transaminases suggests coeliac disease. Duodenal biopsy confirms the diagnosis.
notes: Capsule endoscopy is not needed to diagnose coeliac disease. Biopsy gives the histological diagnosis.
Colonoscopy does not sample the duodenum, where coeliac disease is confirmed.
Viral hepatitis may be checked, but the serology points to coeliac disease, and the transaminase rise is likely related to it.

items.stem: A 43-year-old man, recently taking NSAIDs, presents with 4 melaena stools in 12 hours, BP 95/65, HR 110 and Hb 81 g/L. He stabilises after fluids and transfusion. Endoscopy shows a 2 cm antral ulcer with a visible vessel (platelet plug, Forrest IIa). What is the best management?
options: Early discharge on a PPI and H. pylori eradication
Biopsy for H. pylori, withdraw carefully to avoid dislodging the plug, and continue IV PPI
Surgical consultation for urgent operative treatment
Endoscopic adrenaline injection plus clips, then IV PPI
items.why: A Forrest IIa ulcer (non-bleeding visible vessel) has a high rebleeding risk, so endoscopic haemostasis, ideally with two techniques (adrenaline plus clips), followed by high-dose IV PPI is indicated.
notes: This patient was unstable and has a high-risk lesion; early discharge is unsafe.
With a high-risk stigma, endoscopic therapy is needed rather than just leaving the plug in place and giving a PPI.
Surgery is only considered if endoscopic therapy fails to control bleeding.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has 6 months of fatigue, hoarse voice, slow speech, drowsiness and puffy hands, feet and face. Pulse is 52/min, with a puffy face and dry pale skin. He has mild anaemia, cholesterol 10 mmol/L, creatinine 115 µmol/L, TSH 187 mIU/L and free T4 2.6 pmol/L (normal 11–24). What is the most appropriate management?
items.why: This is severe primary hypothyroidism, treated with levothyroxine; antibodies (anti-TPO) can confirm autoimmune aetiology. Imaging or cytology is needed only if there is a nodule.
notes: Without a palpable nodule, ultrasound is not required before starting treatment.
The high TSH indicates primary thyroid failure, so pituitary MRI and free T3 are unnecessary.
Levothyroxine is the treatment of choice; liothyronine is not, and lipids and creatinine usually improve with thyroid replacement.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman with primary hyperparathyroidism and bone disease (subperiosteal resorption) has a minimally invasive parathyroidectomy for an adenoma. Postoperatively she has severe hypocalcaemia and tetany, and PTH is below 5 ng/L. She responds well to IV then oral calcium and vitamin D. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: After removal of an adenoma in long-standing hyperparathyroidism with bone disease, falling PTH ends resorption while osteoblasts keep taking up calcium, phosphate and magnesium. This causes hungry bone syndrome.
notes: Permanent hypoparathyroidism is rare after minimally invasive removal of a single adenoma.
Vitamin D insufficiency does not explain sudden severe postoperative hypocalcaemia and tetany.
Osteomalacia is a chronic bone mineralisation disorder, not an acute postoperative event.

items.stem: A 76-year-old obese woman with type 2 diabetes on metformin has had 3 days of fever (38.0°C), dysuria, frequency, marked thirst and falling level of consciousness. She is dehydrated, BP 95/54 mmHg, with no focal neurology. WCC is raised and creatinine is 159 µmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: An elderly type 2 diabetic with an infection (likely urinary), profound dehydration, thirst and reduced consciousness fits hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state.
notes: No trauma or focal neurological signs, and the picture is explained by infection and dehydration.
Renal impairment here is more likely prerenal from dehydration and does not explain the thirst and drowsiness.
DKA is typical of type 1 diabetes; this older type 2 patient with marked dehydration and coma fits HHS better.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man, diagnosed with hypertension 2 months ago, has glucose 7.2 mmol/L, LDL 4.1 mmol/L, HDL 1.0 mmol/L, creatinine 97 µmol/L, BMI 38, BP 157/93, oedema, nocturnal dyspnoea, and weaker right pedal pulses. Which test is LEAST useful for detecting hypertensive target-organ damage?
items.why: HbA1c would help diagnose diabetes in this patient but does not assess hypertensive target-organ damage. Echo (LVH), albuminuria (kidney) and ABI (peripheral arteries) do.
notes: Echocardiography detects left ventricular hypertrophy and cardiac dysfunction, which are target-organ damage.
Albuminuria is an early marker of hypertensive renal damage and is routinely assessed.
The ABI detects peripheral arterial disease, a form of vascular target-organ damage, relevant given the pulse asymmetry.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with depression takes a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Which antimicrobial should be avoided because of the risk of serotonin syndrome?
items.why: Linezolid is a reversible non-selective monoamine oxidase inhibitor. Combined with SSRIs it can cause serotonin syndrome, so the combination should be avoided.
notes: Doxycycline has no significant serotonergic activity.
Daptomycin is not serotonergic.
Vancomycin has no serotonergic interaction.

items.stem: A man with Becker muscular dystrophy (partial dystrophin gene deletion, Xp21) attends genetic counselling with his wife. Which information about the risk to their future children is correct?
options: Autosomal dominant: half of their children will be affected, regardless of sex
Daughters will not inherit the disease, but all sons will be carriers
Sons will not be affected, but all daughters will be carriers
Mitochondrial inheritance: there is no risk as males never transmit it
items.why: The disease is X-linked. An affected father passes his Y to his sons, so they are unaffected, and his X to all daughters, who become carriers with a 50% chance of transmitting it.
notes: The condition is X-linked recessive, not autosomal dominant.
Sons receive the father's Y chromosome and the mother's healthy X, so they are not carriers or affected by his mutation.
The gene is on the X chromosome, not mitochondrial DNA.

items.stem: A 32-year-old asymptomatic woman wishes to conceive. A routine check finds a 4 cm uterine fibroid, partly intramural and partly subserosal on the anterior wall, not distorting the endometrial cavity. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: GnRH analogue for three months before trying to conceive
items.why: An asymptomatic fibroid of this size that does not distort the endometrial cavity does not impair fertility or pregnancy, so no treatment is needed.
notes: Surgery is not indicated for an asymptomatic fibroid that does not distort the cavity, and it carries risks including uterine scarring.
Embolisation is not indicated and may compromise ovarian blood supply and future pregnancy.
GnRH analogues only shrink fibroids temporarily and delay conception without benefit.

items.stem: A 76-year-old postmenopausal woman has had vulvar pruritus for 4-5 years, unresponsive to topical treatments. For 3-4 months she has noticed a small lump on the left labium majus, which now bleeds serosanguinous fluid on rubbing, with occasional dysuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Chronic vulvar itching resistant to treatment, followed by a lump or ulcer, dysuria and bleeding in an older woman is typical of vulvar squamous cell carcinoma.
notes: Herpes causes painful, self-limiting vesicles and ulcers, not a chronic itch with a persistent lump.
Vulvar Paget's disease is an erythematous eczematous plaque, much rarer than SCC, and does not usually form a lump with bleeding.
A urethral caruncle is a small red mass at the urethral meatus, not on the labium majus.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension, menopausal since 55, has 2 months of intermittent scant vaginal bleeding. The cervix is atrophic, the uterus is normal and cervical cytology is normal. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 7 mm endometrium. Which test is most sensitive for diagnosis?
options: Examination under anaesthesia with cervical and endometrial biopsy
items.why: Postmenopausal bleeding with a thickened endometrium needs tissue diagnosis. Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy gives the most information about endometrial pathology, including cancer and polyps.
notes: Endometrial cytology samples blindly and has many false negatives.
MRI helps stage known endometrial cancer but does not give a tissue diagnosis.
Examination under anaesthesia with blind sampling is less sensitive than direct visualisation and targeted biopsy.

items.stem: A healthy 35-year-old woman presents with fatigue. FBC: Hb 70 g/L, MCV 68 fL, MCH 24 pg, RDW 20%, reticulocytes 0.3% (30 × 10⁹/L), reticulocyte Hb content 17 pg, platelets 500 × 10⁹/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Hypoproliferative anaemia due to iron deficiency
items.why: Microcytic hypochromic anaemia with low reticulocytes, high RDW, low reticulocyte Hb and reactive thrombocytosis indicates iron deficiency, common in women of reproductive age.
notes: Thalassaemia trait is microcytic but has a normal RDW, and no thrombocytosis or low reticulocyte Hb.
Haemolysis gives a raised reticulocyte count; here the marrow response is inadequate.
Acute haemorrhage is normocytic and normochromic with a regenerative response, not microcytic with low reticulocytes.

items.stem: A 43-year-old woman has fatigue, gum bleeding and petechiae. Hb 80 g/L, platelets 4 ×10⁹/L, white cells 1.2 ×10⁹/L with neutropenia, prolonged APTT, low fibrinogen (0.98 g/L) and raised D-dimer. Bone marrow shows massive infiltration by immature cells with cleaved nuclei and Auer rods. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Pancytopenia with DIC and a marrow full of blasts with Auer rods and cleaved nuclei is acute promyelocytic leukaemia (t(15;17)). It is a haematological emergency needing urgent ATRA.
notes: CML presents with leucocytosis and a chronic phase, with mature myeloid forms and Philadelphia chromosome, not blasts with Auer rods.
Monoblastic leukaemia can cause some coagulopathy, but cleaved nuclei with Auer rods and florid DIC point to promyelocytes.
Lymphoblasts do not contain Auer rods, which occur only in myeloid blasts.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with cerebral palsy has days of dark urine, fever and dry cough. Hb 63 g/L, MCV 109 fL, WCC 16.9 ×10⁹/L, platelets 360 ×10⁹/L, LDH 2408 U/L, bilirubin 116 µmol/L (mostly unconjugated). Film: spherocytes, polychromasia, no blasts. Antibody screen is pan-reactive. Most likely diagnosis and initial treatment?
options: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia after respiratory infection; corticosteroids
Pernicious anaemia; periodic vitamin B12 injections
items.why: Haemolysis (dark urine, high LDH, unconjugated bilirubin, polychromasia, spherocytes) with a pan-reactive antibody screen indicates autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. Corticosteroids are first-line treatment.
notes: Hereditary spherocytosis would not cause a pan-reactive antibody screen.
Pernicious anaemia causes ineffective, intramedullary haemolysis without reticulocytosis, and does not explain the pan-reactive antibodies.
No blasts are seen, and leukaemia does not explain the antibody findings.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man has had 1 week of fever, cough and right pleuritic pain. CXR shows a loculated right effusion filling two thirds of the hemithorax. Pleural fluid: WCC 15,000/µL (92% neutrophils), glucose 1.7 mmol/L, pH 7.0, LDH 3500 U/L, Gram stain negative. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Intravenous antibiotics and repeat diagnostic thoracentesis in 24 hours
Intravenous antibiotics and repeat thoracentesis only if no improvement in 48 hours
Intravenous antibiotics and intercostal drain insertion to drain the pleural fluid
items.why: This is a complicated parapneumonic effusion verging on empyema: pH <7.2, low glucose, very high LDH and loculation. It needs IV antibiotics plus prompt pleural drainage with a chest tube or catheter.
notes: Antibiotics alone are inadequate for a complicated, loculated effusion with pH 7.0.
Repeat diagnostic tapping delays the drainage this effusion clearly needs.
Waiting 48 hours for deterioration delays drainage of an effusion that already meets criteria for it.

items.stem: A 17-year-old woman presents with high fever, sore throat and cervical lymphadenopathy. She was treated for pharyngitis with amoxicillin and then developed a generalised maculopapular rash. Bloods show lymphocytosis with activated lymphocytes, mild thrombocytopenia and mildly raised transaminases. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: This is a typical mononucleosis picture (usually EBV): pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, atypical lymphocytosis and rash after amoxicillin.
notes: Varicella causes a vesicular rash, not this picture of pharyngitis with atypical lymphocytes.
Toxoplasmosis can mimic mononucleosis, but the amoxicillin-related rash and age make EBV more likely.
Lyme disease causes erythema migrans and does not present with atypical lymphocytosis and pharyngitis.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man falls 2 m onto his feet. He is alert, with clear urine in a urinary catheter, left heel swelling, tingling over the left anterior thigh and scrotum, and dysaesthesia in both feet. Arm function is normal. Pelvic compression and leg rotation are painless. What is the next step?
options: Radiology of the lower limbs (feet, femurs, pelvis)
Palpate the abdomen and log roll to palpate the thoracolumbar spine
Place a cervical collar and request lower limb and cervical spine imaging
items.why: A fall onto the feet with calcaneal injury and lower-limb neurology suggests a lumbar fracture with low spinal cord injury. Complete the primary survey with abdominal palpation and a log roll to examine the spine before imaging.
notes: Imaging comes after the clinical secondary survey, and pelvic injury is unlikely given painless compression.
Upper limb function is normal and there is no cervical suggestion, so a cervical focus is not the priority.
Ultrasound is mainly for haemodynamically unstable patients and follows the initial evaluation.

items.stem: A 40-year-old orthopaedic surgeon completed the standard hepatitis B vaccine course 4 years ago. Routine serology shows anti-HBs of 30 mIU/L. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Give hepatitis B immunoglobulin and restart the vaccination schedule
items.why: An anti-HBs level of 10 mIU/L or more indicates immunity after vaccination, so no revaccination or booster is needed.
notes: The level is protective, so a repeat course is unnecessary.
A booster is only considered when anti-HBs is below 10 mIU/L.
Immunoglobulin is for post-exposure prophylaxis in non-immune people, and this person is immune.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman, born in Cochabamba, Bolivia, has lived in Australia for 8 years. She presents with palpitations, dyspnoea and progressive leg oedema, and is diagnosed with heart failure from Chagas cardiomyopathy. Which organism causes this disease?
items.why: Chagas disease is caused by the protozoan Trypanosoma cruzi, endemic in Latin America. Chronic infection can cause dilated cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias years after migration.
notes: Toxoplasma gondii causes toxoplasmosis, not Chagas disease.
Trypanosoma brucei causes African sleeping sickness, not Chagas disease.
Leishmania donovani causes visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), not Chagas disease.

items.stem: A 17-year-old woman has high fever, sore throat and cervical lymphadenopathy. After amoxicillin for presumed pharyngitis she develops a generalised macular rash. Bloods show mild leukocytosis with activated lymphocytes, mild thrombocytopenia and mildly raised transaminases. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, atypical lymphocytes, mild hepatitis and a rash after amoxicillin are characteristic of EBV infectious mononucleosis.
notes: Varicella causes a vesicular rash, not this pharyngitis, atypical lymphocyte and amoxicillin-rash picture.
Can mimic mononucleosis, but fewer than 1% of acute infections present this way.
Presents with erythema migrans and a tick exposure history, and is not acquired in Australia.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation presents with left loin pain and dysuria. Urinalysis shows blood, leucocytes and nitrites. Which organism is the most common cause of urinary tract infection in pregnancy?
items.why: Escherichia coli is the most common cause of urinary tract infection, including in pregnancy.
notes: Proteus mirabilis is a less common cause, associated with struvite stones.
Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a less common cause, mainly in young sexually active women.
Group B streptococcus bacteriuria occurs in pregnancy but is far less common than E. coli.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension has BP 156/92 mmHg, creatinine 141 µmol/L, proteinuria 1.5 g/day and eGFR about 45 mL/min. She stopped verapamil for constipation and cannot tolerate ACE inhibitors (cough). Which drug class is most effective for slowing her diabetic nephropathy?
items.why: ACE inhibitors and ARBs slow progression of diabetic nephropathy. ARBs have proven benefit in type 2 diabetes and avoid the ACE inhibitor cough.
notes: She is intolerant of ACE inhibitors because of cough, so an ARB is the substitute.
Calcium channel blockers lower BP but have not been shown to slow diabetic nephropathy; she also stopped verapamil.
Beta-blockers lower BP but have no proven renoprotective effect in diabetic nephropathy.

items.stem: A 65-year-old retired office worker who smokes 20 cigarettes a day has a 2-year history of persistent dry cough and progressive exertional dyspnoea (mMRC grade 2). Examination is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Chest X-ray and spirometry with bronchodilator response
items.why: This is probably COPD, but it must be confirmed and severity assessed by spirometry before treatment. A chest X-ray is also needed in a smoker to exclude lung cancer or other causes.
notes: Treatment should follow confirmation of airflow obstruction by spirometry.
Oral corticosteroids are not indicated in stable suspected COPD.
CT is not the first investigation; start with chest X-ray and spirometry.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with well-controlled type 1 diabetes has 2 weeks of tingling in both hands. Pain and temperature sensation are lost in both hands and distal forearms, with preserved vibration and position sense. Strength and reflexes are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Dissociated sensory loss (pain and temperature lost, dorsal column modalities preserved) in a cape or hand distribution indicates a central cord lesion such as syringomyelia, affecting crossing spinothalamic fibres.
notes: Diabetic neuropathy is usually length-dependent, starting in the feet, with reduced reflexes. A 2-week onset with normal reflexes argues against it.
Compression would produce other signs such as brisk reflexes, weakness or dorsal column loss.
MS would typically give other findings such as hyperreflexia or other deficits, not isolated dissociated loss.

items.stem: A 42-year-old mother of two school-age children has had recurrent headaches for over a year, worse in the last 2 months. The current 7-day episode is a heavy pressure from the occiput to both temples, barely relieved by paracetamol. She has no nausea or focal neurology and requests a CT, convinced something is wrong. Most likely cause?
items.why: A recurrent, bilateral, heavy or pressing occipital-to-temporal headache in a stressed patient without associated neurological features is typical of tension-type headache.
notes: Migraine is usually unilateral and throbbing with nausea, photophobia or aura, none of which are described.
Temporal arteritis is rare under 50 and presents with temporal tenderness, jaw claudication and raised inflammatory markers.
Tumour headache is progressive and accompanied by neurological signs or raised intracranial pressure, not recurrent episodes.

items.stem: A 78-year-old man has a year of progressive cognitive impairment with memory and orientation lapses. His family reports recurrent visual hallucinations, occasional falls and marked slowing of movement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Early recurrent visual hallucinations in dementia are the hallmark of Lewy body dementia. Parkinsonism (motor slowing) and falls support it.
notes: Alzheimer disease typically presents with amnesia first; early prominent visual hallucinations and parkinsonism are not typical.
Frontotemporal dementia presents with early behavioural or language change, not visual hallucinations and parkinsonism.
Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a triad of gait disturbance, incontinence and dementia, without prominent visual hallucinations.

items.stem: A 1.5-year-old boy presents with abdominal pain, jaundice and a palpable abdominal mass. Ultrasound shows a choledochal (common bile duct) cyst. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Immediate radical resection and bowel reconstruction without further imaging
Exploratory laparotomy with cyst drainage, removing the drain once dilatation settles
MRCP to define the cyst type, then cyst excision with biliary-enteric anastomosis
HIDA scan to delineate the cyst, then percutaneous drainage
items.why: Choledochal cysts are treated surgically by cyst excision with hepaticojejunostomy. MRCP delineates the anatomy (Todani type) to choose the correct technique.
notes: Surgery is right in principle, but operative planning needs MRCP to define the Todani type first.
Simple drainage leaves the cyst in place, with ongoing risk of cholangitis and malignancy; excision is required.
Percutaneous drainage is not definitive; MRCP, not HIDA, is the imaging of choice for planning.

items.stem: An 18-year-old woman had absence seizures at ages 6 to 9 and now has recent generalised tonic-clonic seizures and violent jerks of the upper limbs at breakfast. Symptoms worsen after late weekend nights. EEG shows generalised polyspike-wave discharges at 4 to 6 Hz. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Symptomatic epilepsy due to mesial temporal sclerosis
items.why: Adolescent morning myoclonic jerks, prior absences, generalised seizures, sleep deprivation as a trigger and generalised polyspike-wave EEG are typical of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.
notes: Lennox-Gastaut starts in early childhood with multiple seizure types and intellectual impairment.
Mesial temporal sclerosis causes focal impaired-awareness seizures, with a temporal focus on EEG.
Absence epilepsy does not explain the myoclonic jerks or the polyspike pattern at adolescent onset.

items.stem: A patient has right-sided spastic hemiparesis with hyperreflexia and an extensor plantar response, plus a left facial palsy affecting upper and lower face (cannot close the left eye or retract the left mouth). Where is the lesion most likely located?
options: Medial portion of the left caudal pons
Medulla oblongata, above the decussation of the right corticospinal tract
items.why: Contralateral limb weakness with an ipsilateral lower motor neuron facial palsy is a crossed brainstem syndrome. The facial nucleus lies in the pons, so the lesion is in the left caudal pons.
notes: A right capsular lesion would cause left-sided weakness and a central (upper-face-sparing) facial palsy.
A left peduncular lesion would involve the oculomotor nerve, not the facial nerve.
The medulla contains lower cranial nerve nuclei (IX–XII), not the facial nucleus, which is pontine.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension and mild CKD has somnolence and right hemiparesis. Creatinine 203 µmol/L, Hb 103 g/L, platelets 20 ×10^9/L, normal coagulation. CT shows ischaemic lesions. He deteriorates; LDH and unconjugated bilirubin rise. Direct Coombs is negative; film shows schistocytes. What is the next step?
options: Repeat CT for suspected haemorrhagic transformation
Search for the trigger of disseminated intravascular coagulation
items.why: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with thrombocytopenia, neurological and renal involvement, normal coagulation and negative Coombs indicates TTP. Urgent plasma exchange is the treatment.
notes: Haemorrhagic transformation would not explain the haemolysis, schistocytes or the rise in LDH and creatinine.
Steroids alone are inadequate for a critically unwell patient with TTP. Plasma exchange is the first-line treatment.
DIC causes consumption of clotting factors with abnormal coagulation, which is absent here.

items.stem: A 75-year-old woman with soft drusen seen on fundoscopy 3 years ago reports 2 weeks of metamorphopsia and marked loss of central vision in her right eye, so she can no longer read. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Soft drusen indicate age-related macular degeneration; sudden metamorphopsia with central vision loss suggests conversion to the neovascular (wet) form with subretinal fluid or haemorrhage.
notes: An epiretinal membrane usually progresses more slowly and is not linked to drusen.
A macular hole causes more profound central loss and metamorphopsia is less likely in the acute stage.
CRVO causes more severe visual loss with widespread haemorrhages and rarely prominent metamorphopsia.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of right eye pain. Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining shows a central dendritic corneal ulcer. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: A dendritic corneal ulcer on fluorescein staining is typical of herpes simplex keratitis, which causes modest pain and little or no red eye. Bacterial and fungal keratitis show corneal infiltrates instead.
notes: A resolving abrasion can leave a pseudodendrite, but a true dendrite should first suggest herpes. Pain improves as an abrasion heals.
Fungal keratitis presents with corneal infiltrates rather than a dendritic ulcer.
Bacterial keratitis presents with corneal infiltrates rather than a dendritic ulcer.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man with Child-Pugh A cirrhosis has good performance status and only asthenia. CT shows 4 liver lesions (largest 6 cm) typical of hepatocellular carcinoma, with vascular invasion and a right adrenal metastasis. No ascites. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Systemic therapy with a tyrosine kinase inhibitor such as sorafenib
items.why: This is BCLC-C advanced HCC (vascular invasion, extrahepatic spread) with preserved liver function and good performance status, so systemic targeted therapy is indicated. Sorafenib is the classic option; current practice also uses immunotherapy-based regimens.
notes: He has good performance status and preserved liver function, so best supportive care alone is not appropriate.
TACE is not indicated with extrahepatic spread and vascular invasion.
Conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy such as doxorubicin is not effective in HCC and is not recommended.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man who stopped smoking 3 years ago presents with a first seizure. A CT head shows multiple brain metastases. Which is the most likely primary site?
items.why: Lung cancer is the most common cause of brain metastases, and in 20–30% of cases the brain lesions are the first presentation of the primary tumour.
notes: Head and neck cancers mainly spread locally and to regional nodes; brain metastases are uncommon.
Bladder cancer rarely metastasises to the brain.
Colon cancer more often spreads to liver and lung; brain metastases are uncommon.

items.stem: After direct trauma to the right side of the face, a patient has unilateral periorbital haematoma, diplopia on vertical gaze and difficulty opening the mouth. Which statement is most accurate?
options: This is most likely a Le Fort I fracture
This is probably a zygomatico-orbital fracture, ideally confirmed by CT
This is a skull base fracture at the carotid canal
This is probably a dislocated mandibular condyle fracture
items.why: Vertical diplopia implies involvement of the orbital walls, and trismus fits a zygomatic complex fracture. Le Fort I does not involve the orbit; CT confirms the diagnosis.
notes: Le Fort I is a low maxillary fracture and does not affect the orbital contents.
Nothing in the history suggests a skull base fracture; the findings localise to the orbit and zygoma.
A condylar injury would not explain orbital signs and vertical diplopia.

items.stem: A 64-year-old smoker with heavy alcohol use has 3 months of odynophagia and left otalgia. Dental cause excluded; non-contrast CT neck is normal. There is a 3 cm stony-hard induration of the left tongue base, no mucosal ulceration, no cervical nodes. What is the best presumptive diagnosis and action?
options: Dental cause; reassess with the dentist
Tongue base abscess; incision and drainage
Oropharyngeal malignancy; repeat imaging with contrast and biopsy
items.why: Tongue base cancer can be submucosal without ulceration and is easily missed on non-contrast CT. With risk factors and a stony induration, suspect malignancy and proceed to repeat imaging and biopsy.
notes: The dentist has already excluded a dental cause, and it would not explain a stony tongue base mass.
An abscess would be acute and septic; over 3 months it would have caused serious illness, not a stony induration.
Ankyloglossia is a congenital tongue-tie and does not cause a stony mass, odynophagia or otalgia.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man presents with a right thyroid nodule and has a fine needle aspiration (FNA). Which of the following can cytological analysis of the aspirate reliably identify?
options: Distinguishing follicular adenoma from minimally invasive follicular carcinoma
Areas of capsular or vascular invasion in a follicular carcinoma
Distinguishing a Hürthle cell tumour from an oxyphilic follicular adenoma
The typical cytological features of papillary carcinoma
items.why: FNA gives cytology, not architecture, so it can identify papillary carcinoma nuclear features. Capsular or vascular invasion needs histology of the resected specimen.
notes: Separating adenoma from follicular carcinoma needs capsular or vascular invasion on histology, which FNA cannot show.
Invasion is a histological finding that needs the whole resected nodule, not an aspirate.
Oncocytic (Hürthle) lesions cannot be reliably separated as benign or malignant on cytology; this needs histology.

items.stem: A term newborn has an orogastric/nasogastric tube that cannot be passed in the delivery room. X-ray shows a blind-ending oesophageal pouch with gas in the stomach and bowel. No other anomalies are found and the baby is respiratorily stable. What is the main reason for prompt surgery?
items.why: Gas in the gastrointestinal tract indicates a distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula, so gastric contents can reflux into the airway, causing chemical pneumonitis and pulmonary complications.
notes: Saliva pooling is managed by upper pouch suction and does not drive urgency.
Cardiac anomalies are associated but have been excluded and do not determine surgical priority.
Feeding can be bridged with parenteral nutrition; it is not the priority.

items.stem: A 2-year-old boy has recurrent otitis media, meningococcal meningitis and pneumonias, plus three episodes of thrombocytopenic purpura without antiplatelet antibodies. Maternal male relatives died in childhood of infections. He has atopic dermatitis, raised IgA and IgE, low IgM and mildly reduced T cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is X-linked and combines immunodeficiency, thrombocytopenia and eczema, with raised IgA and IgE, low IgM and variable T-cell defects.
notes: Hyper IgE causes staphylococcal abscesses, eczema and pneumatocoeles but not thrombocytopenia, and is not typically X-linked.
X-linked SCID presents in early infancy with severe T-cell failure and profound hypogammaglobulinaemia, not thrombocytopenia and eczema.
CVID usually presents later with low IgG and IgA, and does not cause thrombocytopenia with eczema in a male infant with X-linked family history.

items.stem: A healthy 12-year-old girl has mild hepatomegaly found at a pre-sport check. ALT 105 U/L, AST 80 U/L, normal protein electrophoresis, negative viral hepatitis serology. Which diagnosis should be excluded, and with what tests?
options: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency; CT chest to confirm emphysema
Wilson disease; serum caeruloplasmin and copper, urinary copper
items.why: Unexplained persistent transaminase elevation in a child or adolescent warrants excluding Wilson disease, using the least invasive tests: caeruloplasmin and copper levels in blood and urine.
notes: Alpha-1 antitrypsin is assessed by serum level or phenotype; chest CT is unnecessary in a child.
Cystic fibrosis liver disease is unlikely without respiratory or GI features.
Autoimmune hepatitis typically shows hypergammaglobulinaemia, and biopsy would not be first-line.

items.stem: A 7-month-old infant has fever, irritability and a bulging fontanelle. CSF shows 110 x10^6 cells/L (75% lymphocytes), protein 1.2 g/L and glucose 1.6 mmol/L (serum glucose 4.9 mmol/L). What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Lymphocytic pleocytosis with raised protein and markedly low CSF glucose (CSF:serum ratio about 0.3) is the typical CSF pattern of tuberculous meningitis.
notes: Viral meningitis gives lymphocytes with raised protein but normal glucose.
Bacterial meningitis typically gives a neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis; lymphocyte predominance argues against it.
Guillain-Barré causes albuminocytologic dissociation (high protein, near-normal cells) and no fever or bulging fontanelle.

items.stem: A 1-month-old exclusively breastfed, thriving infant passes a soft stool with straining every 5 to 6 days. Examination is normal. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Reassure that this is a normal stool pattern
Refer to paediatric gastroenterology to exclude Hirschsprung disease
items.why: Stool frequency in young breastfed infants varies widely, and infrequent soft stools are normal. Hirschsprung disease usually shows delayed meconium passage, abdominal distension or poor weight gain.
notes: Laxatives are not needed for soft stools in a well infant.
Formula supplementation is unnecessary and undermines exclusive breastfeeding.
Hirschsprung disease usually presents with delayed meconium, distension and poor weight gain, none of which are present.

items.stem: A 7-month-old has 5 days of fever to 39.5°C unresponsive to amoxicillin. Over 24 hours he developed a pruritic cephalocaudal erythematous rash, with cough and marked conjunctivitis but no rhinorrhoea. There are fine crackles at both bases and whitish spots on the buccal mucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Whitish buccal mucosal spots are Koplik spots, pathognomonic of measles. With fever, conjunctivitis, cough and a cephalocaudal rash, this is measles complicated by pneumonia.
notes: Kawasaki does not cause Koplik spots or cough, and the presentation here fits measles better.
Scarlet fever gives a sandpaper rash with pharyngitis and strawberry tongue, not Koplik spots or conjunctivitis.
Drug rash would not explain Koplik spots, cough and conjunctivitis; the fever predated the amoxicillin's effect.

items.stem: A 19-year-old university student has 2 months of fatigue, poor appetite, weight loss (90% of ideal weight), poor concentration, loss of interest in friends, thoughts of death without self-harm intent and a pessimistic outlook. She has no weight phobia or body image distortion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Low mood, anhedonia, appetite and weight loss, poor concentration and thoughts of death over 2 weeks or more meet criteria for major depressive disorder. Anorexia requires fear of weight gain and body image disturbance.
notes: Anorexia nervosa requires intense fear of weight gain and body image distortion, both absent here.
There is no prominent excessive worry or anxiety symptom cluster; the picture is depressive.
Persistent depressive disorder requires at least 2 years of symptoms (1 year in adolescents), but this has lasted 2 months.

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman presents to the emergency department very distressed after an argument with her partner. Over the past year she has had several similar presentations, two after self-harm. She has frequent relationship conflicts, job changes and family arguments, and feels misunderstood by everyone, including her psychiatrists. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Unstable relationships, impulsivity, intolerance of rejection and recurrent self-harm in a young woman fit borderline personality disorder.
notes: Histrionic personality centres on attention-seeking, theatricality and seductive behaviour, not recurrent self-harm and unstable relationships.
No sustained low mood is described; persistent depressive disorder does not explain the pattern.
No dissociative syndrome is described; dissociative symptoms alone are not a disorder here.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset bilateral upper limb paralysis that began two hours ago. She smiles and says she does not understand why her family is worried. Her son was arrested yesterday for drug trafficking. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Abrupt neurological deficit after an acute psychological stressor, with marked unconcern (la belle indifférence), suggests conversion disorder. The symptom is not consciously feigned for gain.
notes: Factitious disorder involves deliberate feigning of illness; nothing here suggests intentional production of symptoms.
No fixed false beliefs are described, so delusional disorder does not fit.
She shows no sadness or low mood, so a major depressive episode is not supported.

items.stem: An 84-year-old man with advanced dementia has had his third admission in 6 months for aspiration pneumonia, with 9.5 kg weight loss and a sacral pressure ulcer. He is bed-bound and dependent. Swallow study shows aspiration with all consistencies. His advance care directive refuses artificial nutrition, and his wife is his substitute decision-maker. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
options: Discharge to a nursing home until the pressure ulcer heals
Insert a PEG tube and discharge home
Insert a nasogastric tube and discharge to a nursing home
Discharge home with a community palliative care service
items.why: In advanced dementia with recurrent aspiration, tube feeding does not prolong life or prevent aspiration. His valid advance care directive refuses artificial nutrition, so comfort-focused care at home with palliative support matches his and his wife's wishes.
notes: This ignores his wife's wish to care for him at home and does not address the goals of care or the directive.
A PEG is artificial nutrition, which his directive refuses. It also does not prevent aspiration or improve survival in advanced dementia.
A nasogastric tube is artificial nutrition, which his directive refuses. It does not prevent aspiration in advanced dementia.

items.stem: An 84-year-old woman has sleep-onset insomnia that has not responded to sleep hygiene measures. Pharmacotherapy is considered unavoidable. Which drug is the most appropriate choice, given her risk of falls?
items.why: If a hypnotic is unavoidable in an older person, choose a short-acting benzodiazepine at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Its short half-life limits next-day sedation and falls.
notes: Long half-life with active metabolites causes accumulation, daytime sedation and falls in the elderly.
Barbiturates are not appropriate hypnotics: narrow therapeutic index, heavy sedation and dependence risk.
Long-acting with active metabolites, so it accumulates in the elderly and raises fall risk.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman with photosensitive rash and intermittent hand polyarthritis has 15 days of malaise and pallor. Hb 78 g/L, MCV 108 fL, platelets 150, WCC 3.0, LDH raised, haptoglobin undetectable. Which single test should be done first?
items.why: This picture suggests autoimmune haemolytic anaemia in probable SLE. The direct antiglobulin test confirms it and allows treatment to start; the other tests can wait.
notes: ANA can wait; it will not guide urgent treatment of the haemolysis.
B12 deficiency does not explain low haptoglobin and raised LDH from haemolysis.
Ferritin would not confirm haemolysis; iron deficiency is microcytic.

items.stem: A man with hyperuricaemia, usually taking allopurinol 100 mg daily, presents to the ED with an acutely painful, inflamed right knee. Joint aspirate shows intracellular crystals with negative birefringence under polarised light. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Cease allopurinol and start an NSAID
Continue allopurinol and add an NSAID until the flare settles
items.why: Negatively birefringent intracellular crystals confirm acute gout. Treat the flare with an anti-inflammatory such as an NSAID and continue the existing urate-lowering therapy, as changing it during a flare can worsen the attack.
notes: Stopping allopurinol during a flare is not advised; altering urate levels can prolong or worsen the attack.
Stopping allopurinol is wrong; urate-lowering therapy should not be changed during the acute episode.
Changing the allopurinol dose during an acute flare can worsen it; titrate later once the flare has settled.

items.stem: A 75-year-old woman presents with violaceous lesions on the hands and neck and 3 months of progressive proximal muscle weakness. Which one of the following tests would be most useful in supporting the likely diagnosis?
items.why: The picture suggests dermatomyositis, in which muscle enzymes such as aldolase (and CK) are elevated. Confirmation needs muscle, not subcutaneous, biopsy.
notes: An EEG assesses cortical electrical activity and has no role in inflammatory myopathy.
Biopsy for suspected myositis should be of muscle, not subcutaneous tissue.
Anti-smooth muscle antibodies are associated with autoimmune hepatitis, not dermatomyositis.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man on an ACE inhibitor, with a past duodenal ulcer and uric acid stones, has recurrent podagra. Examination shows tophi on both ears. Urate is 0.60 mmol/L and creatinine 133 µmol/L. Which statement about starting allopurinol is FALSE?
options: It is second choice, used when uricosurics have failed
Long-term use is practically obligatory because of the tophi
It is started low and titrated to a urate below 0.36 mmol/L
Low-dose colchicine in the first months helps prevent flares
items.why: Allopurinol is the first-line urate-lowering drug, especially in tophaceous gout. Uricosurics are second line and could worsen urolithiasis by raising urinary uric acid.
notes: True: tophi indicate severe gout, which needs lifelong urate lowering.
True: start low, titrate gradually, and aim for urate below 0.36 mmol/L.
True: flare prophylaxis with low-dose colchicine is advised for the first months of urate-lowering therapy.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man presents to the emergency department with oral aphthous ulcers, conjunctivitis, urethritis, balanitis and joint pain. Which diagnosis is most likely?
items.why: Conjunctivitis, urethritis, mucocutaneous lesions (oral ulcers, balanitis) and joint symptoms form the classic presentation of reactive arthritis (formerly Reiter syndrome).
notes: Behçet disease causes oral and genital ulcers, but urethritis is not a feature and the typical eye lesion is uveitis.
Sweet syndrome is a neutrophilic dermatosis with fever and tender plaques, not urethritis and conjunctivitis.
Gonococcal infection can cause urethritis and arthralgia, but it does not explain the combination with conjunctivitis, oral ulcers and balanitis as well as reactive arthritis.

items.stem: A 75-year-old has severe knee osteoarthritis with varus deformity, marked functional limitation and constant pain despite regular analgesics, NSAIDs and non-surgical management. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Further rehabilitation of the knee alone
items.why: End-stage osteoarthritis refractory to medical therapy is treated with total knee arthroplasty, which also corrects the varus deformity.
notes: Arthroscopic lavage does not help established severe osteoarthritis.
Non-surgical measures have already been exhausted in this patient.
Osteotomy suits younger patients with early, localised disease; here the joint damage is severe.

items.stem: A 12-year-old obese boy (87 kg) has had 4 months of mechanical pain in the right thigh and knee. He has a 1 cm leg-length discrepancy, and the right leg lies in external rotation with loss of internal rotation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Sequelae of developmental dysplasia of the hip.
items.why: An obese adolescent with hip pain referred to the knee, a shortened externally rotated leg and lost internal rotation has slipped capital femoral epiphysis.
notes: Usually polyarticular or systemic, with no such features here; the picture is confined to one hip.
Perthes disease occurs at about 4–9 years with a limp and hip or knee pain.
Would present earlier in life, not with a new 4-month onset in adolescence.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with a 25-year history of uric acid stones has 2 hours of severe right loin pain and palpitations. Urine pH is 5.5 with leukocyturia. ECG shows new AF. Creatinine 80 µmol/L, calcium 2.75 mmol/L, LDH 950 U/L. Which imaging is most useful?
options: Non-contrast CT of kidneys, ureters and bladder
items.why: CT has the highest sensitivity and specificity (about 94-100%) for ureteric calculi, detecting stones down to 2 mm, including radiolucent uric acid stones. In Australia the non-contrast CT KUB is the standard.
notes: Sensitivity is only about 45-59%, and uric acid stones are radiolucent, so a stone could be missed.
Informative about obstruction and function, but slower and now largely replaced by CT.
Operator-dependent and detects only about 20-45% of stones, though it shows hydronephrosis well.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man with heavy alcohol use and hepatitis C, taking ibuprofen for shoulder tendinitis, develops tense blisters on the dorsum of both hands after two weeks at the beach. He also has mild malar hypertrichosis. Most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Porphyria cutanea tarda causes photosensitive blistering of the hand dorsa with hypertrichosis, linked to alcohol, hepatitis C and iron overload reducing uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity.
notes: Causes trauma-induced skin fragility on extensor surfaces, not photo-distributed blisters with hypertrichosis.
A phototoxic reaction causes sunburn-like erythema, not hypertrichosis or tense blisters in this risk context.
Acute intermittent porphyria causes neurovisceral attacks and has no cutaneous photosensitivity.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with kidney failure from autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease has received a deceased-donor kidney transplant. His asymptomatic 34-year-old brother wants to know if he is affected. What is the most appropriate test to recommend?
items.why: Ultrasound is the first-line, cheapest, sensitive and specific test for diagnosing ADPKD in at-risk relatives. Age-specific cyst number criteria are applied.
notes: Genetic testing is reserved for equivocal imaging or when a young potential living donor needs exclusion; it is not first line.
MRI is not needed for initial screening; cerebral imaging is only for selected patients, such as those with a family history of aneurysm.
Clinical review alone cannot establish or exclude the diagnosis in an at-risk relative.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis has nephrotic-range proteinuria (6 g/day), hypoalbuminaemia and oedema, with no haematuria. Creatinine is 141 µmol/L, eGFR 45 mL/min, glucose 6.1 mmol/L. Severe spinal deformity precludes percutaneous renal biopsy. What is the most appropriate initial step?
options: Start corticosteroids for presumed minimal change disease
Start cyclophosphamide for presumed membranous nephropathy
items.why: Long-standing ankylosing spondylitis with nephrotic syndrome and no haematuria (against IgA nephropathy) suggests AA amyloidosis, which can be diagnosed with a subcutaneous fat biopsy when renal biopsy is not feasible.
notes: Treating empirically for minimal change disease is unjustified without histology, and it is uncommon at this age with reduced GFR.
Cytotoxic therapy for membranous nephropathy should not be started empirically without tissue diagnosis.
Dialysis is not indicated at an eGFR of 45 mL/min without urgent indications.

items.stem: An 80-year-old man with hypertension taking ramipril and spironolactone presents with asthenia and severe muscle weakness. BP is 110/70 mmHg. ECG shows peaked T waves, ventricular ectopics and a short QT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: ACE inhibitor plus potassium-sparing spironolactone causes hyperkalaemia. It produces tall, narrow-based symmetrical T waves and a shortened QT, with conduction disturbances and ectopics at higher levels (above about 6.5 mmol/L).
notes: Hypercalcaemia shortens the QT but does not cause peaked T waves, and is not explained by these drugs.
Hypomagnesaemia causes QT prolongation and arrhythmias, not peaked T waves.
Hypocalcaemia prolongs the QT interval rather than shortening it.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman (130 kg, 155 cm) has mild hypertension, glucose 6.0 mmol/L, no leg oedema, creatinine 177 µmol/L, urea 14 mmol/L, albumin 38 g/L. Urine sediment is bland; 24-hour proteinuria is 6.3 g. Which diagnosis is most likely?
items.why: Obesity, hypertension, renal impairment and nephrotic-range proteinuria with a bland sediment and preserved albumin fit obesity-related focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.
notes: Possible non-proliferative cause, but obesity with hypertension and renal impairment favours FSGS.
IgA nephropathy is proliferative and typically gives haematuria with an active sediment.
Minimal change disease usually causes florid nephrotic syndrome with low albumin and oedema, and normal renal function.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has blood pressure 190/120 mmHg and serum potassium 2.5 mmol/L. Ultrasound shows bilateral renal artery stenosis. Which antihypertensive is contraindicated?
items.why: In bilateral renal artery stenosis, GFR depends on efferent arteriolar constriction by angiotensin II. ACE inhibitors dilate the efferent arteriole, causing a fall in GFR and acute kidney injury.
notes: Beta-blockers are acceptable and reduce renin release.
Amiloride is not contraindicated by renal artery stenosis and helps the hypokalaemia, although potassium needs monitoring.
Calcium channel blockers are safe in renal artery stenosis.

items.stem: A patient with chronic heart failure has prominent v waves in the jugular venous pulse and a holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge and xiphoid area that increases with deep inspiration. Which valvular lesion is responsible?
items.why: Tricuspid regurgitation produces a holosystolic murmur at the xiphoid area that increases with inspiration (Carvallo sign), with giant v waves as blood regurgitates into the right atrium in systole.
notes: Mitral regurgitation is heard at the apex, radiates to the axilla, and doesn't increase with inspiration or cause jugular v waves.
Pulmonary regurgitation is a diastolic murmur, not holosystolic.
Aortic stenosis is an ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge radiating to the carotids, with no jugular v waves.

items.stem: An 82-year-old man has exertional angina and a grade 3/6 ejection systolic murmur. Which investigation should be performed first?
items.why: An ejection systolic murmur with angina suggests aortic stenosis, whose severity must be established first. Doppler echocardiography is the non-invasive first step.
notes: Exercise testing is risky in symptomatic possible severe aortic stenosis and can provoke syncope.
Angiography is invasive and should follow non-invasive assessment of the valve.
In an 82-year-old, heavy calcification limits the value of CT, and it does not first assess valve severity.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetes has a painful right medial malleolar ulcer, with rest pain worse at night. Femoral and popliteal pulses are normal but distal pulses are absent. Which investigation should be done first?
options: Venous duplex ultrasound of the lower limbs
items.why: This is suspected chronic limb ischaemia. The ankle-brachial index is the least invasive, cheapest first test to confirm and grade arterial disease.
notes: Venous duplex assesses venous disease; the varicosities are uncomplicated and the picture is ischaemic.
CT angiography is used for anatomical planning after ischaemia is confirmed.
Invasive angiography is reserved for planning revascularisation, not first-line.

items.stem: A well 14-year-old girl has a 4-day history of intensely itchy, generalised erythematous, oedematous plaques 2–15 cm across, often annular, each resolving within 24 hours without scaling. Mucous membranes are spared. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Acute urticaria causes itchy, erythematous, oedematous, evanescent wheals lasting under 24 hours without scaling, with preserved general condition. Annular lesions are common in children.
notes: Drug eruptions are usually more persistent, and the patient is often unwell; individual lesions do not vanish within 24 hours.
Toxic shock syndrome causes systemic illness and a diffuse erythroderma or blistering rash, not a well child with transient wheals.
Scabies causes burrows and papules, typically in the finger webs, with linear tracks, not transient plaques.

items.stem: A 26-year-old competitive athlete is investigated after his brother's sudden cardiac death. Testing shows obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Which of the following management statements is INCORRECT?
options: Digoxin is useful to reduce the subaortic gradient
Screening of first-degree relatives should be performed
items.why: Digoxin is a positive inotrope and increases the dynamic LV outflow gradient, so it is contraindicated in obstructive HCM. Negatively inotropic beta-blockers relax the myocardium and are first-line.
notes: This statement is correct: beta-blockers relax the myocardium and reduce symptoms.
This statement is correct: competitive sport is discouraged because of the sudden-death risk.
This statement is correct: HCM is hereditary, so relatives should be screened with examination and ECG.

items.stem: A patient with severe COPD presents with acute dyspnoea. ABG on FiO2 0.31 at sea level: PaO2 11.5 kPa, PaCO2 8.7 kPa, pH 7.13, bicarbonate 27 mmol/L. Which statement about this result is INCORRECT?
options: The alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient is elevated.
The patient has a respiratory acidosis.
Initiation of ventilatory support should be considered.
items.why: A raised PaCO2 means the patient is hypoventilating, not hyperventilating. This is an acute respiratory acidosis with bicarbonate not yet compensated by renal retention.
notes: The statement is true: a normal PaO2 on supplemental oxygen means a widened A-a gradient. Without oxygen the patient would be hypoxaemic.
The statement is true: low pH with raised PaCO2 and near-normal bicarbonate is an acute respiratory acidosis.
The statement is true: pH below 7.20 with hypercapnia in severe COPD is a reason to consider non-invasive ventilation.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man with a 45-year, 20-cigarettes-a-day smoking history has progressive exertional dyspnoea and daily sputum. SpO2 is 94% and chest X-ray shows hyperinflation. Spirometry: FEV1 58% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.61, no bronchodilator response. Which is the most appropriate treatment to start?
options: Home oxygen with a portable source for ambulation
items.why: This is moderate COPD (GOLD 2) with modest symptoms. Initial treatment is a long-acting bronchodilator, either a LAMA such as tiotropium or a LABA.
notes: Inhaled corticosteroids are not first-line in COPD; they are added to bronchodilators for frequent exacerbations or high eosinophils.
Long-term oxygen is only indicated with resting hypoxaemia (PaO2 ≤55 mmHg); this patient has SpO2 94%.
Long-term oral corticosteroids have no role in stable COPD and cause significant adverse effects.

items.stem: A 71-year-old retired non-smoking waiter has nocturnal snoring and BMI 31.5 kg/m². Epworth score is 3 with mild postprandial sleepiness only, and no other symptoms or comorbidities. Polysomnography shows an AHI of 18/hour. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Weight loss and lifestyle measures with follow-up
items.why: This is moderate OSA that is essentially asymptomatic, with no high-risk occupation or comorbidity. Weight loss and lifestyle measures with regular review are appropriate.
notes: Surgery is not first-line and is not warranted in an asymptomatic patient.
CPAP is reserved for symptomatic patients, higher AHI, or those with risk occupations or comorbidities.
Non-invasive ventilation is for hypoventilation syndromes, not simple OSA.

items.stem: A 30-year-old asymptomatic woman has anaemia found on routine testing. Examination shows scleral icterus and splenomegaly. Her family has a history of early-onset gallstones. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Chronic haemolysis (anaemia, jaundice, splenomegaly) with pigment gallstones at a young age in the family fits hereditary spherocytosis, which can stay asymptomatic until adulthood.
notes: G6PD deficiency causes episodic haemolysis triggered by drugs, infection or fava beans, none mentioned here.
Thalassaemia minor causes microcytosis with mild anaemia, usually without jaundice or splenomegaly.
Pyruvate kinase deficiency is rarer and usually presents with more severe haemolysis earlier in life.

items.stem: An 18-month-old boy presents with right knee swelling after playing in the park, with no obvious trauma. The mother's uncle had similar problems. Ultrasound shows haemarthrosis. The only abnormality on blood tests is a prolonged APTT of 52 seconds (normal 25–35). What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Spontaneous haemarthrosis in a young boy, an affected maternal relative (X-linked) and isolated prolonged APTT indicate haemophilia A.
notes: Marfan syndrome is a connective tissue disorder with normal coagulation tests.
Von Willebrand disease typically causes mucosal or post-surgical/trauma bleeding, and is less often with haemarthrosis in an X-linked pattern.
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a connective tissue disorder with normal coagulation tests.

items.stem: A patient reports several months of tongue enlargement without other tongue changes, causing him to bite it constantly. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Amyloidosis is deposition of fibrillar protein, localised or systemic. Amyloid deposits in the tongue can cause macroglossia, with the kidneys and heart most often affected.
notes: Hypoglossal palsy causes tongue deviation and atrophy, not enlargement.
Hyperthyroidism does not typically cause macroglossia (hypothyroidism can).
Mastocytosis causes skin lesions and mediator symptoms, not macroglossia.

items.stem: A 29-year-old patient is diagnosed with severe aplastic anaemia. A fully HLA-matched sibling is available. What is the treatment of choice?
options: Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplant from the matched sibling
items.why: In younger patients (under about 40) with severe aplastic anaemia and a matched sibling donor, allogeneic stem cell transplant is first-line because it can cure the disease.
notes: Supportive care only bridges the problem and does not treat the marrow failure.
Autologous transplant is unsuitable because the patient's own marrow is aplastic and cannot provide healthy stem cells.
Immunosuppression is used when no matched donor exists or the patient is older, not first-line here.

items.stem: A 76-year-old woman fears stroke as her mother died of one. She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes on gliclazide, aspirin, enalapril and atorvastatin, smokes 20 cigarettes daily and is sedentary. BP 150/80 mmHg, HbA1c 64 mmol/mol, LDL 2.8 mmol/L. Which action gives the greatest stroke risk reduction?
items.why: Hypertension is the most influential modifiable risk factor for stroke, particularly in older women, and blood pressure lowering gives the largest stroke risk reduction.
notes: Tighter glycaemic control mainly reduces microvascular disease, with a smaller effect on stroke.
Smoking cessation lowers risk, but the effect is smaller than treating blood pressure in this age group.
Further LDL lowering reduces stroke risk modestly compared with blood pressure control.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman with a BMI of 38 kg/m² has been obese since age 17. Despite a supervised 1500 kcal diet and 4 hours of aerobic exercise weekly she has lost 3 kg and needs 7 kg more. Which drug would reduce dietary fat absorption?
items.why: Orlistat inhibits gastric and pancreatic lipases, so about 30% of dietary fat is not absorbed. It is the anti-obesity drug whose mechanism is reduced fat absorption.
notes: Topiramate is an anticonvulsant that causes weight loss through appetite suppression. It does not affect fat absorption.
Liraglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist. It reduces appetite and slows gastric emptying and does not block fat absorption.
Metformin is a glucose-lowering drug with modest weight effects. It does not reduce fat absorption and is not an anti-obesity agent.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man with a previous bowel resection for mesenteric thrombosis has fatigue, bone pain and a Colles' fracture 3 months ago. Hb 95 g/L (microcytic), albumin 35 g/L, calcium 1.88 mmol/L, phosphate 0.65 mmol/L, ALP 224 U/L. Femoral X-ray shows radiolucent bands perpendicular to the inner cortex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Intestinal resection causes malabsorption and vitamin D deficiency, giving low calcium and phosphate, raised ALP, bone pain and fractures. Looser zones (pseudofractures) on X-ray are characteristic of osteomalacia.
notes: Osteoporosis has normal calcium, phosphate and ALP and does not cause Looser zones.
Paget's disease has raised ALP but normal calcium and phosphate, with sclerotic and lytic bone enlargement, not hypocalcaemia.
Prostate metastases are typically sclerotic and would not explain low calcium and phosphate with Looser zones after bowel resection.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has an asymptomatic 2 cm firm, smooth anterior neck lump that moves with swallowing, with no palpable lymphadenopathy. Which test is most useful for establishing whether the nodule is malignant?
items.why: A solitary thyroid nodule needs cytology by fine needle aspiration (usually ultrasound-guided) to assess for malignancy, alongside TSH. A 2 cm nodule is above the usual size threshold for sampling.
notes: Thyroglobulin is not specific for malignancy and is used to monitor differentiated thyroid cancer after treatment.
CT is not first-line for a thyroid nodule and cannot reliably distinguish benign from malignant disease.
Antibodies support autoimmune thyroiditis but do not exclude cancer in a nodule.

items.stem: A 10-year-old boy has brief episodes (<1 minute) of staring, unresponsiveness and blinking. EEG shows 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave discharges. What is the first-line treatment?
items.why: This is typical absence epilepsy. Sodium valproate (or ethosuximide) is first line; note that valproate is avoided in females of childbearing potential.
notes: Carbamazepine can worsen absence seizures.
Phenytoin can worsen absence seizures and is not used for them.
Gabapentin is ineffective for absence seizures and may aggravate them.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman returned from Cuba 3 days ago. She has had fever, severe myalgia, arthralgia and headache since before her return. Now she has a generalised pruritic maculopapular rash with lower-limb petechiae. Platelets are 75 ×10⁹/L, Hct 0.36, WCC 4.1 ×10⁹/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Fever, severe myalgia/arthralgia, rash and petechiae with thrombocytopenia and leukopenia after Caribbean travel indicate dengue.
notes: Mononucleosis would show lymphocytosis, which is absent here.
Nothing in the picture suggests malaria, and Cuba is not a typical falciparum exposure.
Typhoid does not fit the clinical features and tropical exposure here.

items.stem: An 18-month-old fully immunised boy presents with right knee swelling after playing, with no obvious trauma. His mother's uncle had similar problems. Ultrasound shows haemarthrosis and the only abnormality on testing is a prolonged APTT of 52 seconds (normal 25–35). What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: A male toddler with spontaneous haemarthrosis, an isolated prolonged APTT and an affected maternal male relative suggests X-linked haemophilia A.
notes: It can prolong APTT but usually causes mucosal bleeding, and haemarthrosis is less typical.
This connective tissue disorder causes hypermobility and bruising, with normal coagulation tests.
This platelet disorder causes mucocutaneous bleeding with thrombocytopenia and normal APTT.

items.stem: A 13-month-old with 48 hours of fever and no focus is well. Catheter urine shows leukocytes, blood, nitrites and Gram-negative bacilli; CRP is 50 mg/L. He is managed as an outpatient with oral antibiotics. Which empirical oral antibiotic is LEAST appropriate?
items.why: The likely organism is E. coli, and many strains are resistant to amoxicillin alone, so it is unsuitable for empirical UTI treatment.
notes: Clavulanate overcomes many beta-lactamase-mediated resistances, so this is a reasonable choice for E. coli UTI.
Oral cephalosporins are good options for UTI caused by Gram-negative bacilli.
Active against most E. coli and a reasonable empirical option where local resistance is low.

items.stem: A 5-month-old in day care has had 3 days of watery stools (4/day), occasional vomiting, fever 38.3°C and coryza. He is partly breastfed, well hydrated and alert, with a 70 g weight loss. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Fast for 4 hours and rehydrate with oral rehydration solution
Introduce rice cereal for its astringent effect
Send a stool culture urgently to exclude a bacterial cause
Replace each stool's losses with oral rehydration solution and continue usual feeding
items.why: He is not dehydrated, so replace ongoing losses with oral rehydration solution after each stool and continue the usual diet, including breastfeeding. Fasting, dietary changes and routine stool culture are not needed.
notes: Fasting is not recommended; early continued feeding is advised.
Rice cereal has no proven benefit and is a common myth.
Stool culture is not routinely needed in mild, self-limiting viral-type gastroenteritis.

items.stem: A 3-year-old girl from Bangladesh has had 3 weeks of intermittent fever, weakness and anorexia. She has marked splenomegaly and pallor. Hb is 85 g/L, neutrophils 0.3 ×10⁹/L, platelets 54 ×10⁹/L, AST/ALT mildly raised, with polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Prolonged fever, massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia in a child from an endemic area are characteristic of visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar).
notes: Leukaemia is a differential, but polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia and endemic origin favour leishmaniasis.
Burkitt lymphoma usually presents with a rapidly growing mass, not hypergammaglobulinaemia with splenomegaly.
Miliary TB can cause cytopenias but does not typically cause massive splenomegaly with hypergammaglobulinaemia.

items.stem: A 15-month-old boy suddenly develops perioral flushing, urticaria on the trunk and limbs, and cough after a bite of omelette. He is conscious, with suprasternal retraction, watery rhinorrhoea, bilateral reduced air entry without wheeze and capillary refill under 2 seconds. What is the correct management?
options: Priority is to cannulate a vein
Intramuscular methylprednisolone is the treatment of choice
Advise the parents to take him to an emergency department
items.why: This is egg-induced anaphylaxis with respiratory involvement. IM adrenaline is the first-line treatment and must not be delayed; IV access, steroids and antihistamines come later.
notes: Adrenaline IM comes first; IV access is secondary and must not delay it.
Corticosteroids are adjuncts with slow onset and are not first-line.
Anaphylaxis is life-threatening; adrenaline must be given immediately, then transfer by ambulance.

items.stem: A 10-year-old boy has brief episodes (under 1 minute) of staring and blinking, during which he does not respond when called. EEG shows generalised 3 Hz spike-wave discharges. Which drug is an appropriate first-line treatment?
items.why: This is childhood absence epilepsy, shown by brief unresponsiveness with blinking and 3 Hz spike-wave on EEG. Ethosuximide and sodium valproate are the drugs of choice.
notes: Carbamazepine can worsen absence seizures, so it is not used for them.
Phenytoin is not effective for absence seizures and may aggravate them.
Clonazepam is not first line because of sedation and tolerance; it is only a later adjunct.

items.stem: A 77-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has had slowly progressive memory loss for 2 years (MMSE 28/30 then, 24/30 now), including confusion with insulin doses. MRI shows diffuse posterior-predominant cortical atrophy. He has no hallucinations, behavioural change, parkinsonism or focal signs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Insidious, slowly progressive short-term memory loss with posterior cortical atrophy and no focal signs, hallucinations or behavioural change is typical of Alzheimer's disease.
notes: Frontotemporal dementia presents with early behavioural or language change and frontotemporal atrophy.
Vascular dementia needs evidence of cerebrovascular disease on history, examination or imaging, which is absent.
Lewy body dementia features early visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition and parkinsonism, none of which are present.

items.stem: A teenager presents with progressive parkinsonism, tremor, dystonia and behavioural change. Which disease should always be excluded because appropriate treatment can improve neurological symptoms and halt progression?
items.why: Wilson's disease should be excluded in young patients with movement and neuropsychiatric disorders, as copper chelation or zinc can halt and improve the course.
notes: No treatment currently stops the progression of Huntington's disease.
Sydenham's chorea follows streptococcal infection in younger children and usually resolves spontaneously.
Treatment of juvenile Parkinson's disease is symptomatic and does not stop progression.

items.stem: An 87-year-old with chronic bronchitis and heart failure has acute calculous cholecystitis. After 4 days of fasting and IV piperacillin-tazobactam he still has fever, abdominal pain and leukocytosis. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Change antibiotics to ceftriaxone plus metronidazole.
Add gentamicin to the current treatment.
items.why: In a frail, high-risk patient who fails medical therapy, the gallbladder source should be drained percutaneously. Changing antibiotics will not control an undrained infected gallbladder.
notes: Operative risk is prohibitive given age and cardiorespiratory comorbidity.
Piperacillin-tazobactam already gives broad cover; the problem is source control.
Adding an aminoglycoside does not address the undrained source and adds nephrotoxicity risk.

items.stem: A 40-year-old smoker with no other history has had 24 hours of rigors, fever of 39°C and productive cough. Chest X-ray shows right upper lobe alveolar consolidation, and community-acquired pneumonia is diagnosed. Which is the most common causative organism, which empirical therapy must cover?
items.why: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia in adults and must always be covered by empirical treatment.
notes: Mycoplasma is a common atypical cause, especially in younger patients, but is less frequent overall.
Legionella is a less common cause, important in severe disease or particular exposures.
H. influenzae is less common, seen more often in COPD patients.

items.stem: A 75-year-old woman has long-standing leg and arm tingling and burning at rest, worse in the evening, relieved by movement and causing insomnia, consistent with restless legs syndrome. Which statement is FALSE?
options: Diagnosis is based on clinical criteria
Iron studies, thyroid function, B12 and folate should be checked
Treatment is for sleep or quality-of-life impairment and does not alter disease course
Diagnosis is confirmed by muscle biopsy
items.why: Restless legs syndrome is a clinical diagnosis; muscle biopsy has no role in confirming it. Blood tests look for secondary causes such as iron deficiency.
notes: This is true; diagnosis is clinical.
This is true; secondary causes such as iron deficiency should be excluded.
This is true; treatment is symptomatic.

items.stem: A patient has impaired comprehension of spoken and written language, cannot name objects or repeat words, and speaks fluently but incomprehensibly with semantic and phonemic paraphasias. Which aphasia is this?
items.why: Wernicke's aphasia causes fluent speech with paraphasias and impaired comprehension, naming and repetition.
notes: Global aphasia has non-fluent speech as well as impaired comprehension.
Broca's aphasia has non-fluent speech with preserved comprehension.
Transcortical aphasias have preserved repetition.

items.stem: A 43-year-old man presents with chronic diarrhoea and a history of three pneumonias in adulthood. Which immunological investigation is most appropriate?
options: Serum immunoglobulin levels and antibody response to vaccination
Neutrophil phagocytosis and oxidative burst testing
T-lymphocyte receptor repertoire and clonality studies
items.why: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections with diarrhoea suggest antibody deficiency (e.g. CVID). Measure serum immunoglobulins and the specific antibody response to vaccines.
notes: Neutrophil oxidative burst testing assesses chronic granulomatous disease, which causes abscesses and fungal or catalase-positive infections.
Lymphocyte apoptosis testing is for autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome, which does not fit this picture.
T-cell repertoire studies are for combined or T-cell immunodeficiency or lymphoproliferation, not recurrent bacterial pneumonia.

items.stem: A 49-year-old asymptomatic man has a father who died of prostate cancer. A routine check shows PSA 5.9 µg/L with free/total PSA ratio 11%, and DRE shows increased firmness of the right lobe. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Refer for prostate MRI and biopsy to assess for prostate cancer
Perform a CT of the abdomen and pelvis
Start a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor to halve the PSA
Start an LHRH analogue with an antiandrogen
items.why: Raised PSA, a low free/total ratio (<25%), an abnormal DRE and family history strongly suggest prostate cancer. Tissue diagnosis (usually after MRI, with biopsy) is required before any treatment or staging.
notes: CT does not diagnose prostate cancer; staging comes only after histological confirmation.
A 5-ARI would mask the PSA rise and delay diagnosis of possible cancer.
Androgen deprivation therapy is not given without a tissue diagnosis and staging.

items.stem: A woman at 40 weeks is in labour at 6 cm dilation with a decelerative CTG pattern. A fetal scalp blood sample gives pH 7.22. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Severe acidosis; proceed to urgent caesarean section.
Borderline result; repeat the scalp sample in 15–30 minutes.
Moderate acidosis; repeat the scalp sample in 1–2 hours.
Normal result; allow labour to continue without further sampling.
items.why: A fetal scalp pH of 7.20–7.25 is borderline (pre-pathological) and should be repeated within about 15–30 minutes. Below 7.20 is abnormal and needs delivery; above 7.25 is normal.
notes: Delivery is indicated for pH below 7.20, not 7.22.
Waiting 1–2 hours is too long with ongoing decelerations.
A pH of 7.22 is not in the normal range (above 7.25), so resampling is required.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman seeks preconception advice. After cervical excision for a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, she had three second-trimester losses (20–22 weeks), each with painless 8 cm dilatation and bulging membranes. What is the best advice for her next pregnancy?
options: Elective cervical cerclage at about 14 weeks
items.why: Recurrent painless second-trimester dilatation is cervical insufficiency, with prior cervical excision as a risk factor. A planned (history-indicated) cerclage in the late first or early second trimester is the treatment.
notes: Atosiban is given intravenously and is not used as oral prophylaxis; the problem is a structurally weak cervix, not contractions.
Corticosteroids aid fetal lung maturity only when delivery is imminent and do not prevent cervical dilatation.
Successful pregnancy is achievable with cerclage, so advising against pregnancy is not warranted.

items.stem: A 32-year-old man who injects drugs, recently released from prison, has a 10 mm Mantoux induration. His test was negative a year ago. He is asymptomatic, HIV negative, with a normal chest X-ray. What is the most appropriate management?
options: No treatment and annual chest X-ray
items.why: Recent tuberculin conversion with no active disease means latent TB infection in a high-risk person, so preventive therapy is indicated. Isoniazid for 6 months is a standard regimen.
notes: Recent conversion carries a high risk of progression, so observation alone is inappropriate.
Four-drug therapy is for active TB, which has been excluded clinically and radiologically.
Rifampicin plus pyrazinamide is hepatotoxic and not recommended for latent TB.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation has persistent allergic asthma, well controlled on daily inhaled budesonide and as-needed salbutamol. She is worried about teratogenicity. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Stop all asthma treatment, since asthma usually improves in pregnancy
Stop budesonide, as it increases malformation risk, and start oral montelukast
Continue current treatment and reassure her; good asthma control matters in pregnancy
Replace budesonide with omalizumab because it is safer in pregnancy
items.why: Inhaled corticosteroids and salbutamol are safe in pregnancy. Uncontrolled asthma poses greater risk to mother and fetus than the drugs, so current treatment should continue.
notes: Asthma control can worsen in pregnancy, and uncontrolled asthma harms mother and fetus. Stopping preventer therapy is unsafe.
Budesonide is not associated with increased malformations; it is the preferred inhaled steroid in pregnancy. Switching to montelukast gives no benefit.
Omalizumab is not a first-line change in a well-controlled patient, and biologics are not clearly safer than inhaled budesonide.
