items.stem: A 78-year-old woman has 24 hours of left iliac fossa pain, fever and vomiting, with focal tenderness, a sense of fullness, guarding and rebound. Acute diverticulitis is suspected. Which statement is correct?
options: Barium enema is the safest and best initial investigation.
A contained pelvic abscess is managed by CT- or ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage.
Laparoscopic surgery is contraindicated for elective resection after an acute episode.
Elective sigmoidectomy is indicated after a first episode of uncomplicated diverticulitis.
items.why: Contained diverticular abscesses (typically >3-4 cm) are managed with antibiotics plus CT- or ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage, avoiding emergency surgery.
notes: CT (or ultrasound) is the investigation of choice; contrast enema risks perforation in acute disease.
Laparoscopic elective resection is appropriate and commonly used.
Elective resection after a first uncomplicated episode is not routine; it is considered individually after recurrent episodes or persistent symptoms.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man had a truncal vagotomy and antrectomy with Billroth II reconstruction for peptic ulcer disease. Six weeks later, within 30 minutes of eating, he has nausea, sweating, dizziness, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Surgical conversion to an antiperistaltic Roux-en-Y gastrojejunostomy
items.why: This is early dumping syndrome after gastrectomy. First-line management is dietary: small frequent low-carbohydrate meals, separating fluids from solids. Octreotide and surgery are reserved for refractory cases.
notes: Octreotide is second-line, used when dietary measures fail.
Symptoms began after surgery and fit dumping; a carcinoid is not the likely cause.
Revisional surgery is a last resort after failure of dietary and medical therapy.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man has had a painful, swollen right knee with effusion for 24 hours, with fever 38°C. Bloods show neutrophilic leukocytosis and raised CRP. A diagnosis of acute monoarthritis is made. What is the most likely cause?
items.why: A young man with acute febrile monoarthritis and raised inflammatory markers most likely has bacterial septic arthritis. It must always be excluded first because of the risk of joint destruction.
notes: Crystal arthritis can look similar but is less likely in a 19-year-old; septic arthritis must still be excluded first.
Reactive arthritis can present like this but is less common than septic arthritis and is a diagnosis of exclusion.
Mycobacterial arthritis usually has a chronic, indolent course rather than a 24-hour onset.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man presents with dyspnoea and haemoptysis. Creatinine is 620 µmol/L and anti-GBM antibodies are strongly positive. Renal biopsy shows crescents in 75% of glomeruli and linear immunoglobulin deposition on immunofluorescence. Which statement is correct?
options: This is IgA nephropathy with acute kidney injury.
Glomerular injury is caused by circulating immune complexes.
items.why: This is anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome). Treatment is plasma exchange with corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide.
notes: IgA nephropathy shows mesangial IgA deposits, not linear IgG.
Membranous nephropathy shows granular subepithelial deposits, not crescents with linear staining.
Injury is from antibodies binding the GBM (type II hypersensitivity), not circulating immune complexes.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man has a left renal mass suggestive of renal cell carcinoma. Bloods show raised ALT, ALP and alpha-2-globulin and a prolonged PT. The liver is diffusely enlarged with no focal infiltrative lesions. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Hepatotoxic substances secreted by the tumour (paraneoplastic)
items.why: This is a paraneoplastic hepatic dysfunction (Stauffer syndrome) in renal cell carcinoma, with cholestasis, raised enzymes and prolonged PT but no infiltrative lesions.
notes: Metastases are excluded by the absence of focal infiltrative defects on imaging.
Tumour thrombus would present differently and more acutely.
Acute hepatitis does not fit the context of a renal tumour with this pattern.

items.stem: A healthy 30-year-old man has small palpable purpuric lesions over the shins. FBC, coagulation, creatinine and electrolytes are normal. Urine microscopy shows haematuria, which has been found before without a diagnosis. Regarding the likely underlying renal disease, which statement is FALSE?
options: Serum IgA is elevated in 20–50% of cases
Mesangial IgA deposits on renal biopsy are characteristic
Nephrotic-range proteinuria is the usual presentation
Most patients do not progress to renal failure
items.why: This is IgA nephropathy (with IgA vasculitis skin lesions). It typically presents with haematuria and a nephritic picture; nephrotic-range proteinuria is uncommon.
notes: True: serum IgA is raised in up to half of patients, though it is not diagnostic.
True: dominant mesangial IgA deposition is the defining biopsy finding.
True: roughly a quarter of patients progress to renal failure, so most do not.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and stage 5 chronic kidney disease has suspected pulmonary embolism. Which investigation carries the greatest risk of further renal injury and should generally be avoided?
items.why: CT pulmonary angiography needs intravenous iodinated contrast, which risks further kidney injury in severe renal impairment. The other tests need no contrast, and V/Q scanning is a suitable alternative.
notes: Echocardiography uses no contrast and is safe, and can show right ventricular strain.
V/Q scanning uses no nephrotoxic contrast and is a suitable alternative in renal failure.
An ECG is non-invasive, needs no contrast and is safe.

items.stem: A woman presents to the emergency department with 24 hours of fever without a focus and appears severely unwell. She had a splenectomy 2 years ago for staging of Hodgkin lymphoma. Which organism is most frequently responsible?
items.why: Asplenic patients are at risk of overwhelming sepsis from encapsulated organisms, and Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most frequent.
notes: Pseudomonas is not an encapsulated organism classically associated with post-splenectomy sepsis.
Non-typhoidal Salmonella is a lesser concern in asplenia, mainly in sickle cell disease.
Pneumocystis is an opportunistic infection of cellular immunodeficiency, not asplenia.

items.stem: A 20-year-old man has ataxia, headaches and a solid-cystic mass in the right cerebellar hemisphere. The resected lesion shows cells with long, thin cytoplasmic processes, fascicular and microcystic patterns, numerous vessels and Rosenthal fibres. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: A young patient with a cystic cerebellar mass and bipolar hair-like cell processes with Rosenthal fibres and microcysts is characteristic of pilocytic astrocytoma.
notes: Rosenthal fibres can occur here, but the hair-like cell morphology and cerebellar location point to pilocytic astrocytoma.
Central neurocytoma is an intraventricular tumour of small uniform round cells, not a cerebellar tumour with Rosenthal fibres.
Cerebellar liponeurocytoma shows neuronal cells with lipidised cells, not hair-like processes with Rosenthal fibres.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man who has sex with men, living with HIV (CD4 above 200 cells/microlitre), volunteers at an AIDS support centre. He had Td 6 years ago, MMR in childhood and adolescence, and hepatitis B vaccine 3 years ago, with no hepatitis A immunity. Which vaccines should be recommended?
options: Influenza, pneumococcal, quadrivalent meningococcal (ACWY) and hepatitis A
Influenza, Td, pneumococcal and quadrivalent meningococcal (ACWY)
items.why: Adults with HIV need annual influenza, pneumococcal and meningococcal ACWY vaccines, and hepatitis A is also indicated in men who have sex with men. Td and MMR are up to date, and hepatitis B was already given.
notes: Td was given only 6 years ago and is not yet due (booster at 10 years), and this option omits hepatitis A, which is indicated.
This list omits hepatitis A, which is indicated for a non-immune man who has sex with men.
Td is not yet due, and this option omits annual influenza and hepatitis A vaccination.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has had 6 months of exertional dyspnoea, without angina or syncope. Echo shows mean aortic gradient 55 mmHg, valve area 0.7 cm² and ejection fraction 65%. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Diuretics and more frequent specialist review
Percutaneous balloon aortic valvuloplasty if dyspnoea worsens
Surgical aortic valve replacement with a prosthetic valve
items.why: This is severe symptomatic aortic stenosis (area <1 cm², mean gradient >40 mmHg), which needs valve replacement. A young, fit patient is best managed with surgical replacement.
notes: Medical therapy and surveillance allow ventricular decline and reduce survival.
Balloon valvuloplasty is only a bridge or palliation in patients unfit for surgery.
TAVI is for patients at high surgical risk or older; this man is 52 and suited to surgery.

items.stem: An 82-year-old hypertensive woman takes atenolol, hydrochlorothiazide and digoxin. She presents with atrial fibrillation and is given intravenous verapamil. ECG then shows complete atrioventricular block. What is the most likely cause?
options: Digoxin toxicity from a pharmacokinetic interaction with verapamil
Additive pharmacodynamic effect of beta-blocker, digoxin and verapamil on the AV node
items.why: She is already on two AV nodal blocking drugs (atenolol, digoxin); adding verapamil, a third, produces an additive pharmacodynamic effect and complete AV block.
notes: Verapamil does raise digoxin levels, but the question points to the additive nodal blockade of three drugs.
Hypokalaemia promotes ectopy and digoxin toxicity but is not the most likely cause of AV block here.
Verapamil alone is less likely to cause complete block; the combination with other nodal blockers is the cause.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a childhood murmur presents with palpitations, fatigue, ankle oedema and mild hepatomegaly. SpO₂ is 97%. She has AF at 100 bpm, a 2/6 ejection systolic murmur at the pulmonary area, wide fixed splitting of S2, and RBBB. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: A childhood murmur with right heart overload (RBBB, hepatomegaly, oedema), AF from atrial dilatation and wide fixed split S2 indicates an atrial septal defect.
notes: A VSD does not cause atrial dilatation, and wide fixed splitting of S2 is not a feature.
Aortic stenosis is a left-sided lesion and does not produce right heart overload or fixed splitting.
Mitral stenosis can cause AF but not fixed splitting of S2 or RBBB from a congenital murmur.

items.stem: A patient with signs of right-sided heart failure has ascites out of proportion to peripheral oedema. Which underlying condition is most likely?
options: Dilated cardiomyopathy with marked left ventricular dysfunction
items.why: Constrictive pericarditis raises right-sided filling pressures, causing retrograde hepatic congestion with ascites often out of proportion to oedema. Left-sided lesions do not typically present this way.
notes: Aortic stenosis causes left-sided failure (dyspnoea, angina, syncope), not predominant ascites.
Dilated cardiomyopathy with LV dysfunction mainly produces left-sided congestion and pulmonary symptoms.
In pulmonary hypertension the tricuspid valve initially contains the pressure overload, so ascites out of proportion is less typical.

items.stem: A previously healthy 10-month-old has had one day of acute gastroenteritis with mild dehydration, no blood or mucus in the stool, and is vomiting but taking small sips. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Intravenous rehydration, fast for 8 hours, then a bland diet
Low-osmolality oral rehydration solution and continue usual diet or feeds
Oral rehydration solution, usual feeds and 10 days of oral amoxicillin
Oral rehydration solution, then change to lactose-free formula
items.why: Mild dehydration in gastroenteritis is managed with oral rehydration solution given in small frequent amounts, continuing breast milk or the usual diet.
notes: IV fluids are for severe dehydration or failed oral/enteral rehydration. Fasting and a bland diet are not recommended.
Most gastroenteritis is viral; antibiotics give no benefit and are not indicated without a specific bacterial indication.
Routine lactose-free formula is unnecessary; usual feeding should continue.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on sulfasalazine, prednisolone and etanercept presents with 72 hours of right facial herpes zoster involving the auricle, sparing the forehead, with conjunctival chemosis. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Outpatient oral aciclovir, valaciclovir or famciclovir
items.why: She is immunosuppressed and has possible ocular involvement, so there is a high risk of complications. Admission for intravenous antiviral therapy is indicated.
notes: Untreated zoster in an immunosuppressed patient with eye involvement risks serious complications and dissemination.
Topical antivirals are ineffective for zoster.
Oral therapy suits immunocompetent patients without complications; this patient is immunosuppressed with ocular signs.

items.stem: A 4-year-old boy with known cow's milk allergy accidentally ate yoghurt 5 minutes ago. He has facial angioedema, conjunctivitis, nasal congestion, hoarseness, mild hypotension, SpO2 93%, pallor, sweating and scattered wheeze. What is the first treatment of choice?
items.why: This is anaphylaxis, so give intramuscular adrenaline (1 mg/mL, 0.01 mg/kg) first. It acts fastest, whereas corticosteroids take hours to work.
notes: Subcutaneous absorption is slower and less reliable; adrenaline should be given intramuscularly.
Corticosteroids take hours to act and are not first line.
Salbutamol treats only the bronchospasm and does not treat the circulatory or airway compromise of anaphylaxis.

items.stem: A 1-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with 10 days of worsening jaundice. Total bilirubin is 120 µmol/L with an unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin of 26 µmol/L. What is the most likely cause?
items.why: Most of the bilirubin is conjugated, so this is cholestatic jaundice beyond 2 weeks of age. Biliary atresia is the key diagnosis and the main indication for paediatric liver transplantation.
notes: Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated, so it would not give a mainly conjugated rise.
ABO haemolysis causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, not mainly conjugated.
Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man has a pathological femoral fracture. Tests show Hb 95 g/L, total protein 110 g/L, albumin 20 g/L, beta-2 microglobulin 6 mg/L and creatinine 159 µmol/L. Which pair of tests is needed to confirm the most likely diagnosis?
options: Skeletal survey and bone marrow aspirate
Serum and urine electrophoresis and renal function tests
Bone marrow aspirate and serum and urine protein electrophoresis
items.why: This is multiple myeloma. Diagnosis needs clonal plasma cells from bone marrow and a monoclonal protein on serum and urine electrophoresis. Imaging and renal tests stage the disease and guide treatment after diagnosis.
notes: Bone marrow is needed, but a skeletal survey assesses disease extent rather than confirming the diagnosis; the monoclonal protein is still missing.
Electrophoresis finds the paraprotein, but there is no marrow sample to show clonal plasma cells; renal tests are for staging, not diagnosis.
Imaging stages disease and a fracture biopsy is not the standard route; the paraprotein and marrow plasma cell count are the key tests.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman taking clopidogrel presents with headache, fatigue and lower limb petechiae. Hb 82 g/L, MCV 100 fL, platelets 25 ×10⁹/L, raised reticulocytes, numerous schistocytes, normal APTT, PT and fibrinogen, LDH 2700 U/L, bilirubin 44 µmol/L. Most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Thrombocytopenia with microangiopathic haemolysis (schistocytes, high LDH and bilirubin, reticulocytosis), neurological symptoms and normal coagulation is TTP. Thienopyridines such as ticlopidine and clopidogrel are known triggers.
notes: ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia without anaemia or schistocytes.
Drug-induced thrombocytopenia would not explain the haemolysis, schistocytes and raised LDH.
DIC would show prolonged clotting times and low fibrinogen. Here coagulation is normal.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man is in ICU in a coma after a road traffic accident. He has not improved neurologically after several days. CT shows punctate haemorrhagic lesions in the corpus callosum and grey-white matter junction. What is the diagnosis?
items.why: Diffuse axonal injury causes early, sustained coma, often with a near-normal CT. When visible, there are punctate haemorrhages in the corpus callosum, grey-white junction and dorsolateral brainstem.
notes: A subdural would appear as a crescentic extra-axial collection, not punctate lesions.
Contusions are focal, larger cortical lesions (often frontal or temporal poles), not punctate callosal haemorrhages.
Hypoxic-ischaemic injury shows diffuse oedema and loss of grey-white differentiation, not punctate haemorrhages.

items.stem: An 80-year-old man with well-controlled hypertension and a year of cognitive decline presents with sudden aphasia and right hemiparesis. CT shows a left frontal lobar haematoma with no contrast enhancement. What is the most likely cause?
options: Arteriovenous malformation masked by acute haematoma
items.why: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is the commonest cause of spontaneous non-hypertensive lobar haemorrhage in older people, and is associated with cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease.
notes: AVMs typically present in young patients and would usually be seen on contrast imaging.
Hypertensive bleeds typically occur deep (putamen, thalamus, pons, cerebellum), not lobar, and his BP is well controlled.
A tumour is unlikely: no mass is seen, and enhancement would be expected.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man has fever, weight loss, exertional dyspnoea, a new aortic diastolic murmur and peripheral emboli. Echocardiography shows a 1 cm aortic vegetation, and blood cultures grow penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus bovis. Which investigation is most appropriate next?
items.why: Streptococcus bovis (gallolyticus) endocarditis is associated with colorectal neoplasia, so colonoscopy should be performed.
notes: Glucose tolerance testing has no link to S. bovis endocarditis.
A chest X-ray does not address the known association with colonic lesions.
Upper endoscopy is not the source to investigate; the association is with colonic neoplasia.

items.stem: A 76-year-old man has 8 months of cognitive decline, slowness and clumsy movements. His family report visual hallucinations. Low-dose risperidone was started and his motor state worsened markedly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Dementia with Lewy bodies features cognitive decline, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and severe sensitivity to antipsychotics, even at low doses.
notes: Alzheimer's disease typically presents with early memory loss, and early hallucinations and parkinsonism are not typical.
Frontotemporal dementia presents with behavioural or language change, and visual hallucinations are not typical.
Vascular dementia has a stepwise course with focal deficits, and does not explain antipsychotic sensitivity.

items.stem: A 29-year-old obese woman has had a month of severe bilateral pulsating headache, horizontal diplopia and brief episodes of monocular visual loss. Examination is normal apart from bilateral papilloedema. Which test confirms the likely diagnosis?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
items.why: This is idiopathic intracranial hypertension (obese young woman, papilloedema, VI nerve palsy diplopia). Once a mass is excluded, lumbar puncture shows raised opening pressure with normal CSF and confirms it.
notes: Carotid ultrasound assesses extracranial vessels and does not diagnose raised intracranial pressure.
MRI is used to exclude a mass or venous thrombosis but cannot confirm raised CSF pressure.
EEG assesses seizure activity and has no role in diagnosing intracranial hypertension.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man with chronic bronchitis is admitted with pneumonia and Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteraemia, penicillin-susceptible (MIC 0.0125 mg/L). He is given benzylpenicillin 2 million units 4-hourly but is still febrile (38°C) on day 5. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Change to ceftriaxone for greater efficacy
Continue the same treatment, as this is simply a matter of time
items.why: The organism is fully susceptible and the dose adequate, so persistent fever suggests the antibiotic is not reaching the focus, most likely a pleural empyema, which needs to be excluded and drained.
notes: Ceftriaxone offers no advantage against a fully penicillin-susceptible pneumococcus; the problem is the focus, not the drug.
Pneumococcus does not produce beta-lactamase, so clavulanic acid adds nothing.
With a susceptible organism and adequate dosing, persistent fever is not just a timing issue and suggests a complication such as empyema.

items.stem: A 20-year-old woman presents with fever, cervical lymphadenopathy and a rash. Three weeks ago she had sexual exposure with a risk of HIV transmission. Which statement is correct?
options: A negative HIV antibody screening immunoassay excludes HIV infection
This presentation is not consistent with acute HIV infection
A positive screening immunoassay alone is enough to diagnose HIV infection
If the screening immunoassay is negative, HIV RNA PCR can still detect infection
items.why: At 3 weeks she may be in the window period, when antibody-based tests can be negative despite acute infection. HIV RNA PCR can detect the virus in this setting.
notes: Serology can be negative in the window period, and no test excludes disease with certainty.
A mononucleosis-like illness is a classic presentation of acute (seroconversion) HIV infection.
A reactive screening test requires confirmatory testing before diagnosis.

items.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy for leukaemia is admitted with pneumonia and started on cefepime. Chest imaging shows a peripheral infiltrate with a halo sign and crescentic meniscus (air-crescent). Pending biopsy results, which antimicrobial should be added?
items.why: Halo sign and air-crescent in a neutropenic chemotherapy patient suggest invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, treated with voriconazole.
notes: Ganciclovir treats CMV, which does not cause this radiological picture.
Caspofungin is not first-line for invasive aspergillosis; it is used as salvage or in combination.
Aspergillus is resistant to fluconazole, so it is not a valid option.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes returns from overseas travel with 40°C fever, rigors, arthromyalgia and headache. Three days later he develops a maculopapular rash with lower limb petechiae, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia (91 ×10⁹/L) and markedly raised transaminases. Malaria testing is negative. Most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Fever, arthromyalgia, rash with petechiae, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and raised transaminases after travel, with malaria excluded, are classic for dengue. Thrombocytopenia and petechiae reflect capillary fragility.
notes: Coronavirus infection typically causes respiratory symptoms and does not produce this thrombocytopenic, hepatitic picture.
Lymphocytic choriomeningitis mainly causes meningitis or flu-like illness after rodent exposure, not a petechial rash with marked transaminitis.
Chikungunya causes fever and severe arthralgia, but marked thrombocytopenia, petechiae and raised transaminases favour dengue.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man who has sex with men presents with fever and malaise. Two months ago he had a painless penile ulcer with bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy that resolved spontaneously. HIV is negative, RPR titre is 1:320 and TPHA titre is 1:128. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 24 MU daily for 14 days
Benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 MU intramuscularly weekly for 3 weeks
Ceftriaxone 2 g intramuscularly as a single dose
Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g (2.4 MU) intramuscularly as a single dose
items.why: This is early (secondary) syphilis, with a prior chancre and high-titre positive nontreponemal and treponemal tests. Treatment is a single intramuscular dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g (2.4 MU).
notes: Intravenous benzylpenicillin for 14 days is used for neurosyphilis, ocular or otic syphilis, not early syphilis without neurological features.
Three weekly doses are for late latent syphilis or syphilis of unknown duration, not early syphilis of less than 2 years.
Ceftriaxone is not first-line for syphilis and is the treatment for gonorrhoea.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with fever of 38°C and right flank pain. Her white cell count is 25 × 10^9/L with a left shift, and abdominal ultrasound shows a staghorn calculus. Which organism is most likely to be isolated?
items.why: Staghorn (struvite) calculi are associated with urease-producing bacteria, most commonly Proteus, also Pseudomonas, Klebsiella and some staphylococci. Urease splits urea, raising urinary pH.
notes: E. coli does not produce urease, so it is not the typical organism in struvite stones.
Enterococcus faecalis is not a urease-splitting organism and is not classically linked to staghorn calculi.
Candida can cause urinary infection but is not urease-producing and is not linked to struvite stones.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man, whose child has coeliac disease, has iron-deficiency anaemia and a recent increase in stool frequency. HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 are both negative. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
items.why: Iron-deficiency anaemia with a change in bowel habit in a middle-aged man needs colonoscopy to exclude colorectal cancer. Negative HLA-DQ2/DQ8 makes coeliac disease very unlikely.
notes: Negative HLA-DQ2/DQ8 has a high negative predictive value, so serology is low yield.
Coeliac disease is very unlikely with negative HLA typing, so duodenal biopsy is not the priority.
A gluten-free diet trial is not indicated when coeliac disease is unlikely and cancer has not been excluded.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman drinking 60 g alcohol/day (more in the last month) has fever 38.5°C, jaundice, painful hepatomegaly, disorientation and asterixis, without ascites or peritonism. WBC 15×10⁹/L (90% neutrophils), Hb 100 g/L, MCV 115 fL, direct bilirubin 257 µmol/L, AST 300, ALT 120, GGT 635 U/L, prolonged PT. Most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Heavy alcohol use with fever, jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, macrocytosis, neutrophilia and AST:ALT >2 with AST under 5× normal indicates acute alcoholic hepatitis.
notes: Cholecystitis presents with right upper quadrant pain and Murphy's sign, not encephalopathy and coagulopathy.
Cholangitis (Charcot's triad) is possible, but the alcohol history, macrocytosis, AST>ALT and encephalopathy favour alcoholic hepatitis.
Pancreatitis gives epigastric pain radiating to the back with raised lipase, not hepatic failure features.

items.stem: A young patient has recurrent dysphagia to solids and liquids with repeated food bolus impactions but no heartburn. Endoscopy shows multiple concentric oesophageal rings with otherwise normal mucosa (trachealised oesophagus). What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Concentric rings (trachealised or feline oesophagus) with dysphagia and recurrent food impaction in a young patient are typical of eosinophilic oesophagitis. Biopsy confirms it.
notes: Candida causes white plaques on the mucosa, usually with odynophagia and immunosuppression, not fixed rings.
CMV oesophagitis causes discrete ulcers in immunosuppressed patients, with odynophagia rather than rings.
Adenocarcinoma is uncommon in the young and presents as a mass or stricture, usually with long-standing reflux (Barrett oesophagus).

items.stem: A 37-year-old woman with extensive ulcerative colitis has a severe flare. She has had no improvement after one week of intravenous corticosteroids (prednisolone-equivalent 1 mg/kg). What is the next step?
options: Emergency subtotal colectomy, later completion proctectomy and ileoanal pouch
Add oral mesalazine 4 g daily and rectal corticosteroid
items.why: Severe UC not responding to full-dose IV corticosteroids needs rescue therapy with ciclosporin or infliximab. Surgery is reserved for failure of rescue therapy or complications.
notes: Colectomy is for rescue failure, toxic megacolon or perforation, not the first step.
Azathioprine acts too slowly to rescue an acute severe flare.
Mesalazine and topical steroids are inadequate for a steroid-refractory severe flare.

items.stem: A healthy 17-year-old athletic boy has occasional scleral icterus. He takes no drugs and has no abdominal pain. ALT, AST, GGT and ALP are normal; total bilirubin is 55 µmol/L, conjugated 7 µmol/L. No anaemia; liver ultrasound is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Mild, intermittent unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (usually under 85 µmol/L) with normal liver enzymes and no haemolysis in a young healthy person is Gilbert syndrome, often unmasked by stress or fasting.
notes: Rotor syndrome causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, not an unconjugated rise.
Dubin-Johnson syndrome causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, not an unconjugated rise.
Acute hepatitis would show clearly raised transaminases.

items.stem: A 65-year-old woman on NSAIDs for joint pain has iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 110 g/L, MCV 69 fL, ferritin 18 µg/L). Coeliac serology is negative. Gastroscopy (3 cm hiatus hernia), colonoscopy to the caecum, small bowel transit and abdominal ultrasound are unremarkable. Which investigation is most appropriate next?
items.why: Iron deficiency anaemia needs a GI source excluded. With normal gastroscopy and colonoscopy and negative coeliac serology, the small bowel (jejunum and ileum) remains unexamined, so capsule endoscopy is next.
notes: Coeliac disease has already been made unlikely by negative serology, and a biopsy would not examine the ileum.
Angiography is invasive and reserved for active bleeding, not for occult blood loss with an unexplored small bowel.
Radioisotope scans are low-yield here and are not the standard way to survey the small bowel in occult bleeding.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has incidental mild hypercalcaemia (calcium 2.75 mmol/L) with an inappropriately normal PTH (4.8 pmol/L). Her mother and paternal grandfather had parathyroid surgery but stayed hypercalcaemic. Which test best confirms the diagnosis?
items.why: This is familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (autosomal dominant, calcium-sensing receptor mutation), confirmed by a low urine calcium/creatinine ratio. It is benign and not cured by parathyroidectomy.
notes: Vitamin D status does not distinguish FHH from primary hyperparathyroidism.
Phosphate handling is altered in primary hyperparathyroidism but is not diagnostic of FHH.
PTHrP is for malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia, where PTH is suppressed, and does not fit this family history.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man with 10 years of type 2 diabetes takes metformin and sitagliptin and follows diet advice. Over 6 months he has lost weight and become fatigued. HbA1c has risen from 54 to 69 mmol/mol, with fasting glucose now 9.4–11.1 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Increase dietary protein and complex carbohydrate intake
items.why: Poor control on dual therapy with weight loss and fatigue suggests relative insulin deficiency. Adding basal insulin relieves symptoms and lowers HbA1c towards target.
notes: Dietary changes alone will not correct this degree of deterioration, and weight loss reflects insulin deficiency.
Swapping to pioglitazone is unlikely to achieve enough glucose lowering and can cause weight gain and fluid retention.
Removing metformin and substituting a sulfonylurea is a step backward; the patient needs intensification, not substitution.

items.stem: An immunocompromised patient with pneumonia has a halo sign and then an air-crescent (meniscus) sign on chest CT. Which organism is the most likely cause?
items.why: The CT halo sign and air-crescent sign are characteristic of invasive pulmonary aspergillosis in immunocompromised patients. They are not pathognomonic; TB, some neoplasms and granulomatosis with polyangiitis can also cause them.
notes: S. aureus pneumonia causes consolidation, cavitation or pneumatoceles, not the classic halo sign.
Candida rarely causes pneumonia and is not classically linked to the halo sign.
Pseudomonas causes necrotising pneumonia, mostly in hospitalised patients, but not the classic halo or air-crescent sign.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman had a 2 cm pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour in the tail removed by partial pancreatectomy. She has amenorrhoea for 6 months and recurrent renal colic since age 20 needing lithotripsy, and a family history of renal colic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, probable prolactinoma (amenorrhoea) and hyperparathyroidism (recurrent renal stones) form the MEN 1 triad of pituitary, parathyroid and pancreatic tumours.
notes: MEN 2A involves medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism, not pancreatic tumours or pituitary disease.
MEN 2B involves medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas and marfanoid habitus.
A single somatostatinoma would not explain the amenorrhoea, recurrent stones and family history.

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman presents with severe headache, meningism, bilateral visual disturbance and ophthalmoplegia. CT shows a 2 cm sellar mass with haemorrhage, a deviated pituitary stalk and compressed gland. Which statement about her management is INCORRECT?
options: The likely diagnosis is pituitary apoplexy
High-dose corticosteroids with observation only may avoid surgery
Glucocorticoids should be given to prevent life-threatening adrenal insufficiency
Ophthalmoplegia and visual defects mean urgent surgery is never indicated
items.why: Visual deficits or ophthalmoplegia with reduced consciousness or instability are indications for early surgical decompression. Conservative management is considered only for milder cases.
notes: This is a correct statement; the picture is classic for pituitary apoplexy.
This is a reasonable statement; conservative management with steroids is an option in selected stable patients without severe deficits.
This is correct; glucocorticoid replacement is essential because of acute secondary adrenal insufficiency.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman with hypertension and heart failure has a persistent dry cough that starts as an itchy tickle in the throat. Which of her medicines is the most likely cause?
items.why: A persistent dry, irritating cough is a typical ACE inhibitor adverse effect, caused by bradykinin accumulation. Hyperkalaemia is another.
notes: Thiazides cause hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia and hyperuricaemia, not cough.
Beta blockers can cause bradycardia, fatigue and bronchospasm, but not a dry tickly cough.
Loop diuretics cause volume depletion, hypokalaemia and ototoxicity, not cough.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman is found collapsed in the street with SpO2 88% on room air and pinpoint pupils. ABG: pH 7.25, PaCO2 8.0 kPa, PaO2 7.7 kPa, HCO3 26 mmol/L, base excess −1. Na 137, Cl 100 mmol/L. What is the acid–base disturbance?
options: Venous sample; arterial interpretation is not possible
items.why: Low pH with raised PaCO2 and normal bicarbonate indicates acute, uncompensated respiratory acidosis. With pinpoint pupils, the likely cause is hypoventilation from opioid intoxication.
notes: Type 1 failure has hypoxaemia with normal or low PaCO2. Here PaCO2 is raised.
Bicarbonate and base excess are normal and the anion gap is normal (137 − 100 − 26 = 11), so there is no metabolic component.
The PaO2 of 7.7 kPa and the picture are consistent with an arterial sample, and nothing suggests it is venous.

items.stem: A 65-year-old man receiving chemotherapy for pancreatic cancer is suspected of having a deep vein thrombosis of the leg. Which investigation is the most appropriate and cost-effective to confirm the diagnosis?
items.why: Venous duplex ultrasound is accurate, non-invasive and cheap, and allows follow-up. D-dimer is unhelpful in cancer patients as it is often raised.
notes: D-dimer is commonly raised in malignancy, so it has low specificity and is unhelpful here.
MRI is costly and not first line for suspected DVT.
Venography is invasive and carries contrast risk; it is rarely used now.

items.stem: A patient with cirrhosis and ascites develops a pleural effusion. Pleural fluid LDH is 45 U/L (serum 220), pleural/serum protein ratio 0.3 and pleural/serum LDH ratio 0.2. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Extend fluid analysis with cell count, glucose, pH, ADA, cholesterol and culture
Continue treatment of the liver disease
items.why: The fluid meets transudate criteria by Light's criteria, consistent with hepatic hydrothorax from decompensated cirrhosis, so no further pleural work-up is needed; treat the liver disease.
notes: Extended testing is for exudates; this is a transudate.
Thoracoscopy is not indicated for a clear transudate.
Nothing suggests infection; parapneumonic effusions are exudates.

items.stem: A 50-year-old has a pleural effusion: straw-coloured, pH 7.3, pleural/serum protein 0.8, pleural/serum LDH 0.9, Gram and Ziehl-Neelsen stains negative, normal lipids, mesothelial cells <5%, marked lymphocytosis without atypia, ADA 64 U/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: This is a lymphocytic exudate with high ADA and no malignant cells, which points to tuberculous pleurisy. The main alternative for a lymphocytic exudate is malignancy.
notes: Empyema would show purulent fluid with neutrophils, low pH and often positive Gram stain.
Mesothelioma would typically show atypical or malignant cells on cytology, and ADA would not be markedly raised.
Infarction gives a bloody or exudative effusion that is not lymphocyte-predominant with high ADA.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with asthma has a severe exacerbation. After an hour of oxygen and two nebulised salbutamol doses he is no better: RR 42/min, accessory muscle use, diffuse wheeze, PEF 220 (from 310) L/min. On 28% O2, PaO2 is 7.2 kPa and PaCO2 4.7 kPa. Which is LEAST indicated?
options: Nebulised ipratropium with salbutamol every 20 minutes
items.why: In severe asthma with hypoxaemia but a normal PaCO2, escalate oxygen, bronchodilators, steroids and magnesium first. NIV is not a routine step and invasive support is reserved for deterioration with hypercapnia or acidosis.
notes: Hypoxaemia persists on 28% oxygen, so increasing oxygen is indicated.
Combined ipratropium and salbutamol every 20 minutes is standard for severe asthma not responding to initial treatment.
IV magnesium is an accepted adjunct in severe or life-threatening asthma not responding to initial bronchodilators.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man is admitted with severe pneumonia and improves on antibiotics. On day 4 of his admission he develops severe diarrhoea. What is the most likely causative organism?
options: The pneumonia-causing bacterium, now antibiotic resistant
items.why: Severe diarrhoea developing in hospital during or after antibiotic therapy is most commonly due to Clostridioides difficile infection.
notes: Salmonella is community-acquired from food and does not typically arise after antibiotics in hospital.
Resistance emerging within days and causing diarrhoea is implausible.
Campylobacter is a community-acquired foodborne cause, not a typical hospital antibiotic-associated one.

items.stem: A young man presents with a flame burn covering 10% of his body surface area, circumferential around the right arm. There is no Doppler arterial signal in the hand. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Occlusive silver sulfadiazine dressings and review of burn depth at one week
Lymphatic drainage and assessment for vascular bypass
items.why: A circumferential burn with loss of distal pulses indicates compartment-like compression from the rigid eschar and oedema. Emergency escharotomy relieves pressure and saves the limb.
notes: Topical dressings suit a small burn, but they ignore the limb-threatening circumferential constriction.
Bypass and lymphatic drainage don't address the constricting eschar causing the ischaemia.
Amputation is not indicated when decompression can restore perfusion.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man has had extensive ulcerative colitis for 15 years, in clinical remission for 3 years. He asks about colorectal cancer risk and prevention. Which advice is correct?
options: Risk is increased only if he smokes
Remission means population screening is adequate
Periodic surveillance colonoscopy with biopsies or chromoendoscopy is appropriate
Faecal occult blood testing at higher frequency than the general population is appropriate
items.why: Extensive colitis for over 8–10 years raises colorectal cancer risk regardless of remission or smoking. Surveillance colonoscopy at intervals set by risk, with targeted biopsies (chromoendoscopy) or random biopsies, is recommended.
notes: Colitis itself raises cancer risk whether or not the patient smokes.
Risk persists despite remission; population screening is insufficient.
FOBT is not adequate for surveillance in colitis, as dysplasia is often flat and may be missed.

items.stem: An 18-year-old man with asthma and allergies to pollen, dust mites and cats presents with food sticking retrosternally and inability to swallow saliva. Similar episodes have resolved spontaneously. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Intermittent dysphagia with food impaction in a young man with marked atopy suggests eosinophilic oesophagitis.
notes: Barrett oesophagus occurs with chronic reflux in older patients; any stricture would cause progressive dysphagia.
A Schatzki ring is possible, but the strong atopic history favours eosinophilic oesophagitis.
Infectious oesophagitis is typical in immunocompromised patients and causes odynophagia.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has two weeks of progressive abdominal distension and malaise, with shifting dullness and no oedema. Diagnostic paracentesis shows 2,300 cells/µL, 60% polymorphs. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
items.why: Ascitic polymorphs above 250/µL (here about 1,380/µL) define spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Start a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime) promptly, with albumin.
notes: Ascites measures can wait; infection must be treated first.
Diuretics can wait until the infection is treated and are not the immediate priority.
There is no tense ascites to justify urgent drainage.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a colonoscopy after a positive screening test. A 2 cm pedunculated sigmoid polyp is removed by diathermy snare. Histology shows carcinoma in situ (high-grade dysplasia) confined to the polyp head. CT chest/abdomen is normal. What is the correct management?
options: Local excision of the polyp base
items.why: Carcinoma in situ does not breach the basement membrane, so it has no metastatic potential. Complete polypectomy is curative and only endoscopic surveillance follows.
notes: Surgery is unnecessary for non-invasive disease that has been completely removed.
The polyp has already been removed by snare; further local excision of the base adds nothing.
Lymphadenectomy is for invasive cancer with adverse features, not in situ disease.

items.stem: A 20-year-old woman has a 15 cm solid-cystic ovarian tumour found on ultrasound. Histology shows teeth, hair, intestinal, bronchial and squamous epithelium (15%), plus neuroectodermal and embryonic elements. What is the correct diagnosis?
items.why: Embryonic and neuroectodermal (immature) elements within a solid-cystic teratoma indicate an immature teratoma, which occurs in young women. A mature cystic teratoma contains only fully differentiated tissues.
notes: Teratocarcinoma is an outdated term implying overt malignant epithelial elements; no atypia is described here.
A mature cystic teratoma (dermoid) has only well-differentiated tissues; embryonic elements exclude it.
Dysgerminoma is a uniform tumour of germ cells resembling seminoma, without teeth, hair or varied tissue types.

items.stem: A 59-year-old woman has 4 months of chronic watery diarrhoea. Colonoscopy shows normal mucosa with no ulcers. Transverse colon biopsy shows a thickened subepithelial band (highlighted by Masson's trichrome), epithelial damage and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. What is the diagnosis?
items.why: A thickened subepithelial collagen band (shown by Masson's trichrome) with increased intraepithelial lymphocytes in a macroscopically normal colon is diagnostic of collagenous colitis. It is a cause of chronic watery diarrhoea.
notes: Ulcerative colitis causes crypt architectural distortion and visible mucosal inflammation or friability, not a subepithelial collagen band.
Pseudomembranous colitis shows adherent pseudomembranes with volcano-like exudate, usually after antibiotics.
Crohn's disease shows transmural inflammation and architectural crypt changes, often with granulomas, not an isolated collagen band.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man has a pre-employment chest X-ray showing a bilateral reticular interstitial pattern with bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. BAL: lymphocytes 50%, macrophages 40%, eosinophils 2%, neutrophils 8%, CD4/CD8 ratio 5. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Bilateral hilar and mediastinal adenopathy with interstitial infiltrates in a young adult, plus lymphocytic BAL with a raised CD4/CD8 ratio (>3.5), indicates sarcoidosis.
notes: Extrinsic allergic alveolitis also gives BAL lymphocytosis, but with a low CD4/CD8 ratio and usually no hilar adenopathy.
Pneumoconiosis needs an occupational exposure and does not typically give a lymphocytic BAL with a high CD4/CD8 ratio.
Carcinomatous lymphangitis occurs with known malignancy and does not give a lymphocytic BAL with a high CD4/CD8 ratio.

items.stem: A 59-year-old woman has 4 months of chronic watery diarrhoea. Colonoscopy is macroscopically normal. Transverse colon biopsy shows a subepithelial band thickening highlighted by Masson's trichrome, surface epithelial damage and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. What is the diagnosis?
items.why: Collagenous colitis shows a subepithelial collagen band (trichrome-positive) with surface epithelial damage, increased intraepithelial lymphocytes and a lamina propria chronic infiltrate, despite normal-looking mucosa.
notes: Ulcerative colitis would show visible mucosal inflammation and ulceration with crypt distortion and abscesses, not a normal mucosa.
Pseudomembranous colitis shows endoscopic pseudomembranes and a 'volcano' exudate, usually after antibiotics (C. difficile).
Crohn's disease shows transmural inflammation, granulomas and skip lesions; a subepithelial collagen band is not a feature.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman has 2 hours of oppressive chest pain. BP 68/32 mmHg, HR 124/min, RR 32/min, SpO2 91% on 50% oxygen, bilateral crackles. ECG shows anterior ST elevation with inferior reciprocal change; CXR shows bilateral alveolar infiltrates. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Arrange urgent coronary angiography and percutaneous coronary intervention
items.why: Anterior STEMI with hypotension and pulmonary oedema is cardiogenic shock. Urgent coronary angiography with PCI (primary reperfusion) is the treatment of choice, as it improves survival.
notes: Nitrates are contraindicated in hypotension and cardiogenic shock; they would worsen perfusion.
Fibrinolysis is less effective in cardiogenic shock; mechanical reperfusion is preferred when PCI is available.
Diuretic alone will not treat the cause and may worsen hypotension; reperfusion is the priority.

items.stem: A 73-year-old woman has progressive dyspnoea now at rest, orthopnoea and 4 kg weight gain. BP 150/84 mmHg, HR 100/min, raised JVP, bibasal crepitations and ankle oedema. She takes enalapril 5 mg twice daily and furosemide 80 mg daily. What is the most appropriate treatment now?
options: Uptitrate enalapril as tolerated and give intravenous furosemide
items.why: She has decompensated heart failure with hypertension. Give intravenous diuretic for congestion and uptitrate the ACE inhibitor as tolerated, which also helps control her blood pressure.
notes: This treats congestion but leaves the suboptimal ACE inhibitor dose and the raised blood pressure unaddressed.
Beta-blockers should not be started during acute congestion; they are introduced once the patient is stable and euvolaemic.
Amlodipine has no benefit in heart failure; neurohormonal blockade is preferred for blood pressure control.

items.stem: A 76-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes has had 72 hours of palpitations and reduced exercise tolerance. The ED ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of about 120 bpm. Which of the following statements is FALSE?
options: He should be anticoagulated orally long term unless contraindicated
Cardioversion in the ED would require a prior transoesophageal echocardiogram
As this is a first episode, he is the ideal candidate for catheter ablation
Beta-blockers may be used to control the heart rate
items.why: A first episode of AF in an older patient with comorbidities is not an ideal indication for catheter ablation, which is usually considered for symptomatic AF refractory to drug therapy.
notes: True: his CHA2DS2-VASc score is high, so long-term anticoagulation is indicated.
True: onset is over 48 hours or unknown, so thrombus must be excluded before cardioversion.
True: beta-blockers are a standard rate-control option.

items.stem: A man had an antrectomy with Billroth II gastrojejunostomy for gastric ulcer 20 years ago. He now has postprandial abdominal pain, distension, diarrhoea, and fat and vitamin B12 malabsorption. What is the most likely complication?
options: Afferent loop syndrome with bacterial overgrowth
items.why: Partial obstruction of the afferent loop leads to stasis and bacterial overgrowth, causing postprandial pain, steatorrhoea and vitamin B12 malabsorption.
notes: Bile reflux gastropathy is an endoscopic diagnosis and does not cause diarrhoea or malabsorption.
Cancer would more likely present with weight loss and systemic or metastatic features.
Dumping causes vasomotor symptoms such as palpitations and flushing, which are absent here.

items.stem: A 58-year-old gardener has a 3-week history of mildly painful, progressive nodular lesions up his left arm, starting on the thumb, with linear erythematous streaks joining them. He is afebrile and recalls no injury. Skin biopsy culture is diagnostic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: A sporotrichoid (lymphocutaneous) pattern after gardening, often with unnoticed trauma from plants or soil, indicates sporotrichosis from Sporothrix. M. marinum requires aquarium or water exposure.
notes: Dermatophytes cause scaly annular lesions, not ascending nodular lymphangitic spread.
Staphylococcal infection is usually acute, with pus and systemic features, not a subacute nodular chain.
M. marinum also gives a sporotrichoid pattern but follows aquarium or fish/water exposure, not gardening.

items.stem: An 8-year-old child has had superficial pustules, erosions and honey-coloured crusts around the mouth for 3 days. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Perioral pustules, erosions and honey-coloured crusts in a child are classic for impetigo, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.
notes: Erythema multiforme causes target lesions, not crusted perioral pustules.
Acne occurs with comedones and inflammatory papules, not honey-coloured crusts in an 8-year-old.
Pustular psoriasis is rare in children and gives sterile pustules on erythematous skin, not honey crusts.

items.stem: A man presents with malaise and psoriasiform skin lesions on the trunk, palms and soles. He also has asymmetric non-suppurative arthritis, bilateral red eyes and erosions on the glans penis. He reports a high-risk sexual contact 20 days ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Keratoderma of the palms and soles, asymmetric arthritis, conjunctivitis and balanitis after a probable chlamydial urethritis are classic for reactive arthritis (formerly Reiter syndrome).
notes: HIV may coexist but does not explain this classic combination of features.
Syphilis can involve palms and soles, but the arthritis, conjunctivitis and balanitis together point to reactive arthritis.
Erythema multiforme causes target lesions and mucosal erosions, not keratoderma with arthritis and conjunctivitis.

items.stem: A patient presents to the emergency department with erythroderma, fever and malaise. Examination shows nail pitting and distal yellowish 'oil-drop' discolouration. Which underlying disease is most likely?
items.why: Any of these can cause erythroderma, but nail pitting and oil-drop discolouration are highly suggestive of psoriasis, making it the most likely cause.
notes: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma can cause erythroderma but does not typically produce pitting and oil-drop nail changes.
Atopic dermatitis can cause erythroderma but is not characterised by oil-drop nail changes.
Ichthyosis can cause erythroderma but is not associated with these nail findings.

items.stem: A 3-year-old girl has had surgery for tetralogy of Fallot. She had thymic dysfunction and hypocalcaemia as a neonate, and now has a nasal voice and psychomotor delay. Which genetic test is most appropriate to establish the aetiological diagnosis?
items.why: Conotruncal heart disease, thymic hypoplasia, hypocalcaemia from parathyroid hypoplasia and palatal anomalies (nasal voice) point to 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge) syndrome.
notes: Fragile X causes intellectual disability and a characteristic face, not thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia with conotruncal defects.
Noonan syndrome involves short stature and cardiac disease (usually pulmonary stenosis), mostly from PTPN11 variants, and not thymic or parathyroid hypoplasia.
Williams syndrome features supravalvular aortic stenosis and hypercalcaemia, not hypocalcaemia and thymic dysfunction.

items.stem: A 5-year-old child from Nigeria has a normal examination. Hepatitis B serology: HBsAg positive, anti-HBs negative, HBeAg negative, anti-HBe positive, anti-HBc IgM negative, anti-HBc IgG positive, HBV DNA positive. What is the clinical situation?
items.why: Persistent HBsAg with anti-HBc IgG (no IgM) and detectable HBV DNA indicates chronic infection with ongoing viral replication. Anti-HBe positivity does not exclude it.
notes: Acute infection would have anti-HBc IgM positive and usually HBeAg positive with anti-HBe negative.
Vaccination produces only anti-HBs. HBsAg, anti-HBc and HBV DNA would all be negative.
An inactive carrier is HBsAg positive but has undetectable or very low HBV DNA. Here DNA is positive.

items.stem: A 47-year-old smoker who injects drugs has had 2 weeks of fever, malaise and dry cough, then sudden pleuritic chest pain and severe dyspnoea. He has tracheal deviation, absent left breath sounds, SpO2 81%, BP 75/47 mm Hg. HIV is positive, CD4 176 cells/µL. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
items.why: Subacute fever and dry cough with CD4 below 200 suggests PJP. Pneumatoceles form in about 10% and can rupture into the pleura, causing tension pneumothorax.
notes: A bulla rupture explains the abrupt pneumothorax but not the preceding 2 weeks of fever and cough.
Bacterial pneumonia does not explain the pneumothorax picture, and a dry cough with subacute onset is atypical.
TB can cause pneumothorax, but PJP is more typical with CD4 below 200, a dry cough and pneumatoceles.

items.stem: A 58-year-old gardener has had weeks of progressive, mildly painful skin lesions up his left arm, starting on the thumb, linked by reddish streaks. He is afebrile and recalls no injury. Skin biopsy culture made the diagnosis. What is the most likely causative agent?
items.why: Sporothrix schenckii is found in soil and plants and is inoculated by thorns or other minor trauma. It causes a slow, indolent, ascending lymphocutaneous spread, without systemic symptoms.
notes: Dermatophytes are keratinophilic and do not invade deep tissue or spread along lymphatics.
Usually acute (days) with systemic features, not an evolution over weeks.
Needs exposure to fish or water through broken skin, which is not described here.

items.stem: A 25-year-old previously well man presents with fever, headache, myalgia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, jaundice and conjunctival suffusion, 2 weeks after taking part in a freshwater regatta in Thailand. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Freshwater exposure in an endemic area with fever, jaundice and conjunctival suffusion points to leptospirosis (Weil disease).
notes: Malaria has no link to freshwater exposure and rarely causes conjunctival suffusion.
Schistosomiasis follows freshwater exposure, but acute illness (Katayama fever) is not typified by jaundice and conjunctival suffusion.
Rabies follows an animal bite and causes neurological features, not this picture.

items.stem: A 46-year-old man who injects drugs presents with 24 hours of rigors, confusion, myalgia and severe left hand pain without obvious local inflammation or trauma. T 38.9°C, HR 120, RR 30, BP 90/54. WCC 25 ×10⁹/L (80% neutrophils), creatinine 141 µmol/L. Most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Pain out of proportion to local signs with early septic shock and organ dysfunction suggests necrotising fasciitis, most often due to Streptococcus pyogenes in people who inject drugs.
notes: Clostridial gangrene usually follows trauma or contaminated wounds, with crepitus and markedly raised CK from myonecrosis.
Mycobacterial infection is indolent, not an acute fulminant sepsis over 24 hours.
Erysipelas shows clear, raised, well-demarcated erythema and is rarely this septic.

items.stem: A 76-year-old woman has painless jaundice, pruritus and anorexia. Bilirubin is 140 µmol/L, mostly conjugated. Imaging shows biliary dilatation, a 3.5 cm pancreatic head mass and a single peripheral liver nodule under 2 cm, which biopsy confirms as adenocarcinoma. What is the best management?
options: Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, with surgery depending on response
Palliative surgical biliary bypass with or without gastrojejunostomy
Endoscopic metal biliary stent with option of palliative chemotherapy
Pancreaticoduodenectomy with ablation of the liver lesion
items.why: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma with liver metastasis is unresectable, so treatment is palliative. In a reasonably fit patient, an endoscopic (ERCP) metal biliary stent for permanent drainage plus palliative chemotherapy is best.
notes: Neoadjuvant therapy aims at resection, which is not possible with metastatic disease.
Surgical bypass is more invasive; endoscopic stenting is preferred in metastatic disease.
Resection is not indicated in metastatic pancreatic cancer.

items.stem: A 32-year-old Cameroonian man has had fever, cough and left pleuritic pain for 1 month despite a week of amoxicillin-clavulanate. Chest X-ray shows a loculated left effusion. Pleural fluid: leukocytes 2.5×10⁹/L (90% lymphocytes), protein 49 g/L, LDH 550 U/L, glucose 3.7 mmol/L, cytology negative. Which test is most useful for the diagnosis?
items.why: A lymphocytic exudate with subacute illness unresponsive to antibiotics in a person from a high-prevalence region suggests tuberculous pleurisy. Pleural ADA (above about 70 U/L) supports it, and fluid should go for TB culture.
notes: CT would not give the aetiology of a lymphocytic exudate.
Pleural pH helps assess parapneumonic effusion or empyema, not a lymphocytic exudate.
A tuberculin test cannot distinguish latent infection from active pleural disease and may be negative or positive regardless.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman notices groin lumps. She has no local symptoms or features suggesting a sexually transmitted infection. Examination shows one 1 cm lymph node in each groin, soft, mobile and painless, with no skin lesions on the legs, anus or perineum. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Syphilis serology as the most likely diagnosis
Reassurance; no further investigation, as these are normal nodes
EBV serology to exclude infectious mononucleosis
items.why: Palpable inguinal nodes up to about 2 cm are common and normal in healthy adults. Small, soft, mobile, painless nodes without a local source need no further investigation.
notes: No genital ulcer or risk features; syphilis is not the likeliest cause of normal-feeling bilateral small nodes.
Nothing suggests malignancy; ovarian cancer does not present as small bilateral inguinal nodes.
No fever, pharyngitis or systemic features suggest mononucleosis.

items.stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis taking methotrexate, prednisolone and indomethacin develops acute oedema and a rise in plasma creatinine. Urine sediment is bland and proteinuria is under 100 mg/24 h. What is the most likely cause?
items.why: NSAIDs cause prerenal AKI by blocking vasodilatory prostaglandins, with fluid retention and a bland sediment with minimal proteinuria.
notes: Amyloidosis would cause significant proteinuria, which is absent here.
Glomerulonephritis would give an active sediment and proteinuria; neither is present.
Interstitial nephritis from methotrexate is unlikely without rash, fever or eosinophilia.

items.stem: An 87-year-old independent man with hypertension and knee osteoarthritis takes perindopril, a thiazide diuretic and ibuprofen 1800 mg/day. Clinic BP is persistently 190/80 mmHg. What is the most reasonable change to achieve BP control?
options: Replace ibuprofen with paracetamol and recheck BP
Add an alpha blocker for probable prostatic symptoms
items.why: Regular NSAIDs raise BP through renal effects and blunt ACE inhibitor and diuretic action. Remove possible causes before intensifying therapy: stop ibuprofen, use a non-NSAID analgesic such as paracetamol and reassess BP.
notes: Escalating therapy before removing the NSAID treats a reversible, drug-induced cause incorrectly and adds polypharmacy risk in an elderly patient.
A higher diuretic dose does not address NSAID interference and increases risks of electrolyte disturbance and AKI, especially with an ACE inhibitor and NSAID.
Alpha blockers are not first-line for hypertension and the stem gives no prostatic symptoms; they also risk postural hypotension in the elderly.

items.stem: An 87-year-old independent man with hypertension and knee osteoarthritis takes perindopril, a thiazide diuretic and ibuprofen 1800 mg/day. At review his BP is persistently 190/80 mmHg. What is the most reasonable change to improve control?
options: Increase the hydrochlorothiazide dose to 25 mg daily
Add an alpha-blocker for likely prostatic symptoms
items.why: NSAIDs inhibit vasodilatory prostaglandins and renal perfusion, antagonising ACE inhibitors and diuretics. Switching to paracetamol, then reassessing BP, is preferred before escalating therapy.
notes: Adding drugs before removing the NSAID treats the interaction rather than the cause.
Increasing the thiazide does not remove the NSAID effect and raises risk of electrolyte disturbance and AKI in the elderly.
Alpha-blockers are not first-line for hypertension and risk postural hypotension in the elderly.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man is hit in the left eye by a tennis ball. He has marked eyelid bruising, subconjunctival haemorrhage, and vertical diplopia on upgaze with limited elevation of the left eye. What injury do you suspect?
options: Orbital floor fracture with entrapment of the inferior rectus
Orbital roof fracture with entrapment of the superior rectus
items.why: An entrapped inferior rectus cannot relax, so the eye cannot elevate, causing vertical diplopia on upgaze after blunt orbital trauma. This is a blowout fracture of the orbital floor.
notes: A zygomatic arch fracture typically causes trismus and a cheek or arch deformity, not limited upgaze.
Roof fractures are much less common, and superior rectus entrapment would limit depression, not elevation.
A dentoalveolar fracture involves the tooth-bearing bone and does not affect eye movements.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man is hit in the left orbit by a tennis ball. He has marked eyelid haematoma, subconjunctival haemorrhage, and diplopia on upgaze with restricted elevation of the left eye. What injury do you suspect?
options: Orbital floor fracture with inferior rectus entrapment
Orbital roof fracture with superior rectus entrapment
items.why: A blunt blow to the orbit with restricted upgaze suggests an orbital floor (blow-out) fracture. The trapped inferior rectus cannot stretch, causing restrictive diplopia on looking up.
notes: A zygomatic arch fracture is too far from the extraocular muscles to cause diplopia.
The orbital roof rarely fractures, and the restriction here is of elevation, which points to inferior rectus entrapment.
A dentoalveolar fracture is too far from the extraocular muscles to cause diplopia.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man with high myopia, who had cataract surgery 2 years ago, presents with profound, painless loss of vision in his right eye. Which diagnosis best explains this presentation?
items.why: High myopia and previous cataract surgery are risk factors for retinal detachment, which causes painless, profound loss of vision.
notes: Endophthalmitis usually occurs soon after surgery and is painful with rapidly falling acuity.
AMD occurs in older patients and vision loss is usually progressive, not sudden and profound.
Posterior vitreous detachment causes floaters and flashes with little acuity loss, and may cause some discomfort.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man with high myopia, who had cataract surgery 2 years ago, presents with profound painless loss of vision in his right eye. Which diagnosis should be most strongly suspected?
items.why: High myopia and previous intraocular surgery are both risk factors for retinal detachment, which causes painless, marked visual loss and must be excluded first.
notes: Endophthalmitis is typically painful and usually occurs soon after surgery.
Wet AMD is more typical in older patients; myopic macular degeneration is a different entity.
PVD usually causes floaters or flashes without major vision loss, though a haemorrhagic PVD can occasionally reduce vision.

items.stem: A man with asthma takes budesonide 200 micrograms twice daily and salbutamol as needed. Over 3 months he has had no exacerbations, but uses salbutamol daily, becomes dyspnoeic climbing stairs and has some nights disturbed by cough. What is the most appropriate treatment change?
options: Change to low-dose inhaled corticosteroid plus long-acting beta2 agonist
items.why: He remains symptomatic (daily reliever use, exertional dyspnoea, night cough), so asthma is uncontrolled and treatment should be stepped up. The next step is combined low-dose inhaled corticosteroid with a long-acting beta2 agonist.
notes: Quadrupling the corticosteroid dose gives less benefit and more adverse effects than adding a LABA at low dose.
Tiotropium is an add-on for patients still uncontrolled on ICS-LABA, not the next step.
Continuing is wrong because he has ongoing symptoms and frequent reliever use, so he is not controlled.

items.stem: A father brings his 2-year-old son to the emergency department saying he hit his right eye while playing. There is an eyelid haematoma. Fundoscopy shows intraretinal haemorrhages in both eyes. The child is drowsy and hypotonic. Which statement is most appropriate?
options: The history is highly suggestive of child abuse
This is the normal course of non-perforating ocular trauma
The most likely diagnosis is Berlin oedema
This is the characteristic picture of Purtscher retinopathy
items.why: Bilateral retinal haemorrhages with drowsiness and hypotonia suggest abusive head trauma (shaken baby syndrome), which also causes cerebral oedema and subdural haematoma. A minor blow does not explain this.
notes: Nothing suggests perforating trauma, and a blow to one eye would not cause haemorrhages in the other eye.
Berlin oedema is macular oedema seen as a whitish lesion, and it is not described here. It would not explain bilateral haemorrhages.
Purtscher retinopathy also has cotton-wool exudates and oedema, not isolated haemorrhages.

items.stem: An 84-year-old woman has had 4 days of left eye vision loss with metamorphopsia. The macula shows hard exudates, two small deep haemorrhages and a localised neurosensory retinal detachment. The other eye has abundant soft drusen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Metamorphopsia with macular exudates, deep haemorrhages and neurosensory detachment, plus drusen in the fellow eye, indicates neovascular AMD.
notes: Posterior vitreous detachment causes floaters and flashes, not macular lesions, metamorphopsia or vision loss.
Artery occlusion gives a pale, oedematous retina with a cherry-red spot and no haemorrhages or exudates.
NAION causes optic disc swelling and visual loss without metamorphopsia or macular lesions.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man had resection of a T3N1M0 colon adenocarcinoma and 6 months of adjuvant FOLFOX. Two years later CEA is 30 ng/mL (previously <2). He is asymptomatic. CT and PET show a single 3 cm right hepatic lobe lesion and no other disease. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Assessment for surgical resection of the liver lesion
items.why: This is probable oligometastatic (single liver) recurrence of colon cancer. Resection, if feasible, offers prolonged survival and potential cure, so surgical assessment comes first.
notes: Systemic chemotherapy is reserved for unresectable disease, to try to convert it to resectable.
Capecitabine alone gives lower response rates than combination regimens and is not a good first choice.
SBRT can be considered if surgery is ruled out, but surgical assessment comes first.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with stage IV pancreatic adenocarcinoma takes modified-release oral morphine 200 mg 12-hourly, senna and lactulose. For 15 days he has had paraesthesias and lancinating right lumbar and periumbilical pain unrelieved by breakthrough morphine; neurological examination is normal. What is the most appropriate management?
options: CT scan only, to assess nerve compression
Neurolytic procedure now, as neuropathic pain is hard to control
Reduce the morphine dose because it is ineffective for this pain
Add amitriptyline or gabapentin and dexamethasone, and increase morphine
items.why: This is likely neuropathic pain from tumour infiltration, so adjuvants (gabapentinoid or antidepressant, plus corticosteroid) should be added while opioids continue. Imaging and plexus blockade can be considered afterwards.
notes: Imaging is useful but should not delay symptom relief.
A neurolytic block can be considered later, but pain needs treating now.
Opioids are less effective in neuropathic pain, but the dose is not reduced; adjuvants are added.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man has 3 days of fever and a hot swollen right knee after diarrhoea 2 weeks ago. Aspirate: cloudy, low viscosity, WCC 40 x10^9/L (85% neutrophils), glucose 2.2 mmol/L, no crystals, Gram stain negative. Which statement is INCORRECT?
options: Empirical flucloxacillin and ceftriaxone should start while awaiting culture
Daily joint aspiration helps relieve symptoms and limit joint damage
If culture is negative, reactive arthritis is likely
A negative Gram stain rules out septic arthritis
items.why: A negative Gram stain or even culture never excludes infection, so septic arthritis must be treated until proven otherwise. The other statements are correct.
notes: Empirical antibiotics are appropriate while awaiting culture, so this statement is correct.
Repeated drainage is standard in septic arthritis, so this statement is correct.
Post-diarrhoeal inflammatory arthritis with negative culture suggests reactive arthritis, so this is correct.

items.stem: A 37-year-old man has arthritis of the metacarpophalangeal joints, right pleuritis and malar rash. ANA is positive at 1:640 and anti-dsDNA is positive. What is the most appropriate initial treatment of this lupus flare?
options: No treatment, as it is likely self-limiting
items.why: This is SLE with joint, skin and serosal involvement, and the flare is treated with moderate-to-high dose glucocorticoids (alongside hydroxychloroquine). Mycophenolate is for maintenance or organ-threatening disease.
notes: Mycophenolate is used for maintenance or organ-threatening disease, not as initial therapy for joint and serosal flares.
NSAIDs and antimalarials are insufficient for serositis such as pleuritis. Antimalarials work slowly.
SLE with serositis is active disease and needs treatment.

items.stem: A patient with diagnosed epilepsy has episodes of unresponsiveness, asynchronous irregular limb movements, eye closure, crying and pelvic thrusting lasting 5–20 seconds, unresponsive to antiseizure medication. Which investigation is most likely to clarify the diagnosis?
items.why: Asynchronous limb movements, pelvic thrusting, eye closure, crying and no response to antiseizure medication suggest psychogenic non-epileptic seizures. Video-EEG capturing typical events is the diagnostic test.
notes: Arrhythmic syncope does not produce this prolonged semiology with pelvic movements and crying.
A routine interictal EEG can be normal in either condition and cannot confirm the nature of events.
MRI shows structural lesions but cannot determine whether these events are epileptic.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man has a 5-day hot, swollen right knee and temperature 37.7°C, no trauma. Aspirate: 30 000 cells/µL, mostly neutrophils; rhomboid crystals with weakly positive birefringence. X-ray shows meniscal calcification. Which management statement is INCORRECT?
options: Initial treatment is NSAIDs plus aspiration of synovial fluid
Synovial fluid culture should be sent to exclude septic arthritis
Allopurinol should be started after the flare to prevent recurrences
The most likely diagnosis is pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate deposition)
items.why: This is CPPD arthritis (pseudogout) with chondrocalcinosis. There is no disease-modifying therapy; only flares are treated (NSAIDs, colchicine, corticosteroids). Allopurinol works in gout, not CPPD.
notes: This statement is correct: NSAIDs and aspiration treat the flare.
This statement is correct: infection must be excluded in any acute monoarthritis.
This statement is correct: the crystals and chondrocalcinosis indicate CPPD.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man with granulomatosis with polyangiitis diagnosed 10 years ago, untreated for 5 years, is asymptomatic at review. Chest X-ray, blood tests and urine sediment are normal, but PR3-ANCA is positive at 1/320 (previously negative). What is the most appropriate management?
items.why: ANCA titres relate to disease activity but should not alone prompt treatment changes. With no clinical or laboratory evidence of activity, monitor closely without restarting treatment.
notes: Treatment should not be started on ANCA titre alone in an asymptomatic patient with no evidence of activity.
Cyclophosphamide is for active organ-threatening disease, not an isolated ANCA rise.
Mycophenolate is not indicated for an isolated serological change without disease activity.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man with hyposmia has absent secondary sexual characteristics and infertility. Testicular volume is 4 mL bilaterally. FSH is 1.2 U/L (low), LH 0.6 U/L (low), testosterone 3.5 nmol/L (low) and prolactin is normal. Which treatment is most appropriate to achieve fertility?
options: Pulsatile GnRH via an infusion pump
items.why: This is Kallmann syndrome (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia). Fertility can be induced with pulsatile GnRH by pump, or with hCG plus FSH.
notes: Triptorelin is a GnRH agonist. Continuous exposure suppresses FSH and LH, so it is used in hormone-dependent cancers and precocious puberty.
LH is not given as treatment; pulsatile GnRH stimulates endogenous LH. Gonadotropin therapy uses hCG with FSH.
Bromocriptine treats hyperprolactinaemia and some pituitary tumours. His prolactin is normal.

items.stem: A 12-month-old boy has a right testis palpable in the inguinal canal that cannot be brought down into the scrotum. Which statement is correct?
options: The most likely diagnosis is a retractile testis
Surgery should wait until 3 years for spontaneous descent
Human chorionic gonadotropin is the first-line treatment
Orchidopexy should not be deferred any further
items.why: This is cryptorchidism (undescended testis). Spontaneous descent is unlikely after about 6 months, hormonal therapy is not used, and orchidopexy is the treatment of choice, ideally early in the first 1–2 years.
notes: A retractile testis can be manipulated into the scrotum; this one cannot.
Spontaneous descent is unlikely at this age, and delay risks impaired fertility and malignancy.
Hormonal treatment is not first-line and is now largely abandoned.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman, 4 days after an anterior STEMI treated with PCI and stenting of the LAD, suddenly becomes hypotensive needing volume, inotropes/vasopressors and intubation. Echocardiography shows pericardial effusion, and a mechanical complication is suspected. Which statement is correct?
options: Mortality with medical treatment alone is about 20%
Free wall rupture causes an oximetric step-up in the right ventricle
In free wall rupture there is no palpable thrill
Mechanical complications usually occur on the first day after infarction
items.why: A thrill and oximetric step-up occur with ventricular septal rupture, not free wall rupture. Free wall rupture, suggested by effusion and shock, has no thrill.
notes: Mortality with medical treatment alone is far higher than 20%.
A right ventricular oximetric step-up indicates septal rupture (left-to-right shunt), not free wall rupture.
Mechanical complications typically occur from days 3 to 7, and can occur up to the first couple of weeks.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man has had fever for 5 days and dyspnoea at rest for 6 hours. He has heart failure and ECG shows complete heart block (ventricular escape 45/min). Echo shows severe aortic regurgitation (EROA 0.5 cm²). Blood cultures grow Streptococcus gallolyticus. Heart failure is refractory to medical therapy. What is the best management?
options: Aortic valve replacement surgery plus targeted antibiotics
Antibiotics, intra-aortic balloon pump and temporary pacing, then permanent pacemaker
Temporary pacing, antibiotics and transcatheter aortic valve implantation
Urgent permanent pacemaker plus 6 weeks of targeted antibiotics
items.why: Heart failure and new conduction disturbance (suggesting perivalvular extension) are both indications for surgery in infective endocarditis. Surgery is combined with directed antibiotics.
notes: Medical bridging does not address refractory heart failure and the destroyed valve.
TAVI is not used for active infective endocarditis.
Pacing and antibiotics alone do not treat refractory heart failure from valve destruction.
