items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has 3 months of anxiety, 6 kg weight loss and tachycardia, with hyperreflexia and no goitre. TSH is <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 is raised and thyroglobulin is low. Thyroid scintigraphy shows no uptake. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Thyrotoxicosis with suppressed TSH, high T4, low thyroglobulin and absent uptake and no goitre indicates exogenous thyroid hormone intake. The gland is suppressed and makes little thyroglobulin.
notes: Graves' disease gives diffuse high uptake, usually with goitre and often eye or skin signs, and thyroglobulin is not low.
Struma ovarii is very rare. Uptake would be seen in the pelvis rather than the neck, and it does not best fit this picture.
Subacute thyroiditis is painful with raised thyroglobulin from gland destruction, though uptake is also low.

items.stem: A 49-year-old man is diagnosed with type 2 diabetes (glucose 17.9 mmol/L, HbA1c 84 mmol/mol) and started on metformin 850 mg twice daily plus glimepiride 6 mg daily. At 4 months, fasting glucose is 5.2 mmol/L and HbA1c 41 mmol/mol. He has sweating, tremor and dizziness in late morning and afternoon, relieved by food. What change would you make?
options: Review the distribution of dietary carbohydrate
Replace metformin with a DPP-4 inhibitor
items.why: His symptoms are recurrent hypoglycaemia relieved by food, now that glycaemic control is excellent. The sulfonylurea is the drug causing hypoglycaemia, so it should be stopped.
notes: Diet changes would not remove the drug-induced cause of the hypoglycaemia.
Metformin does not cause hypoglycaemia when used alone, so stopping it would not fix the problem.
Metformin is not the cause of the hypoglycaemia, and replacing it leaves the sulfonylurea in place.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has established ischaemic heart disease. Which pair of targets for LDL cholesterol and HbA1c is most appropriate for him?
items.why: Diabetes with established cardiovascular disease is very high risk, so the LDL-C target is <1.8 mmol/L (about 70 mg/dL). The general HbA1c target is about 7% (53 mmol/mol), individualised.
notes: An LDL-C of 0.4 mmol/L (15 mg/dL) is unrealistic and not a guideline target. Tight HbA1c targets also risk hypoglycaemia in older patients.
An LDL-C <2.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) is the older target for high-risk patients, not for established cardiovascular disease.
An LDL-C <3.0 mmol/L (115 mg/dL) is too lenient for secondary prevention in diabetes.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man with hyposmia has absent secondary sexual development and infertility. Testes are 4 mL bilaterally. FSH 1.2 IU/L, LH 0.6 IU/L, testosterone 3.5 nmol/L (low), prolactin normal. Which treatment could restore his fertility?
options: Pulsatile GnRH via an infusion pump
items.why: Hyposmia with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism indicates Kallmann syndrome (GnRH deficiency). Pulsatile GnRH restores the pituitary-gonadal axis and fertility.
notes: Continuous GnRH agonist such as triptorelin suppresses gonadotropins and would worsen hypogonadism.
Weekly dosing of FSH and LH does not reflect physiological replacement, and LH is replaced as hCG, not by this regimen.
Bromocriptine treats hyperprolactinaemia, and prolactin is normal here.

items.stem: A hospitalised patient has been unable to eat orally for more than 6 days. In which clinical situation is parenteral nutrition necessarily required?
options: Cardioembolic stroke with complete neurogenic dysphagia
Cachexia due to chronic empyema in an immunocompromised patient
Advanced Alzheimer's disease with high risk of aspiration
items.why: Paralytic ileus is a failure of intestinal propulsion without mechanical obstruction, so the gut cannot be used for feeding and parenteral nutrition is needed.
notes: Dysphagia with a functioning gut can be managed with enteral feeding via a nasogastric tube or gastrostomy.
Cachexia with a working gut is managed with enteral nutrition; parenteral is not mandatory.
Advanced dementia with aspiration risk is a goals-of-care issue, and the gut remains functional, so parenteral nutrition is not required.

items.stem: A woman with type 1 diabetes for 24 years has 3 months of bilateral foot tingling in a sock distribution, with burning paraesthetic pain worse at night that disturbs her sleep. Which drug is most appropriate first-line for her condition?
items.why: This is painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy. First-line treatment for neuropathic pain is a serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor such as duloxetine (or a tricyclic or gabapentinoid).
notes: NSAIDs are not effective for neuropathic pain and carry renal and cardiovascular risks in diabetes.
Opioids are not first-line for neuropathic pain because of limited benefit and risks of dependence and harm.
Simple analgesics such as paracetamol have little effect on neuropathic pain.

items.stem: An 88-year-old man has fallen three times in 6 months, with no dizziness or syncope. He has hypertension without postural blood pressure drop, gout, osteoarthritis and depression, and takes five regular medications. Which of his medications is most likely contributing to the falls?
items.why: Antidepressants such as SSRIs increase fall risk in older people independent of dizziness or postural hypotension. Antihypertensives typically cause falls with dizziness or postural drops.
notes: Allopurinol is not associated with falls.
Thiazides can cause falls via volume depletion or hypotension, usually with dizziness; no postural drop here.
ACE inhibitors cause falls mainly via hypotension and dizziness, which are absent here.

items.stem: A 20-year-old woman has a 15-cm solid-cystic ovarian mass on ultrasound. The resected specimen contains teeth, hair, and well-differentiated intestinal, squamous and bronchial epithelium. What is the diagnosis?
items.why: Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst) is a common benign ovarian tumour of young women. It is composed of well-differentiated tissues, often with teeth, cartilage and bone.
notes: Malignant germ cell tumour with carcinomatous elements; not a well-differentiated benign picture.
Immature teratoma contains immature, mainly neuroectodermal, tissue and is malignant.
Dysgerminoma is a solid tumour of uniform germ cells, without teeth, hair or mixed differentiated tissues.

items.stem: A 20-year-old woman has a 15 cm solid-cystic ovarian mass found on ultrasound. The specimen contains teeth, hair, and intestinal, bronchial and squamous epithelium, plus mature neural tissue, with no immature elements. What is the diagnosis?
items.why: Mature teratomas are made of adult tissues from all three germ layers, with ectodermal elements (skin, pilosebaceous structures, neural tissue) predominating. It is an ovarian germ cell tumour.
notes: Teratocarcinoma implies a malignant component, which is not described here.
Immature teratoma contains immature (embryonic) neuroepithelial tissue, which is absent here.
Dysgerminoma is a solid tumour of uniform germ cells and does not contain teeth, hair or multiple tissue types.

items.stem: A 20-year-old woman has a 15 cm solid-cystic ovarian mass. Histology shows teeth, hair, and well-differentiated intestinal, squamous and bronchial epithelium and neuroectodermal tissue. What is the diagnosis?
items.why: Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst) is the common ovarian tumour of young women. It is a cyst with skin-type wall, sebum and hair, containing well-differentiated tissues such as teeth, cartilage and bone.
notes: A malignant tumour combining teratoma with embryonal carcinoma; not suggested by mature tissues.
Contains immature, mainly neuroepithelial, tissue and is usually solid.
A solid germ-cell tumour of uniform cells resembling seminoma, without teeth or hair.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman is diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast and has no family history of cancer. Which additional tumour studies are needed to guide treatment?
options: Complete phenotypic study by flow cytometry
Hormone receptors, E-cadherin and first-degree relative testing
BRCA1/2 testing and first-degree relative testing
items.why: All breast carcinomas need oestrogen/progesterone receptor and HER2 testing for prognosis and to select therapy (endocrine, anti-HER2).
notes: Flow cytometry is used for haematological malignancies, not breast carcinoma.
Relative testing is not indicated without a family history, and E-cadherin only distinguishes lobular from ductal histology.
BRCA testing is not indicated without a family history or other risk features.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman is diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast. She has no family history of cancer. Which additional tumour testing has the most important clinical and therapeutic implications?
options: Hormone receptor status, E-cadherin and testing of first-degree relatives
BRCA1/2 testing and testing of first-degree relatives
items.why: Hormone receptor and HER2 status guide endocrine therapy and anti-HER2 therapy in every invasive breast cancer. With no family history there is no suggestion of hereditary cancer, so BRCA testing and family testing are not indicated.
notes: E-cadherin helps distinguish lobular from ductal histology, and family testing is not warranted without a family history suggesting hereditary breast cancer.
With no family history, hereditary breast cancer is unlikely, so BRCA1/2 and first-degree relative testing are not indicated.
Flow cytometry is used for haematological malignancies, not solid breast tumours.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman is diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast. She has no family history of cancer. Which additional tumour testing is most important for guiding prognosis and adjuvant treatment?
options: Complete phenotypic study by flow cytometry
Oestrogen and progesterone receptors and HER2 status
Hormone receptors, E-cadherin and testing of first-degree relatives
BRCA1/2 testing and testing of first-degree relatives
items.why: Oestrogen and progesterone receptor and HER2 status determine prognosis and the choice of adjuvant therapy (endocrine therapy, anti-HER2 therapy). They are tested on all invasive breast cancers.
notes: Flow cytometry is used for haematological malignancies, not breast carcinoma.
E-cadherin helps distinguish lobular from ductal carcinoma and is not needed here. Relatives' testing is not indicated without a family history.
BRCA testing is not indicated with no family history and it does not guide routine adjuvant therapy choice.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has a spontaneous miscarriage at 7 weeks. Histology of the products of conception shows a hydatidiform mole. What should she be told?
options: The risk of another molar pregnancy is 50%
She should avoid pregnancy until hCG surveillance is complete with normal levels
No follow-up is needed if the evacuation was complete
Follow-up is needed because 40% will develop gestational trophoblastic neoplasia
items.why: All molar pregnancies need serial hCG follow-up, even after complete evacuation, and pregnancy should be avoided until hCG has normalised and surveillance is complete. Recurrence risk is low.
notes: Recurrence risk is only about 1–2%, not 50%.
Follow-up is required regardless of whether evacuation appears complete, to detect persistent disease.
Only a minority (roughly 15–20% of complete moles, fewer of partial moles) develop neoplasia, not 40%.

items.stem: A 24-year-old primigravid woman has a miscarriage at 7 weeks. Histopathology of the products of conception shows a hydatidiform mole. What should she be counselled about?
options: The risk of a molar pregnancy in a future pregnancy is about 50%
She should avoid pregnancy until hCG surveillance is complete and hCG stays undetectable
No follow-up is needed if the trophoblastic tissue was completely evacuated
Surveillance is needed because 40% of cases develop gestational trophoblastic neoplasia
items.why: After molar pregnancy, serial hCG surveillance is essential until hCG is undetectable and for a set period afterwards (longer for complete mole). Pregnancy should be avoided during this time, as a rising hCG would be confused with new pregnancy or persistent disease.
notes: Recurrence risk is increased but only about 1–2%, not 50%.
Surveillance is needed even after complete evacuation because of the risk of persistent trophoblastic disease.
Neoplasia develops in roughly 5% (partial mole) to 15–20% (complete mole), not 40%.

items.stem: A 69-year-old woman presents with several months of vaginal bleeding. She takes no hormone therapy or anticoagulants. Her recent cervical screening test was normal, general and pelvic examination is unremarkable, and her BMI is 38 kg/m². What is the most appropriate next step?
items.why: Postmenopausal bleeding requires exclusion of endometrial cancer, particularly with obesity as a risk factor. Endometrial sampling, by pipelle or hysteroscopy, is indicated.
notes: Cyclic progestogen is not appropriate for postmenopausal bleeding before malignancy is excluded.
Normal cervical screening and a normal cervix on examination make random cervical biopsies unhelpful.
Hormone levels do not help diagnose endometrial neoplasia.

items.stem: A 69-year-old woman reports several months of vaginal bleeding. She takes no hormone therapy or anticoagulants. Her cervical screening test is normal, general and pelvic examination are unremarkable, and her BMI is 38 kg/m². What is the most appropriate next step?
items.why: Postmenopausal bleeding needs exclusion of endometrial cancer, and obesity raises risk through peripheral conversion of androgens to oestrone. Endometrial sampling is required before any treatment.
notes: Treatment should not start before organic causes, especially endometrial cancer, are excluded.
A normal cervical screening test makes a cervical source unlikely, and random biopsies are not indicated.
Hormone levels are not useful; she is clearly postmenopausal and the priority is excluding malignancy.

items.stem: A 69-year-old woman reports several months of vaginal bleeding. She is not on hormone therapy or anticoagulants. Her cervical screening result is normal, general and pelvic examination are unremarkable, and her BMI is 38 kg/m². What is the most appropriate next step?
items.why: Postmenopausal bleeding needs exclusion of endometrial hyperplasia or cancer, so endometrial sampling is required. Obesity raises the risk further.
notes: Progestogen would treat bleeding without excluding malignancy, so it delays diagnosis.
Cervical screening is normal and the cervix looks normal; the source is more likely endometrial.
Hormone levels are not useful in an established postmenopausal woman and do not exclude cancer.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman, parity 3, has a cervical screening test reporting a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) on cytology. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Colposcopy with directed biopsy if indicated
Hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy and ovarian conservation
Fractional dilatation and curettage of the uterus
items.why: HSIL on cytology requires referral for colposcopy with biopsy as indicated, regardless of age or parity.
notes: Repeating cytology delays assessment of a high-grade lesion.
Hysterectomy is not first-line; histological diagnosis by colposcopy and biopsy comes first.
Curettage assesses the endometrium, not the cervical lesion.

items.stem: A 56-year-old man has had 6 months of difficulty walking on the right leg. Examination shows 4/5 weakness of ankle dorsiflexion, eversion, plantarflexion and inversion, with brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response. Sensation is normal. What is the syndromic diagnosis?
options: Focal upper motor neuron lesion, probably with lower motor neuron involvement
Multiple mononeuropathy of the right common peroneal and tibial nerves
items.why: Weakness across several myotomes with brisk reflexes and Babinski sign indicates an upper motor neuron (pyramidal) lesion. Probable lower motor neuron involvement fits a motor neuron pattern.
notes: A peroneal neuropathy would not explain pyramidal signs (brisk reflexes, Babinski) or the plantarflexion weakness.
Brown-Séquard would also cause contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation. Sensation is normal here.
Two peripheral nerve lesions could explain the weakness but not the pyramidal signs.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has cervical screening that shows a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion on cytology. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy and ovarian conservation
items.why: HSIL suggests CIN2 or CIN3. It must be confirmed histologically, so she needs colposcopy with directed biopsy.
notes: Repeat cytology is inadequate for HSIL; histological assessment is needed.
Hysterectomy is not done before histological diagnosis; treatment is guided by colposcopic biopsy.
Uterine curettage assesses the endometrium, not the cervical squamous lesion.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman has 8 months of dyspareunia, cyclical dyschezia with occasional rectal bleeding for 3 months, long-standing dysmenorrhoea and 16 months of infertility. She is tender in the posterior vaginal fornix. Which investigation provides the definitive (gold standard) diagnosis of her likely condition?
items.why: The picture suggests endometriosis. Imaging and history suggest the diagnosis, but definitive diagnosis is direct visualisation of implants at laparoscopy, ideally with histological confirmation.
notes: Ultrasound can suggest endometriomas or deep disease but cannot give a definitive diagnosis.
MRI helps map deep infiltrating disease but remains a suspicion-level diagnosis, not histological proof.
Colonoscopy may exclude other bowel pathology but typically cannot confirm endometriosis, which lies outside the mucosa.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman has 8 months of dyspareunia, 3–4 months of dyschezia and cyclical rectal bleeding, and longstanding dysmenorrhoea. She has been unable to conceive for 16 months. Examination shows tenderness in the posterior vaginal fornix. Which test gives a definitive diagnosis?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis
items.why: The picture suggests deep endometriosis. Laparoscopy with visualisation and histological confirmation remains the reference standard for a definitive diagnosis.
notes: Ultrasound can suggest endometriomas and deep disease but does not give a definitive diagnosis.
MRI maps deep disease for planning but is not the definitive test.
Colonoscopy may show extrinsic compression or exclude bowel pathology but cannot confirm endometriosis.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman has 8 months of dyspareunia, 3–4 months of cyclical dyschezia and rectal bleeding, long-standing dysmenorrhoea and 16 months of infertility. Examination shows tenderness of the posterior vaginal fornix only. Suspected deep endometriosis. Which test gives a definitive (histological) diagnosis?
items.why: The picture is deep endometriosis. Definitive diagnosis requires laparoscopic visualisation with histology of the lesions; imaging can suggest but not confirm it.
notes: Ultrasound can show endometriomas or deep disease but gives no histological confirmation.
MRI maps deep disease for surgical planning but cannot give a histological diagnosis.
Colonoscopy may exclude other bowel pathology but usually looks normal in endometriosis, as disease is serosal or extrinsic.

items.stem: A woman at 10 weeks' gestation presents with a blood pressure of 160/105 mmHg and mild headache. After 4 hours' rest it is 150/95 mmHg. Full blood count is normal and there is no proteinuria. What type of hypertension is this?
items.why: Hypertension present before pregnancy or diagnosed before 20 weeks' gestation is chronic hypertension. At 10 weeks this is chronic hypertension.
notes: Pre-eclampsia occurs after 20 weeks and needs proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction.
Gestational hypertension begins after 20 weeks.
Eclampsia requires seizures, which are absent.

items.stem: A woman at 10 weeks' gestation presents with blood pressure 160/105 mmHg and a mild headache. She is otherwise well. After 4 hours' rest her blood pressure is 150/95 mmHg. Full blood count is normal and urine protein is negative. What type of hypertension does she have?
items.why: Hypertension detected before 20 weeks' gestation (or before pregnancy), or persisting beyond 12 weeks postpartum, is chronic hypertension. At 10 weeks this cannot be a pregnancy-specific disorder.
notes: Pre-eclampsia is diagnosed after 20 weeks, with hypertension plus proteinuria or other maternal organ or uteroplacental involvement.
Gestational hypertension is new hypertension arising after 20 weeks' gestation; this woman is at only 10 weeks.
Eclampsia is seizures in a woman with pre-eclampsia, which occurs after 20 weeks; she has had no seizure.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents after noticing groin lumps. She has no local symptoms or features suggesting a sexually transmitted infection. Examination shows bilateral 1 cm inguinal nodes that are soft, mobile and painless, with no lesions of the legs, anus or perineum. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Syphilis serology, as this is most likely syphilis
Gynaecological assessment to exclude ovarian cancer
Reassure: these are likely normal nodes and no further investigation is needed
Monospot (heterophile antibody) test to exclude infectious mononucleosis
items.why: Inguinal nodes up to 1–1.5 cm can be normal. These are small, soft, mobile and painless without other signs, so there is no suspicion of malignancy or infection and no tests are needed.
notes: Nothing in the history or examination suggests an STI, so syphilis is not likely.
There are no features of malignancy, so ovarian cancer work-up is not warranted.
There are no systemic features of mononucleosis, so testing is unnecessary.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents after noticing groin lumps. She has no local symptoms and no features of sexually transmitted infection. There are two 1 cm, soft, mobile, painless inguinal nodes, one per side, and no skin lesions on the legs, anus or perineum. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Syphilis serology, as this is most likely Treponema pallidum infection
Gynaecological assessment to exclude ovarian cancer
Reassure: these are normal nodes and no further investigation is needed
Monospot (heterophile antibody) test to exclude infectious mononucleosis
items.why: Inguinal nodes up to about 1.5 cm can be normal. Soft, mobile, painless, bilateral small nodes with no local lesion or STI features need no investigation.
notes: No genital ulcer, rash or STI features make syphilis unlikely as the cause of these nodes.
Nothing suggests pelvic malignancy; small soft mobile nodes are not a reason to look for ovarian cancer.
No fever, pharyngitis or generalised lymphadenopathy suggests mononucleosis, so testing is not warranted.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman has Hb 96 g/L, haematocrit 0.32, MCV 85 fL, serum iron 4.5 µmol/L (6.6–26) and ferritin 350 µg/L (15–150). Which condition is this pattern most suggestive of?
items.why: Normocytic anaemia with low serum iron but raised ferritin is the pattern of anaemia of chronic disease, as seen in inflammatory conditions such as polymyalgia rheumatica.
notes: Recent blood loss would lower ferritin, not raise it.
Iron malabsorption would give low ferritin, and B12 malabsorption would give a clearly raised MCV.
Thalassaemia minor causes microcytosis with normal or high iron and ferritin, and is not a chronic disease pattern.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman has a mechanical mitral valve replacement. After starting warfarin she develops skin necrosis of the abdomen and limbs. Which underlying abnormality best explains this?
items.why: Warfarin-induced skin necrosis is rare and linked to protein C (or S) deficiency. Warfarin rapidly lowers protein C, which has a short half-life, causing a transient hypercoagulable state and microvascular thrombosis.
notes: Antithrombin deficiency causes heparin resistance, not warfarin skin necrosis.
Factor V Leiden is a thrombophilia but is not classically linked to warfarin necrosis.
Hyperhomocysteinaemia is a thrombotic risk factor but is not linked to warfarin necrosis.

items.stem: A 51-year-old man has macrocytic anaemia (Hb 63 g/L, MCV 120 fL) with deficiencies excluded and a low reticulocyte count. Bone marrow is consistent with myelodysplastic syndrome and cytogenetics shows del(5q). Which statement is correct?
options: Del(5q) is a good prognostic feature and has specific treatment (lenalidomide)
HLA typing should be arranged now for an allogeneic transplant
He has high-risk disease by the International Prognostic Scoring System
Treatment would be transfusion support only
items.why: Isolated del(5q) MDS has favourable cytogenetics and responds to lenalidomide.
notes: Transplant is for high or intermediate-2 risk disease. Risk cannot be calculated here, and cytogenetics is favourable.
IPSS needs blast percentage and other cytopenias, which are not given. Del(5q) alone is favourable.
He is young without comorbidity and has a specific therapy, so transfusion alone is not the only option.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman receiving two units of red cells for a bleeding peptic ulcer develops fever, rigors, hypotension and loin pain 5–10 minutes after the transfusion starts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Febrile reaction due to plasma contaminating the red cells
items.why: Fever, rigors, loin pain and shock within minutes of starting a transfusion indicate an acute haemolytic reaction (usually ABO incompatibility), which may cause DIC.
notes: Contamination can cause fever and shock but loin pain and onset within minutes fit haemolysis better.
A febrile non-haemolytic reaction is milder and does not cause hypotension and loin pain.
Plasma-related febrile reactions are mild and do not cause shock.

items.stem: A 78-year-old asymptomatic woman (ECOG 0) has grade 2 follicular lymphoma with 2 years of small neck nodes. Hb 120 g/L, platelets 220 ×10⁹/L, LDH normal. CT shows nodes <3 cm in multiple regions, with normal liver and spleen. No B symptoms. What is the most appropriate management?
items.why: She has low tumour burden and meets none of the GELF criteria, and early treatment gives no survival benefit, so watch and wait is recommended.
notes: Immunochemotherapy is not indicated without GELF criteria, and anthracycline is risky with her heart failure.
Immunochemotherapy is reserved for high tumour burden or symptoms; none are present.
Bendamustine-rituximab is for patients needing treatment, which she does not yet.

items.stem: A 64-year-old farmer, ex-smoker with COPD and rheumatoid arthritis on corticosteroids, has had a month of productive cough, haemoptysis, fever and weight loss after influenza. He now has headache and a right facial palsy. He has multiple skin abscesses, some with fistulae, apical lung infiltrates and a small pleural effusion. Most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Nocardia affects patients with impaired cell-mediated immunity, such as those on steroids, causing pulmonary disease, brain abscess and skin abscesses.
notes: Cancer would not explain the multiple skin abscesses with fistulae and the fever in this immunosuppressed host.
Tuberculosis can involve lung and brain but does not typically cause cutaneous abscesses.
Aspergillus can involve lung and brain but does not typically cause skin abscesses.

items.stem: A 32-year-old man from Cameroon has had 1 month of fever, cough and left chest pain unresponsive to amoxicillin-clavulanate. CXR shows a loculated left effusion. Pleural fluid is a lymphocytic exudate (protein 49 g/L, glucose normal) with negative cytology. Which test is most useful for diagnosis?
items.why: A lymphocytic exudate in a person from a high-TB-burden region suggests tuberculous pleurisy. Raised pleural adenosine deaminase strongly supports it, though pleural biopsy confirms.
notes: CT adds anatomical detail but does not establish the cause.
pH helps assess parapneumonic effusion or empyema, not TB diagnosis.
A tuberculin test cannot confirm active pleural disease and may be falsely negative or positive.

items.stem: A 38-year-old non-smoking woman with atopic rhinitis has a two-month history of intermittent cough and nocturnal wheeze. Chest X-ray is normal, and spirometry and bronchodilator response are normal. Which test is most appropriate next?
items.why: The picture strongly suggests asthma, and normal spirometry with no bronchodilator response does not exclude it. A methacholine challenge shows bronchial hyperresponsiveness and supports the diagnosis.
notes: Sinus imaging would not explain or confirm the lower airway symptoms.
CT chest is not indicated with a normal chest X-ray and a picture suggesting asthma.
Prick testing shows atopy but does not confirm variable airway obstruction or asthma.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man with acute respiratory failure has a chest X-ray showing atelectasis of two-thirds of the right lung. After intubation and ventilation with FiO2 1.0, ABG shows pH 7.23, PaO2 8.0 kPa and PaCO2 4.0 kPa. What is the mechanism of his hypoxaemia?
items.why: Hypoxaemia that persists despite FiO2 1.0, with a low PaCO2, indicates a V/Q disturbance with shunt through the collapsed, perfused lung.
notes: A low PaCO2 excludes hypoventilation, which would raise PaCO2.
FiO2 of 1.0 means inspired oxygen pressure is maximal.
Neuromuscular disease would cause hypoventilation with a raised PaCO2, and is not suggested here.

items.stem: A 78-year-old woman has sudden left monocular vision loss, a pale swollen optic disc, 3 weeks of fever, headache and shoulder/hip girdle pain, Hb 97 g/L and ESR 115 mm/h. Temporal arteries are normal to palpation. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Arrange a temporal artery Doppler ultrasound before treating
Start high-dose prednisolone (about 1 mg/kg, e.g. 60 mg) daily now
Wait for temporal artery biopsy results before starting steroids
items.why: This is giant cell arteritis with arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, an emergency. Start high-dose corticosteroids immediately to protect the other eye; do not delay for biopsy, which remains positive for days to weeks.
notes: Imaging may assist diagnosis but must not delay treatment when vision is threatened.
10 mg is far too low to prevent further visual loss in active GCA with ocular involvement.
Biopsy is still needed, but it stays diagnostic after starting steroids and treatment must not wait for it.

items.stem: An ex-smoker with known COPD attends for review. Examination shows finger clubbing of recent onset. What is the most likely explanation for this finding?
items.why: Newly developed clubbing in a smoker should prompt exclusion of bronchogenic carcinoma first. COPD itself does not cause clubbing.
notes: Bronchiectasis can cause clubbing but usually develops gradually with chronic productive cough.
Pulmonary fibrosis causes clubbing, but typically in the context of known interstitial disease and not as a sudden new sign in COPD.
Cyanotic heart disease causes clubbing from childhood, not recent onset in an adult ex-smoker.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man has dysphonia, a month of fatigue and weight loss. Chest X-ray shows increased density in the left upper lobe and a filled aortopulmonary window. Bronchoscopy shows left vocal cord paralysis but no visible tumour. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: The most common cause of recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy is bronchogenic carcinoma, here with aortopulmonary window nodes. A normal bronchoscopic view does not exclude it.
notes: Sarcoidosis typically gives bilateral hilar adenopathy and rarely causes recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy.
Silicosis needs occupational exposure and gives nodular upper zone disease, not nerve palsy.
Tuberculosis can cause this, but lung cancer is much more common in a smoker-age man with weight loss and a mass.

items.stem: A 31-year-old man has progressive headache and bitemporal hemianopia. MRI shows a 35 × 30 × 20 mm pituitary tumour compressing the chiasm and cavernous sinus. Prolactin is 480 µg/L (normal <15), testosterone 5.5 nmol/L (low), FSH and LH low; cortisol, TSH and free T4 are normal. What is the initial treatment?
items.why: This is a macroprolactinoma with hypogonadism from stalk and gonadotroph compression. Dopamine agonists are first-line, shrink the tumour and improve visual fields, even with chiasmal compression.
notes: Surgery is second line for dopamine-agonist failure or intolerance; cavernous sinus invasion makes it riskier and unlikely to cure.
Radiotherapy is a later adjunct for resistant tumours, being slow and risking hypopituitarism.
Testosterone does not treat the tumour and gonadal function usually recovers once prolactin normalises.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man presents with 2 days of headache and fever (37.8°C), then difficulty naming and understanding speech. There is no neck stiffness. CT shows a faint left temporal hypodensity without mass effect or enhancement. Which statement is correct?
options: Bacterial meningitis is most likely; start a third-generation cephalosporin alone
CSF likely shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose
Limbic encephalitis is the most likely diagnosis
This is an early brain abscess
items.why: Fever, aphasia and temporal lobe change suggest viral (herpes) encephalitis, whose CSF typically shows moderate lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose.
notes: Bacterial meningitis would show higher fever, neck stiffness and neutrophilic CSF with low glucose; this picture is not that.
Limbic encephalitis is usually afebrile with behavioural change and memory disturbance.
An abscess appears as a well-delimited ring-enhancing lesion, not a faint non-enhancing hypodensity.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man is investigated for possible meningitis with fever, headache and vomiting. MRI brain and lumbar puncture are done. Twenty hours later, he develops severe headache on sitting up that disappears on lying down. Fever and vomiting have resolved. What is the most likely cause?
options: Ongoing meningitis, as the headache is the same as at presentation
Another cause, as this is not typical of post-lumbar puncture headache
Subarachnoid haemorrhage, as the headache eases on lying flat
items.why: A postural headache that is worse upright and relieved supine after lumbar puncture is classic for CSF leak (post-dural puncture headache), usually within 24–48 hours.
notes: Meningitic headache is not relieved by lying down, and nothing says the earlier headache was similar.
The postural pattern is so typical that a post-puncture headache is the most probable cause, even though onset is slightly early.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage headache does not characteristically vary with posture.

items.stem: A 65-year-old woman presented two years ago with apraxia of speech. She now has asymmetric right-sided rigid-akinetic parkinsonism with myoclonus and alien limb phenomenon. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Initial apraxia, then asymmetric akinetic-rigid parkinsonism with myoclonus and alien limb, is typical of corticobasal degeneration.
notes: Parkinson's disease does not begin with apraxia and does not typically cause alien limb or cortical myoclonus.
Alzheimer's disease does not typically produce asymmetric parkinsonism with alien limb.
Huntington's disease rarely starts at this age and presents with chorea rather than rigidity.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man has a year of progressive memory loss and word-finding difficulty. Which investigation is most useful to characterise the pattern of his cognitive deficits?
items.why: Characterising cognitive decline is clinical; formal neuropsychological testing measures each cognitive domain in a standardised way, defines the syndrome and allows monitoring over time.
notes: MRI shows structural changes but does not characterise the cognitive domains affected.
PET is a supportive tool and does not define the cognitive deficit pattern.
EEG is not useful for characterising cognitive deficits.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has had a week of yellow eyes, after a year of generalised pruritus, fatigue, dry mouth and dry eyes. She has no risk factors for viral hepatitis and takes no alcohol or hepatotoxins. She has excoriations, jaundice and non-tender hepatomegaly. Bilirubin is 51 µmol/L, ALP 400 U/L, ESR 40 mm/h. Which test best establishes the aetiology?
items.why: Middle-aged woman with pruritus, sicca symptoms, cholestatic jaundice and hepatomegaly suggests primary biliary cholangitis, which is confirmed by anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA).
notes: No viral risk factors are present, and the cholestatic picture with sicca symptoms points to PBC rather than viral hepatitis.
Copper studies are for Wilson disease, which presents in younger patients with hepatic, neurological or psychiatric features.
MRI (MRCP) is for large-duct disease such as sclerosing cholangitis; it does not give the aetiological diagnosis of PBC.

items.stem: A 25-year-old develops severe neck and left eye pain playing tennis. Next morning he has gait instability, left ptosis and a smaller left pupil, with good visual acuity. Where is the lesion most likely located?
items.why: Ptosis with miosis is Horner syndrome, but the added gait ataxia indicates a brainstem (lateral medullary) lesion, as from vertebral artery dissection, rather than a peripheral sympathetic lesion.
notes: III nerve palsy gives ptosis with a dilated pupil, not miosis.
A chiasm lesion causes visual field defects, not Horner syndrome.
A superior cervical ganglion lesion, such as from carotid dissection, would not explain ataxia.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman with weight loss, anorexia, proximal muscle and joint aching and jaw pain presents with sudden painless monocular vision loss (hand movements) and a relative afferent pupillary defect. Which test should be requested first?
items.why: The picture suggests giant cell arteritis with arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. Inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) are the first test, alongside urgent corticosteroids and temporal artery biopsy.
notes: Lumbar puncture is not relevant to ischaemic optic neuropathy from vasculitis.
MRA is not the first-line test; diagnosis rests on inflammatory markers and temporal artery biopsy.
Carotid ultrasound would be considered for non-arteritic embolic causes, without this systemic symptom cluster.

items.stem: An 88-year-old man, independent in daily activities, has well-controlled hypertension, atrial fibrillation on aspirin, and prostate cancer at 73 now in remission. He presents 45 minutes after sudden aphasia and right hemiparesis. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Urgent non-contrast CT brain; if no haemorrhage or contraindication, give IV thrombolysis
Urgent CT brain; if no haemorrhage, start anticoagulation immediately
CT brain, then admit to rehabilitation as management is the same for any aetiology
No CT brain needed; just stop the aspirin
items.why: Sudden focal deficit within the window needs CT to exclude haemorrhage, then IV thrombolysis if no contraindication. Controlled cancer, good baseline function and age alone do not exclude it.
notes: Immediate anticoagulation in acute stroke raises haemorrhage risk and is not first-line; reperfusion is preferred.
Management differs by aetiology, and he is within the thrombolysis window.
Imaging is essential to distinguish ischaemic from haemorrhagic stroke before treatment.

items.stem: A 12-month-old boy has had a right testis fixed in the inguinal canal since birth that cannot be manipulated into the scrotum. Which statement is correct?
options: The most likely diagnosis is a retractile testis
Wait until 2 years of age for spontaneous descent
Human chorionic gonadotropin is first-line treatment
items.why: A persistently undescended testis is cryptorchidism, and orchidopexy is the treatment, ideally at 6–12 months and certainly before 2 years. Spontaneous descent is unlikely after 6 months.
notes: A retractile testis can be manually brought down to the scrotum; this one cannot.
Spontaneous descent is unlikely after 6 months, and surgery should not wait until 2 years.
Hormonal therapy with hCG is largely abandoned due to low efficacy and risk of re-ascent.

items.stem: A 3-year-old girl has had isolated breast development (Tanner stage II) for 3 months. There is no pubic or axillary hair, no medication use, and normal external genitalia. Ultrasound shows a prepubertal-sized uterus and bone age is 3 years. What is the most appropriate management?
items.why: This is most consistent with premature thelarche: isolated breast development with no pubic hair, a prepubertal uterus and normal bone age. It is often self-limiting, so close clinical follow-up is appropriate.
notes: Biopsy is only considered if there are warning signs such as a suspicious mass; it is not indicated here.
Breast ultrasound, not mammography, is used in children, and only for concerns such as asymmetry or a mass.
GnRH analogues treat central precocious puberty, which is not supported by the normal bone age and prepubertal uterus.

items.stem: A newborn has microcephaly, intrauterine growth restriction, congenital heart disease, rocker-bottom (vertical talus) feet, micrognathia, small palpebral fissures, dysplastic ears, and overlapping fingers with the index and little finger over the middle and ring fingers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Overlapping clenched fingers (index over middle, fifth over fourth) with rocker-bottom feet, growth restriction and cardiac defects are characteristic of Edwards syndrome.
notes: Patau shares heart defects but is typified by holoprosencephaly, cleft lip/palate and polydactyly.
Down syndrome has hypotonia, upslanting fissures and a single palmar crease, not overlapping fingers.
Trisomy 9 is rare and the finger overlap is much more characteristic of trisomy 18.

items.stem: A 5-month-old exclusively breastfed infant was given formula by bottle, then cereals with and without gluten. There is a family history of asthma, atopy and coeliac disease, and formula was given on day 1 of life. She now has abdominal distension, diarrhoea, perioral erythema after bottle feeds and vomiting, but tolerates breast milk. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Family atopy, early formula exposure (sensitisation) and digestive symptoms plus rash coinciding with formula intake indicate cow's milk protein allergy.
notes: Coeliac disease would not explain perioral erythema after bottle feeds, and symptoms track formula, not gluten.
Gastroenteritis would not be linked to formula feeds with perioral rash and tolerance of breast milk.
There is no such entity as bottle allergy; the reaction is to cow's milk protein in the formula.

items.stem: A 13-year-old boy has heartburn during and after meals and dysphagia to solids such as meat. He has allergies to pollen, dust mites and latex, and flexural eczema. Eosinophilic oesophagitis or reflux is suspected. Which test is LEAST appropriate?
options: 13C urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori
items.why: Atopy with heartburn and solid-food dysphagia suggests eosinophilic oesophagitis (or GORD). H. pylori testing is not relevant to either diagnosis.
notes: Endoscopy with biopsy is the key investigation for eosinophilic oesophagitis.
pH monitoring helps assess for coexisting reflux, which is in the differential.
Barium study can show strictures, rings or anatomical problems, and is reasonable in dysphagia.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman had breast cancer treated 10 years ago with surgery and radiotherapy. She now has spinal and sacroiliac metastases and has received monthly IV zoledronic acid for 2 years. She has 2 cm of spontaneous exposed mandibular bone, no acute infection and normal surrounding gum. CT shows bone sclerosis. What is the diagnosis?
items.why: Spontaneous exposed jaw bone without infection in a patient on long-term IV bisphosphonate is bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis of the jaw. Sclerosis fits this better than a metastasis, which is usually destructive.
notes: An abscess would show signs of infection, which are absent here.
Radiotherapy was directed at the breast, not the mandible, so osteoradionecrosis is unlikely.
A metastasis would typically be destructive rather than sclerotic, and would not explain the bone exposure.

items.stem: An 80-year-old man, found lost at night, lives alone and refuses support services. He has diabetes, is underweight and was treated for a urinary tract infection, hyperglycaemia and warfarin-related INR problems. He is now stable, wants to go home, but cannot self-administer insulin. What is the next step in determining his safety at home?
options: Refer to primary care and community social work to determine home safety
Formal assessment of his decision-making capacity about his health
items.why: Decision-making capacity should be assessed first, by the treating doctor. It checks that he understands his condition, the options and the consequences of choosing to go home. It protects vulnerable patients rather than removing autonomy.
notes: Referral may follow, but his ability to decide about discharge and treatment must be established first.
Dementia work-up may follow if capacity is impaired, but it does not itself determine his ability to decide about going home.
Depression screening may be relevant later, but capacity assessment is the immediate step for this decision.

items.stem: A 26-year-old man has not left home for 3 months because he believes his jaw is asymmetrical and his face crooked. He is ashamed, anxious at the mirror and preoccupied all day. Several maxillofacial surgeons found no asymmetry and referred him on. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Major depressive disorder with mood-incongruent delusions
items.why: Preoccupation with a perceived, non-existent or slight physical defect that causes distress and impairs function is body dysmorphic disorder.
notes: There is no pervasive low mood or other depressive features described; the focus is a single appearance concern.
OCD has obsessions and compulsions more broadly. Here the preoccupation is confined to a perceived appearance defect.
There are no hallucinations, disorganisation or other psychotic features suggested by the history.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman with two prior major depressive episodes is started on escitalopram 10 mg for a new episode. At 2 weeks she feels very well, wakes early with lots of energy, is more talkative, not irritable, and sleeps 6 hours continuously. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Early activation or normal response to escitalopram
items.why: Two weeks is too early for the full antidepressant effect, but early activation can occur. Preserved, continuous sleep argues against a hypomanic switch. Continue treatment and review within a month.
notes: Bipolar I requires a past manic episode; nothing here suggests one, and the history is of depressive episodes only.
Sleep is maintained (6 hours continuous) and there is no irritability, which makes a hypomanic switch unlikely.
Nothing suggests dementia; the presentation is a new depressive episode with a short-term change after starting treatment.

items.stem: A patient has a long history of multiple physical symptoms: memory loss, headache, dizziness, vomiting, genital and limb pain, abdominal distension and menstrual irregularity. Extensive investigation has found no medical illness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Chronic multiple symptoms across pain, gastrointestinal, sexual/reproductive and pseudoneurological domains without a medical explanation is the classic somatisation pattern (somatic symptom disorder).
notes: Conversion disorder involves specific neurological deficits, usually linked to a psychological trigger, which is not described.
Illness anxiety centres on fear of having a serious illness with minimal or no somatic symptoms.
Dissociative disorders involve disrupted identity, memory or awareness, not widespread bodily symptoms.

items.stem: A 53-year-old man is distressed by a behaviour he finds absurd but cannot avoid: every time he arrives home from work he must first turn the handle of the upstairs bathroom door, before greeting his family. Resisting only increases his distress. What is this symptom called?
items.why: A compulsion is a repetitive behaviour or mental act performed to reduce anxiety or according to rigid rules, and is not realistically connected to what it aims to prevent. The question asks for the symptom, not the disorder.
notes: This is the name of the disorder, not the symptom being asked about.
An obsession is a recurrent intrusive thought, urge or image, not the behaviour performed in response.
An impulse is an urge to act, typically ego-syntonic and gratifying, without a ritualised anxiety-reducing purpose.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man has 3 days of a painful swollen right knee and fever, after self-limiting diarrhoea 2 weeks ago. Aspirate: cloudy, low viscosity, WCC 40 ×10⁹/L (85% neutrophils), glucose 2.2 mmol/L, no crystals, Gram stain negative. Which statement is INCORRECT?
options: Start flucloxacillin and ceftriaxone pending culture.
Daily joint aspiration is advisable to relieve symptoms and limit joint damage.
If cultures are negative, reactive arthritis is likely.
A negative Gram stain excludes septic arthritis.
items.why: A negative Gram stain never rules out septic arthritis, as its sensitivity is limited. Treat empirically until cultures are back.
notes: Empirical antibiotics are appropriate while septic arthritis cannot be excluded.
Repeated aspiration or drainage of a purulent joint is standard.
Post-diarrhoeal inflammatory arthritis with negative cultures suggests reactive arthritis.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man has had 3 days of a hot swollen painful right knee with fever, after diarrhoea 2 weeks ago. Aspirate: cloudy, WCC 40 x10^9/L (85% neutrophils), glucose low, no crystals, Gram stain negative. Which statement is INCORRECT?
options: Flucloxacillin and ceftriaxone should be started pending culture
Repeated joint aspiration may be used to drain the joint and relieve symptoms
If culture is negative, reactive arthritis is likely
A negative Gram stain rules out septic arthritis
items.why: Gram stain has limited sensitivity, so a negative result does not exclude septic arthritis. An inflammatory aspirate with this cell count should be treated as infection until cultures return.
notes: Empirical antibiotics are appropriate while awaiting culture.
Joint drainage is a recognised part of managing a septic joint.
A culture-negative inflammatory effusion after enteric infection suggests reactive arthritis.

items.stem: A 64-year-old smoker with heavy alcohol use has a 2-month history of a progressively enlarging, painless right jugulodigastric lymph node. Fine needle aspiration shows squamous cell carcinoma. Which primary site is most likely?
items.why: In a smoker who drinks heavily, upper level II neck nodes with squamous cell carcinoma most often come from the upper aerodigestive tract, such as the larynx. Parotid squamous primaries are rare.
notes: Scalp skin primaries are possible but less likely than upper aerodigestive tract cancer in this risk profile.
Primary parotid squamous cell carcinoma is rare.
Lung cancer more often spreads to lower cervical or supraclavicular nodes.

items.stem: A 13-year-old boy has had thoracic back pain for several months. It occurs only when standing and walking. There are no other features of note. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Malignant tumour of a vertebral body
items.why: The pain is mechanical, and mechanical overload is the most common cause of mechanical back pain in adolescents. Nothing in the history points to another cause.
notes: Scheuermann's disease is not suggested by anything in the stem, and the pain is not described with kyphotic deformity.
Scoliosis is usually painless, and there is no deformity described.
A malignant tumour would typically cause night or rest pain, systemic features or neurological signs, none of which are present.

items.stem: A 13-year-old boy has had several months of thoracic back pain only when standing or walking, with no rest or night pain and no other features. Which is the most likely cause?
items.why: Pain only with upright activity, with no rest pain or specific examination findings, fits mechanical overload. Malignancy would also cause rest or night pain.
notes: Scheuermann would need a fixed kyphosis on examination to suggest it.
Scoliosis is usually painless and diagnosed by a visible curve on examination.
A malignant tumour would also hurt at rest or at night.

items.stem: A 15-year-old girl in the emergency department, being observed after a faint at school, asks her junior doctor if she can send him a Facebook friend request. What is the best response?
options: Agree and accept, since his page has nothing inappropriate for a girl her age
Let her send it but restrict what she can see on his page, as she is vulnerable
Explain that professional boundaries must be kept and he will not accept the request
Tell her to send it but he will not accept it
items.why: Doctors should maintain professional boundaries with patients, particularly vulnerable adolescents, including on social media. The kind approach is to explain this openly and decline.
notes: Accepting blurs the doctor-patient boundary, whatever the page contains.
Partial access still creates a personal online relationship with a vulnerable minor.
Agreeing then ignoring the request is deceptive and may hurt the patient; be honest and explain.

items.stem: A 25-year-old man has severe neck and left eye pain while playing tennis. Next morning he has unsteady gait, left ptosis and anisocoria with the left pupil smaller. Visual acuity is preserved. Where is the lesion most likely located?
items.why: Ptosis with miosis is Horner syndrome from loss of sympathetic supply. Neck pain after exertion suggests carotid dissection affecting the sympathetic fibres at the superior cervical ganglion along the carotid sheath.
notes: Third nerve palsy causes ptosis with a dilated pupil and ophthalmoplegia.
Chiasmal lesions cause bitemporal visual field loss, not ptosis or anisocoria.
A cord lesion would give other neurological signs, and this picture fits a postganglionic lesion near the carotid.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman with weight loss, proximal muscle and joint aching and jaw pain presents with sudden painless loss of vision in one eye (hand movements) and a relative afferent pupillary defect. Which test should be requested first?
items.why: This is giant cell arteritis with anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. Inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) are requested first, and steroids are started without waiting for biopsy.
notes: Lumbar puncture has no role in suspected giant cell arteritis.
MRA is not the first test and would delay treatment.
Carotid ultrasound does not diagnose giant cell arteritis.

items.stem: A 20-year-old woman has a 15 cm solid-cystic ovarian mass on ultrasound. Histology shows teeth, hair, intestinal, squamous and bronchial epithelium, plus neuroectodermal and embryonic elements in several sections. What is the diagnosis?
items.why: Teratomas contain tissue from all three germ layers. Embryonic and neuroectodermal elements indicate immature tissue, so this is an immature teratoma rather than a mature cystic one.
notes: Not the best term; the picture is of immature teratoma, with embryonic tissue elements.
A mature cystic teratoma has only well-differentiated adult tissues, with no embryonic or immature neuroectodermal elements.
Dysgerminoma is a solid tumour of uniform germ cells, without multiple tissue types such as teeth and hair.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman is diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast. She has no family history of cancer. Which additional tumour studies have the greatest therapeutic implications?
options: Hormone receptors (oestrogen and progesterone) and HER2
Hormone receptors, E-cadherin and study of first-degree relatives
BRCA1/2 testing and study of first-degree relatives
items.why: Breast cancer classification and treatment depend on oestrogen/progesterone receptor and HER2 status (with proliferation index, Ki-67). These guide endocrine therapy and anti-HER2 treatment.
notes: Flow cytometry is used for haematological malignancies, not routine breast cancer work-up.
E-cadherin helps distinguish lobular from ductal histology but does not guide therapy here, and relatives need no study without a family history.
BRCA testing is not indicated without a suggestive family history or other criteria, and it does not guide routine management here.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has 3 months of anxiety, 6 kg weight loss, tachycardia and hyperreflexia, with no goitre. TSH is <0.01 mU/L, T4 is raised, thyroglobulin is low and a thyroid scan shows no uptake. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Exogenous thyroid hormone causes thyrotoxicosis without goitre, with suppressed TSH, absent scan uptake and, unlike other causes, low thyroglobulin.
notes: Graves' disease causes a diffuse goitre and high uptake, with raised thyroglobulin.
Struma ovarii gives absent neck uptake but thyroglobulin would be raised, and it is rare.
Subacute thyroiditis has low uptake but a painful tender thyroid and raised thyroglobulin.

items.stem: A patient in poor general condition has fever (axillary 39.5°C), bilateral submandibular swelling for six days, mouth pain and trismus. Which statement is correct?
options: The most likely diagnosis is floor of mouth carcinoma with bilateral nodal metastases
Ensuring nutrition is the therapeutic priority
Risk of airway obstruction must be treated as the priority
items.why: Fever, trismus and bilateral submandibular swelling suggest a deep neck space infection (e.g. Ludwig's angina), where airway obstruction is the immediate threat.
notes: Six days of fever and trismus point to infection, not carcinoma.
Nutrition is not the priority when the airway is at risk.
Mediastinitis is a possible complication but is not almost certain, and the airway comes first.

items.stem: An 87-year-old hypertensive woman, 48 hours after an anterior STEMI, becomes dyspnoeic. A new systolic murmur with a thrill is heard, radiating to the right sternal border. Which complication is most likely?
options: Heart failure due to extensive necrosis
items.why: A new harsh holosystolic murmur with a thrill radiating to the right sternal border days after MI, especially in elderly women, indicates post-infarct ventricular septal rupture.
notes: Heart failure alone would not produce a new murmur with a thrill.
Aneurysm forms later and typically causes persistent ST elevation, not an acute new murmur.
Free wall rupture usually causes tamponade, shock or sudden death rather than a murmur.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with a recent febrile illness and chest pain presents with dyspnoea and tachypnoea. He is hypotensive with raised JVP showing a prominent x descent, and has pulsus paradoxus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Preceding febrile pericarditis with effusion, now with hypotension, raised JVP with preserved x descent and pulsus paradoxus, is classic for cardiac tamponade.
notes: Dilated cardiomyopathy does not produce pulsus paradoxus or a prominent x descent.
Constrictive pericarditis has a prominent y descent, and pulsus paradoxus is uncommon.
Ischaemic heart disease would not explain the febrile prodrome, pulsus paradoxus and JVP pattern.

items.stem: A 78-year-old woman with dementia in aged care has severe abdominal pain, distension and clinical deterioration. She has leukocytosis, raised haematocrit, renal failure, metabolic acidosis and atrial fibrillation. CT shows oedematous small bowel loops with portal venous gas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Atrial fibrillation with severe abdominal pain, SIRS, acidosis and portal venous gas on CT indicates embolic mesenteric ischaemia until proven otherwise.
notes: Would expect NSAID use or ulcer-type pain history and free air (pneumoperitoneum) on imaging.
Would expect biliary colic or right upper quadrant pain, with aerobilia and dilated small bowel from gallstone ileus.
Would expect weight loss, altered bowel habit, pneumoperitoneum and peritonitis, possibly a palpable mass.

items.stem: A 78-year-old woman with dementia in residential care has severe abdominal pain, distension and deterioration. Bloods show leucocytosis, haemoconcentration, renal impairment and metabolic acidosis; ECG shows atrial fibrillation. CT shows oedematous small bowel loops with portal venous gas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Elderly patient with AF (embolic source), sudden abdominal pain, lactic acidosis, haemoconcentration and bowel wall oedema with portal venous gas indicates acute mesenteric ischaemia.
notes: Would show free intraperitoneal air and epigastric peritonitis, not small bowel oedema with portal gas.
Would not explain AF-related embolic picture or bowel ischaemic changes.
A sigmoid perforation would show a large bowel obstruction or free air or faecal contamination, not small bowel ischaemia.

items.stem: An 80-year-old woman presents with epigastric pain migrating to the left iliac fossa. CT shows sigmoid wall inflammation and a 2 cm mesenteric abscess. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Admission, nil by mouth and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics
Urgent sigmoidectomy with primary colorectal anastomosis
items.why: This is complicated diverticulitis with a small abscess (under 4–5 cm), which does not need drainage. Treat with bowel rest and intravenous antibiotics.
notes: A colostomy is not needed as there is no obstruction.
Surgical drainage is not indicated for a small abscess responding to antibiotics.
Urgent resection is not required without peritonitis or failure of conservative treatment.

items.stem: An 80-year-old woman presents with epigastric pain that migrated to the left iliac fossa. CT shows sigmoid wall inflammation and a 2 cm pericolic/mesenteric abscess. She is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Admission with bowel rest and intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics
Urgent sigmoidectomy with primary colorectal anastomosis
items.why: This is Hinchey I–II diverticulitis with a small abscess (<3 cm) in a stable patient, which is managed conservatively with IV antibiotics and bowel rest. Larger abscesses need CT-guided percutaneous drainage.
notes: Colostomy is not needed for localised, contained disease in a stable patient; surgery is reserved for failed conservative treatment or peritonitis.
Abscesses under 2–3 cm do not need drainage, and operative drainage risks spreading contents; larger abscesses are drained percutaneously under CT.
Urgent resection is reserved for generalised peritonitis (Hinchey III–IV), often as a Hartmann procedure if unstable.

items.stem: A 18-month-old boy presents with abdominal pain, jaundice and a palpable abdominal mass. Ultrasound shows a common bile duct cyst. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Percutaneous puncture and drainage to confirm bile content
Laparotomy and radical resection of the entire biliary tract with bowel replacement
Laparotomy for cyst drainage, removing the drain when the dilatation resolves
MRCP to delineate the anatomy, then cyst excision with biliary-enteric anastomosis
items.why: Choledochal cyst is congenital and needs definitive surgery: delineate the biliary anatomy with MRCP, then excise the cyst and reconstruct with a biliary-enteric anastomosis (Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy).
notes: Percutaneous puncture risks bile leak and does not treat the cyst, which has malignant potential.
Resecting the entire biliary tract is excessive and not indicated.
Drainage alone leaves the cyst in place with ongoing risk of cholangitis and malignancy.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man presents with rectal bleeding, tenesmus and narrowing of stool calibre. Sigmoid adenocarcinoma without distant metastases is diagnosed and resected. Which finding is a poor prognostic factor that should influence adjuvant chemotherapy planning?
options: Size of the primary lesion and histological differentiation
Tumour perforation or adherence to adjacent organs
items.why: Perforation or invasion of adjacent organs indicates T4 disease, which carries a much higher risk of recurrence and favours adjuvant chemotherapy.
notes: Anaemia at diagnosis is not the prognostic feature that drives adjuvant chemotherapy decisions here.
Family history affects screening and risk, not prognosis after resection.
Tumour size alone is not a key prognostic factor; depth of invasion (T stage) matters more.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man had a sigmoid adenocarcinoma without distant metastases resected and is referred to medical oncology to consider adjuvant chemotherapy. Which histopathological or operative finding is a poor prognostic factor to be considered?
options: Size of the primary lesion and histological differentiation
Tumour perforation or adherence to adjacent organs
items.why: Tumour perforation or obstruction and invasion of adjacent organs (T4 disease) are poor prognostic features. They determine stage and guide adjuvant chemotherapy.
notes: Anaemia is a presenting feature, not a recognised key factor for adjuvant decisions.
Family history affects risk and surveillance, not prognosis after resection.
Tumour size carries less weight than depth of invasion; differentiation matters but this option is less decisive.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man has Cushing disease due to a 22 mm pituitary macroadenoma. What is the first-line treatment?
options: Medical therapy first, with surgery only if this fails
Transsphenoidal selective resection of the adenoma
Pituitary radiotherapy to shrink the tumour
items.why: Selective transsphenoidal adenomectomy is always the first-line treatment of Cushing disease, even though recurrence is common. Drugs only reduce cortisol effects or ACTH release and are not curative.
notes: Drugs such as ketoconazole or metyrapone lower cortisol but are not curative; they are used as adjuncts or bridging therapy.
Adrenalectomy is a later option after failed pituitary surgery, and it risks Nelson syndrome with tumour growth.
Radiotherapy is slow and is used as adjuvant treatment when surgery is incomplete or fails.

items.stem: A 55-year-old obese woman with type 2 diabetes on metformin has an HbA1c of 64 mmol/mol (8%) and a history of recurrent urinary tract infections. Which add-on therapy is LEAST appropriate?
items.why: SGLT2 inhibitors cause glycosuria, and their commonest adverse effects are genitourinary tract infections (including genital candidiasis). With recurrent UTIs, they are the least suitable add-on.
notes: A DPP-4 inhibitor is weight neutral and does not raise the risk of urinary infection, so it is acceptable.
A GLP-1 receptor agonist helps weight loss and glycaemia and does not predispose to UTI, so it is appropriate.
Basal insulin lowers HbA1c effectively and has no excess UTI risk. It can cause weight gain and hypoglycaemia.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman has had secondary amenorrhoea for one year, with no iatrogenic cause. Serum oestradiol is low and prolactin is normal (12 µg/L). Which first-line test is most useful to identify the cause?
items.why: Low oestradiol with normal prolactin in a young woman should raise suspicion of premature ovarian insufficiency. Basal FSH is the first test and would be elevated in ovarian failure.
notes: MRI is for suspected central causes (e.g. prolactinoma) once gonadotropins are low or prolactin is raised.
Karyotype is used after premature ovarian insufficiency is confirmed by raised FSH, not as the first step.
hCG stimulation tests testicular Leydig cell function and is not used for amenorrhoea work-up.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has polyuria and polydipsia, with a 24-hour urine output of 8.2 L. Blood glucose is 5.3 mmol/L, sodium 148 mmol/L and plasma osmolality 309 mOsm/kg; urine osmolality is 89 mOsm/kg. What is the most appropriate next test?
options: Hypertonic saline infusion with serial antidiuretic hormone measurement
Desmopressin administration with serial urine osmolality monitoring
items.why: Normal glucose with high plasma osmolality and dilute urine confirms diabetes insipidus. Desmopressin then distinguishes central (urine concentrates) from nephrogenic (no response) disease.
notes: Reserved for equivocal cases; the plasma osmolality is already high, so diabetes insipidus is established.
Unnecessary and potentially unsafe here: the patient is already hypernatraemic and hyperosmolar with inappropriately dilute urine.
A single ADH level is unstable and hard to assay, and does not alone separate central from nephrogenic causes as well as the desmopressin response.

items.stem: A 73-year-old man has complete neurogenic dysphagia after a cardioembolic stroke in the left middle cerebral artery territory. He is expected to need enteral nutrition for several months. Which route of feeding is most appropriate?
items.why: For enteral feeding expected to last beyond about 4 to 6 weeks, a gastrostomy is the route of choice. Nasal tubes suit short-term feeding, and jejunostomy is reserved for when the gastric route cannot be used.
notes: Nasogastric tubes are for short-term feeding and are poorly tolerated long term.
Nasoduodenal tubes are also short-term and are used mainly when gastric feeding is not tolerated.
Jejunostomy is reserved for cases where the stomach cannot be used, such as gastric outlet problems or gastric surgery.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with confusion and dysphonia. She has a palpable neck mass and a serum calcium of 3.75 mmol/L (15 mg/dL; normal up to 2.55 mmol/L). Which diagnosis should be suspected?
items.why: A palpable neck mass with severe hypercalcaemia (above about 3.2 mmol/L) and dysphonia from local infiltration suggests parathyroid carcinoma.
notes: Medullary thyroid carcinoma does not cause hypercalcaemia.
MEN 1 would need other features such as pituitary, pancreatic or duodenal tumours.
Adenomas are usually small and impalpable, with milder hypercalcaemia and no local invasion.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man with recurrent UTIs, on cefuroxime for a week, presents febrile, tachycardic and hypotensive (90/60). Urine shows pyuria, nitrite negative; chest X-ray is clear. Urine and blood cultures grow Gram-positive cocci in chains. What is the best empirical change pending identification?
options: Continue cefuroxime until the antibiogram is available
Change to ertapenem for presumed multiresistant organisms
Change to therapy covering Enterococcus, e.g. ampicillin plus gentamicin
Change to imipenem for presumed MRSA
items.why: Gram-positive cocci in chains with a nitrite-negative urinary source suggest Enterococcus, which lacks nitrate reductase and is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins. Empirical therapy must cover Enterococcus.
notes: Enterococci are intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins, and he is worsening on cefuroxime.
Ertapenem has poor activity against Enterococcus.
Staphylococci form clusters, not chains, and imipenem is not an anti-MRSA agent.

items.stem: A 10-year-old girl is seen for a check-up. She is asymptomatic, with normal examination, growth and BP. Urinalysis shows blood 2+, no protein, and 5–10 red cells per high-power field on sediment. What is the most appropriate next step?
items.why: Isolated asymptomatic microscopic haematuria without proteinuria or hypertension is often benign or transient. Confirm persistence with repeat urine microscopy before any investigation.
notes: Renal function is not indicated before persistence is confirmed; there is no proteinuria or hypertension.
Cystoscopy is rarely needed in children with isolated microscopic haematuria.
Autoimmune screening is not indicated without systemic features or proteinuria.

items.stem: A 65-year-old woman, 30 days after haematopoietic stem cell transplant and severely neutropenic, has fever, cough, haemoptysis and exertional dyspnoea despite 5 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics. Chest X-ray shows multiple ill-defined nodules, some cavitating. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Prolonged severe neutropenia after stem cell transplant with fever unresponsive to antibiotics, haemoptysis and cavitating nodules is the classic picture of invasive Aspergillus infection.
notes: Septic emboli would suggest endocarditis or a septic focus, which is not described here.
S. aureus pneumonia is unlikely after failure of prior antibiotic therapy, and it would not typically present like this.
Systemic candidiasis rarely causes cavitating pulmonary nodules with haemoptysis.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man returns from Equatorial Guinea without antimalarial prophylaxis with fever, reduced consciousness, creatinine 3.4 mg/dL (300 micromol/L), raised transaminases and P. falciparum parasitaemia of 6%. Which treatment should be started now?
items.why: This is severe falciparum malaria (cerebral features, renal impairment, hyperparasitaemia). IV artesunate is the treatment of choice and should start immediately.
notes: Oral therapy is inappropriate for severe malaria with impaired consciousness.
Doxycycline is used as an adjunct or prophylaxis, not alone for severe malaria.
Oral quinine is not suitable for severe malaria; IV artesunate is preferred.

items.stem: An 85-year-old man with a peripheral intravenous cannula develops rigors and fever one week after admission for a stroke. Blood cultures grow Gram-positive cocci in clusters. Pending susceptibility results, what is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic?
items.why: Hospital-acquired staphylococcal line infections are often methicillin-resistant (MRSA or coagulase-negative staphylococci), so empirical vancomycin is the standard choice until susceptibilities return.
notes: Cefazolin is a beta-lactam that is inactive against methicillin-resistant staphylococci, which are common in hospital-acquired line infections.
Flucloxacillin is inactive against methicillin-resistant staphylococci, so it is unsafe as empirical therapy here.
Linezolid has little clinical data supporting its use for systemic catheter-related bloodstream infection, so it is not the empirical choice.

items.stem: A 38-year-old veterinarian who assists with livestock births develops high fever, chills, headache, myalgia, dry cough and chest pain. Chest X-ray shows bilateral lower-zone infiltrates and Q fever pneumonia is diagnosed. Which statement about acute disease is TRUE?
options: It is transmitted mainly by ticks
Both doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine are standard treatment for acute disease
Acute disease typically shows predominant antibodies against phase I antigens
Mortality in acute disease is very low
items.why: Acute Q fever (Coxiella burnetii) has very low mortality. Higher mortality and phase I antibody predominance belong to chronic Q fever.
notes: Transmission is mainly by inhaled aerosols from infected animal birth products, not ticks.
Doxycycline alone treats acute disease; adding hydroxychloroquine is for chronic Q fever such as endocarditis.
Raised phase I antibodies characterise chronic Q fever; acute disease shows predominant phase II antibodies.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has a 48-hour history of productive cough, right pleuritic pain and fever. SpO2 is 88% and there are right basal crackles; chest X-ray shows right basal consolidation. He has well-controlled HIV (CD4 550 cells/µL, undetectable viral load). Which empirical therapy is most appropriate?
options: Ceftriaxone 2 g and azithromycin 500 mg, each every 24 hours
Ceftriaxone, azithromycin and high-dose co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim 5 mg/kg 8-hourly)
items.why: With CD4 above 500 and an undetectable viral load, this is most likely community-acquired bacterial pneumonia, usually pneumococcal. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin covers pneumococcus and atypicals; Pneumocystis cover is not needed.
notes: Pneumocystis jirovecii is unlikely with CD4 above 500 and suppressed viral load, so co-trimoxazole is not needed.
Steroids and co-trimoxazole are for suspected moderate-severe Pneumocystis pneumonia, which is unlikely here.
Too broad; reserved for hospital-acquired pneumonia with resistant organisms such as Pseudomonas, which is uncommon here.

items.stem: A 38-year-old veterinarian who assists with livestock births develops high fever, rigors, headache, myalgia, dry cough and chest pain. Chest X-ray shows bilateral lower-zone infiltrates, and serology shows raised phase II antibodies (Q fever, Coxiella burnetii). Which statement is TRUE?
options: Ticks are the usual route of transmission to humans.
Doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine are both used to treat acute disease.
Acute infection typically shows high phase I antibody titres.
Mortality from acute infection is very low.
items.why: Acute Q fever, usually acquired by inhaling aerosols from birth products, is mostly self-limiting or treated with doxycycline. Mortality is very low (about 1–2%). Chronic disease causes most of the morbidity.
notes: Transmission is mainly by inhaling aerosols from infected animals' birth products, milk or dust; ticks are an uncommon route.
Doxycycline alone treats acute disease; hydroxychloroquine is added for chronic Q fever such as endocarditis.
Phase II antibodies predominate in acute infection; high phase I titres suggest chronic Q fever.

items.stem: A 28-day-old term, breastfed infant has had 8 days of vomiting, now projectile after every feed, and is always hungry. The abdomen is soft. Gas: pH 7.49, HCO3 30 mmol/L, pCO2 53 mmHg, K 3.1, Cl 94 mmol/L. Which investigation best confirms the likely diagnosis?
items.why: This is classic hypertrophic pyloric stenosis with hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Abdominal ultrasound confirms it by showing a thickened, elongated pyloric muscle.
notes: A plain film is non-specific and does not confirm pyloric stenosis.
pH monitoring assesses reflux, which does not cause projectile vomiting with this alkalosis.
Sweat chloride tests for cystic fibrosis, which is not the picture here.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has had 2 weeks of lower abdominal pain, worse after recent intercourse. She has a new partner and inconsistent condom use. Temp 38.6°C, WCC 16 ×10⁹/L, CRP 30 mg/L, abundant abnormal discharge and cervical motion tenderness. Which management statement is INCORRECT?
options: Start antibiotics as soon as the diagnosis is suspected.
Hysterosalpingography is the preferred initial test to assess the tubes.
Delayed diagnosis and treatment increases the risk of sequelae.
A tubo-ovarian abscess is an indication for hospital admission.
items.why: This is pelvic inflammatory disease. Hysterosalpingography is contraindicated in acute infection because it can spread infection into the pelvis and abdominal cavity.
notes: Empirical treatment should start promptly on clinical suspicion, as delay worsens outcomes.
Delay is a well-established risk factor for tubal damage, infertility and ectopic pregnancy.
Abscess is a recognised criterion for admission, often with IV antibiotics and possible drainage.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with recurrent postcoital bleeding. Cytology shows a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. Colposcopy-directed biopsy of a mosaic area shows a 2 mm focus of invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Repeat a more extensive punch biopsy
