items.why: A lesion with minimal invasion (<3 mm deep) needs excision of the whole transformation zone to confirm depth, margins and lymphovascular space invasion. Conisation is both diagnostic and, if margins are clear, therapeutic.
notes: Hysterectomy is overtreatment before an excision specimen confirms depth, margins and LVSI; it is considered only if excision shows adverse features or fertility is not wanted.
Radiotherapy is reserved for more advanced disease or patients unfit for surgery, not for microinvasive disease.
A further punch biopsy cannot reliably assess depth or margins; a diagnostic excision is required.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman has had a wide local excision and sentinel node biopsy for right breast cancer: grade 3 invasive ductal carcinoma, 2.2 cm, ER and PR positive, HER2 negative, Ki67 25%, one macroscopically involved sentinel node (pN1). Which adjuvant systemic treatment is most appropriate?
options: Endocrine therapy with an aromatase inhibitor alone
Anthracycline and taxane chemotherapy, followed by endocrine therapy
Chemotherapy plus trastuzumab, followed by endocrine therapy
Anthracycline and taxane chemotherapy alone, without endocrine therapy
items.why: This is luminal B-type disease (hormone receptor positive, grade 3, high Ki67, node positive), so chemotherapy is indicated because of high grade and proliferation. Endocrine therapy then follows because the tumour is receptor positive.
notes: Endocrine therapy alone undertreats a high-grade, highly proliferative, node-positive luminal B tumour that warrants chemotherapy.
Trastuzumab is only for HER2-positive disease, and this tumour is HER2 negative.
Omitting endocrine therapy is wrong: the tumour is ER/PR positive, so endocrine therapy is needed after chemotherapy.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman, G2P2, has had heavy menstrual bleeding for a year. Ultrasound shows a stable 2 cm subserosal fibroid and endometrial biopsy is normal. Haemoglobin is 100 g/L despite oral iron, and bleeding persists on tranexamic acid and mefenamic acid. What is the most appropriate next treatment?
items.why: Levonorgestrel IUD is first-line when medical non-hormonal therapy fails in heavy menstrual bleeding without significant cavity distortion; it is less invasive than surgery and also provides contraception.
notes: Hysterectomy is definitive but invasive, reserved for failure of less invasive options.
COCP is an option but is less suitable at 45 and less effective than the LNG-IUD.
Ablation is a second-line option after less invasive therapy.

items.stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department with macroscopic haematuria. Which urinalysis finding would best support a glomerular cause?
options: Dysmorphic red blood cells and/or red cell casts
Proteinuria of 1 g/day with a negative dipstick and albuminuria above 300 mg/24 hours
Clots visible to the naked eye
items.why: Glomerular bleeding is characterised by dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts in the urinary sediment.
notes: Isolated microalbuminuria is not the typical glomerulonephritis pattern, and this description is internally inconsistent with a negative dipstick.
Haematuria with sterile pyuria is not characteristic of glomerulonephritis.
Clots suggest lower urinary tract bleeding, not glomerular disease.

items.stem: A 25-year-old man has had foamy, dark urine for 2 months. Urine: haematuria ++, protein ++, proteinuria 1.5 g/24 h. Creatinine 141 µmol/L, urea 13 mmol/L. Anti-dsDNA, ANCA, anti-GBM and RF negative; C3 0.2 g/L (low), C4 0.1 g/L (low). Which biopsy finding is most likely?
items.why: Low C3 and C4 with a nephritic-nephrotic picture point to membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. Of the options listed, only it typically causes hypocomplementaemia.
notes: Membranous nephropathy presents with nephrotic syndrome and normal complement levels.
Minimal change disease causes nephrotic syndrome with normal complement and a bland sediment.
IgA nephropathy has normal complement levels.

items.stem: A 59-year-old woman presents with new seizures, left pyramidal signs and papilloedema. MRI shows a right hemispheric mass with oedema, midline shift and signs of tentorial herniation. Which feature of her week-long progressive headache is most likely?
items.why: A mass lesion with raised intracranial pressure causes headache that is worse in the morning, as ICP rises overnight when lying flat. It is also worsened by coughing, straining or bending.
notes: Headache from raised ICP typically worsens with exertion, coughing and straining.
Photophobia is characteristic of migraine, not raised ICP.
Phonophobia is characteristic of migraine, not raised ICP.

items.stem: A 13-year-old boy has subacute headache and diplopia. He has vertical gaze palsy (Parinaud syndrome). MRI shows a contrast-enhancing pineal region lesion obstructing the aqueduct of Sylvius. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Germ cell tumours are the commonest pineal region tumours in children. They enhance homogeneously and cause obstructive hydrocephalus and Parinaud syndrome.
notes: Glioblastoma usually occurs in adults, in the cerebral lobes, not the pineal region.
Medulloblastoma is the commonest malignant posterior fossa tumour in children (vermis, roof of fourth ventricle) but is rare in the pineal region.
Meningiomas are rare in children and rare in the pineal region.

items.stem: A 9-year-old asymptomatic boy with an innocent murmur has an ECG showing Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern. Which statement about his management is INCORRECT?
options: He requires treatment for heart failure
He may present with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
Holter monitoring and exercise testing are appropriate
Radiofrequency ablation of the accessory pathway is appropriate in selected patients
items.why: He is asymptomatic, so heart failure treatment is not indicated. Heart failure is a rare complication of WPW, not a usual presentation.
notes: True: accessory pathways predispose to re-entrant supraventricular tachycardia.
True: these help risk-stratify the pathway's conduction properties.
True: ablation is a therapeutic option in selected patients, such as those with symptoms or high-risk pathways.

items.stem: A man has loss of pain and temperature sensation in the left leg, loss of vibration and position sense in the right leg, and right distal leg weakness with an extensor right plantar response. Which syndrome best explains this?
items.why: This is a right hemicord lesion (Brown-Séquard): ipsilateral weakness, upper motor neuron signs and loss of dorsal column function, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature below the lesion.
notes: Central cord syndrome causes a suspended, bilateral dissociated sensory loss in the arms, not a unilateral pattern like this.
A complete transverse lesion would cause bilateral loss of all modalities and motor function below the level.
A lateral medullary lesion affects the face and body with brainstem signs, not a crossed pattern limited to one leg.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man has sudden severe pain down the back of his right leg to the foot. Straight leg raise is positive at 10°. He has weak right plantar flexion, reduced sensation on the lateral border of the foot and an absent right ankle jerk. Lumbar X-ray is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Weak plantar flexion, lateral foot sensory loss and an absent ankle jerk indicate S1 radiculopathy, typically from posterolateral L5/S1 disc herniation.
notes: An L1/L2 herniation would affect the L2 root, not cause this S1 picture.
Cauda equina syndrome would cause more widespread features (bilateral signs, saddle anaesthesia, sphincter dysfunction), not isolated S1 involvement.
L4/L5 herniation affects the L5 root, causing foot dorsiflexion weakness rather than loss of the ankle jerk.

items.stem: A woman has a seizure with an epigastric aura, an unpleasant smell, loss of awareness, oral automatisms (sucking, swallowing), repetitive hand opening and closing, and postictal amnesia. What is the most likely seizure type?
options: Generalised non-convulsive seizure or typical absence
Focal impaired-awareness seizure of temporal lobe origin
items.why: An epigastric rising aura, olfactory hallucination, impaired awareness, oral automatisms and postictal amnesia are characteristic of a temporal lobe focal impaired-awareness (complex partial) seizure.
notes: Typical absence seizures are brief, lack an aura and have no prolonged postictal state.
Epilepsia partialis continua is continuous focal motor jerking with preserved awareness.
Atonic seizures cause sudden loss of tone and falls, not aura and automatisms.

items.stem: A 25-year-old man presents with tremor. Examination shows dysarthria and dystonia. There is a family history of psychiatric illness and movement disorders. Which investigation is most useful to confirm the likely diagnosis?
items.why: Tremor, dystonia and dysarthria in a young adult with psychiatric features suggests Wilson disease. Copper studies (raised 24-hour urinary copper, with low ceruloplasmin) support the diagnosis.
notes: DaTscan assesses presynaptic dopaminergic loss as in Parkinson disease; juvenile parkinsonism is unlikely here.
Nerve conduction studies assess peripheral neuropathy, which does not explain this picture.
An EEG would be used for epilepsy, which is not suggested.

items.stem: A 65-year-old woman has right hand weakness that over months spread to both arms and legs, distal predominant. There is atrophy and fasciculations in multiple myotomes, preserved sensation and bilateral Babinski signs. Which test best confirms the suspected diagnosis?
items.why: Mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs with preserved sensation suggest motor neurone disease (ALS). EMG showing widespread denervation supports the diagnosis.
notes: Imaging helps exclude mimics but cannot confirm the diagnosis.
MRI helps exclude structural mimics such as cervical myelopathy but does not confirm ALS.
Evoked potentials assess sensory and motor pathway conduction and do not confirm ALS.

items.stem: A 70-year-old hypertensive man develops sudden right hemiplegia with mild dysarthria. Language expression and comprehension are intact. Which type of stroke is most likely?
options: Left frontotemporal cortico-subcortical infarction in the middle cerebral artery territory
items.why: Pure motor hemiparesis with mild dysarthria and no cortical signs (aphasia) in a hypertensive patient is the classic pure motor lacunar infarction, typically in the internal capsule.
notes: A cortical MCA infarct would cause aphasia and a more extensive, florid deficit.
Brainstem infarction would give a more extensive picture, usually with cranial nerve signs or crossed deficits.
A haemorrhage would usually produce a more extensive picture with headache and reduced consciousness, not a pure motor deficit.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man with diabetes and asthma has bilateral primary open-angle glaucoma. His intraocular pressure is 34 mmHg in the right eye and 31 mmHg in the left. Which class of topical agent is the most appropriate first-line choice?
items.why: Prostaglandin analogues lower intraocular pressure the most and are dosed once daily, so they are first-line. Beta-blockers are contraindicated in asthma.
notes: These lower pressure less, so they are not first-line when a large reduction is needed.
Topical beta-blockers can cause bronchospasm and are avoided in asthma.
These lower pressure less than prostaglandin analogues and are second-line or adjunctive.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man had a superficial parotidectomy for a right pleomorphic adenoma 6 months ago. He now has preauricular sweating, flushing and pain of the skin while chewing. What is the treatment of choice?
options: Extended total parotidectomy for suspected tumour recurrence
items.why: This is Frey syndrome: aberrant reinnervation after auriculotemporal nerve injury causes gustatory sweating and erythema. Intradermal botulinum toxin is the treatment.
notes: Symptoms are not from recurrence; re-operating is not indicated for Frey syndrome.
Pregabalin treats neuropathic pain, not the underlying gustatory sweating.
There is no infection; antibiotics have no role.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man had a superficial parotidectomy for a right pleomorphic adenoma 6 months ago. He now has preauricular sweating and skin flushing during chewing. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Extended total parotidectomy for suspected recurrence
items.why: This is Frey syndrome (gustatory sweating), from aberrant reinnervation after auriculotemporal nerve injury during parotid surgery. Intradermal botulinum toxin gives good results.
notes: Recurrence would present as a mass, not gustatory sweating and flushing.
Pregabalin treats neuropathic pain and does not address aberrant autonomic sweating.
There is no infection; the symptoms are autonomic, so antibiotics have no role.

items.stem: A 1-year-old boy is asymptomatic with a normal examination, negative tuberculin skin test and normal chest X-ray. His mother has just been diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis and has started appropriate treatment. What is the most appropriate management for the child?
options: Separate him from his mother until her treatment is complete.
Isoniazid for 6–9 months, with repeat test and X-ray at the end.
Isoniazid until the mother's sputum smear is negative.
Isoniazid for 8–12 weeks, then repeat the test; stop if negative, X-ray if positive.
items.why: A young child exposed to infectious TB with a negative test needs window-period prophylaxis for 8–12 weeks, then repeat testing. If still negative, stop; if positive, do a chest X-ray to assess for disease.
notes: Separation is not required for the whole course; the mother is much less infectious after the first 2–4 weeks of treatment.
The long course is for latent infection once confirmed, not for the window period.
Duration is fixed by the window period, not by the mother's smear conversion.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman with insulin-treated diabetes has had several weeks of right shoulder pain, worse at night, with no trauma. Examination shows both active and passive limitation of all shoulder movements. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Malignant tumour of the proximal humerus
items.why: Middle-aged woman with diabetes, insidious shoulder pain worse at night and global loss of active and passive movement is typical of adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder).
notes: Less likely without bone pain, systemic features or a mass, and it would not usually restrict all movement globally.
Would present with fever, a hot swollen joint and severe pain, not weeks of gradual stiffness.
Causes localised pain at the top of the shoulder, not global restriction of passive movement.

items.stem: A 59-year-old woman has new seizures, left pyramidal signs, papilloedema and a week of progressive headache. MRI shows a right hemispheric mass with oedema, midline shift and tentorial herniation. Which headache feature is most likely?
items.why: Headache from raised intracranial pressure is typically worse in the morning, and worse with Valsalva manoeuvres and bending forward.
notes: Headache from raised ICP typically worsens with exertion, Valsalva and bending down.
Photophobia is typical of migraine, not of raised ICP headache.
Phonophobia is typical of migraine, not of raised ICP headache.

items.stem: A 13-year-old boy has subacute headache and diplopia. Examination shows vertical gaze palsy, and MRI shows a contrast-enhancing pineal region lesion obstructing the cerebral aqueduct. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Vertical gaze palsy from midbrain compression and hydrocephalus point to a pineal region mass. Germ cell tumours are the most frequent tumours there, especially in adolescent boys.
notes: Glioblastoma is rare in this age group and not typical of the pineal region.
Medulloblastoma arises in the posterior fossa (cerebellum), not the pineal region.
Meningioma is uncommon in children and rarely arises in the pineal region.

items.stem: A woman with hypotension and tissue hypoperfusion has pulmonary artery catheter readings: cardiac index 1.4 L/min/m², pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 25 mmHg and systemic vascular resistance 2000 dyn·s/cm⁵. What type of shock is this?
items.why: Low cardiac index with raised wedge pressure and raised SVR (normal about 800–1200) indicates pump failure with compensatory vasoconstriction: cardiogenic shock.
notes: Septic shock is distributive: high or normal cardiac output with low SVR.
Hypovolaemic shock has a low wedge pressure (low preload), not a raised one.
Anaphylactic shock is distributive, with low SVR and typically low wedge pressure.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man presents three weeks after an ankle injury with dyspnoea, syncope and hypotension (BP 80/40 mmHg). He is intubated and started on noradrenaline. Echocardiography shows pulmonary hypertension, and CT pulmonary angiography shows bilateral central filling defects. Which treatment gives the most rapid haemodynamic improvement?
options: Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg intravenously
items.why: This is high-risk (massive) pulmonary embolism with shock. With no contraindication, systemic thrombolysis is rapid to give and acts quickly.
notes: Heparin alone is for haemodynamically stable patients and does not lyse clot quickly.
Surgical embolectomy or thromboendarterectomy is reserved for patients with contraindications to thrombolysis, in experienced centres.
A vena cava filter is for patients with contraindication to anticoagulation and does not improve haemodynamics acutely.

items.stem: An 11½-year-old premenarchal girl with idiopathic scoliosis has a thoracolumbar curve that has progressed from 18° to 28° (Cobb) in 6 months. Risser grade is 2. Which treatment is most appropriate to halt progression?
items.why: In a skeletally immature adolescent with a progressing curve of about 20–40°, bracing is used to prevent progression. Surgery is reserved for larger curves, typically over 40–50°.
notes: Exercise does not alter curve progression.
Postural exercises do not prevent progression of a structural curve.
Fusion is for larger curves (over about 40–50°), not a 28° curve.

items.stem: A woman has difficulty walking after gynaecological surgery. She has mild thigh pain and her leg gives way on weight-bearing. Examination shows weak hip flexion and knee extension, and altered sensation over the anterior thigh. Which nerve is most likely injured?
items.why: The femoral nerve can be injured in pelvic or lower abdominal surgery. It supplies iliopsoas and quadriceps (hip flexion, knee extension) and anterior thigh sensation.
notes: This nerve is purely sensory (lateral thigh), so it would not cause motor weakness.
The obturator nerve supplies the adductors and medial thigh, not knee extension or anterior thigh sensation.
Sciatic injury affects knee flexion and structures below the knee, not knee extension or the anterior thigh.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man has had non-radiating lumbar pain for 1 week, progressively worsening, with marked limitation of spinal movement and fever. Lumbar spine X-ray is normal. Which diagnosis should be excluded first, and with which investigation?
options: Bone metastases, with technetium bone scan
Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis, with thoracolumbar X-ray
items.why: Fever, acute progressive back pain and marked spinal stiffness suggest pyogenic spondylodiscitis. MRI is the investigation of choice (sensitivity about 90%) and allows early diagnosis when plain X-ray is normal.
notes: A crush fracture would be visible on plain X-ray, and there is no history of trauma or fever explanation.
Nothing in the history suggests metastases (no cancer history, weight loss), and fever with acute course favours infection.
DISH would be visible on plain X-ray and does not explain fever and acute pain.

items.stem: A 93-year-old woman with COPD, hypertension, AF and ischaemic heart disease (EF 53%, stable) falls and has a painful, shortened, externally rotated right leg, consistent with hip fracture. What is the best management?
options: Admit for echocardiogram and cardiology review, then plate-and-screw fixation
Admit for nephrology and cardiology review, then surgeon chooses arthroplasty or nail
Medical admission with comorbidity stabilisation and non-operative management
Surgical fixation within 48 hours with early analgesia and orthogeriatric co-management
items.why: Hip fracture surgery should occur within 48 hours, ideally sooner, once medically optimised; delay increases mortality. Her comorbidities are stable, so orthogeriatric co-management and early surgery are appropriate.
notes: Routine investigations and consultations delay surgery without clear benefit.
Specialty reviews should not delay surgery in stable patients.
Non-operative management carries high mortality and morbidity.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy has a painful 3 cm boggy scalp swelling in the right occipital area with overlying hair loss and three firm tender posterior cervical lymph nodes. Which treatment is most appropriate?
items.why: This is a kerion, an inflammatory tinea capitis with cervical lymphadenopathy. It needs systemic oral antifungal therapy (terbinafine or griseofulvin) because topical agents do not penetrate the hair follicle.
notes: Kerion is not a bacterial abscess; drainage is not needed and does not treat the fungal infection.
Antibiotics are not indicated unless there is proven secondary bacterial infection; this is a fungal process.
Topical antifungals alone do not reach the hair follicle and are inadequate for tinea capitis.

items.stem: A 73-year-old obese woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension and dyslipidaemia has had severe right knee pain for 5 days, without trauma. The knee is swollen with mild varus deformity and painful limited movement. X-ray shows osteophytes and mild medial joint space narrowing. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Education, relative rest, weight and exercise advice, and simple analgesia
Urgent referral for total knee replacement
Urgent MRI for meniscal tear, Baker cyst or tendinitis
items.why: This is an acute pain flare of knee osteoarthritis. Initial management is conservative: explain the diagnosis, relative rest, analgesia and lifestyle measures.
notes: Arthroplasty is not a first-line option; conservative measures come first.
Debridement would be considered for suspected septic arthritis, which is not suggested here (no fever or systemic features).
Degenerative meniscal change is expected in osteoarthritis, and tendinitis is a clinical diagnosis; MRI is not needed initially.

items.stem: A 7-year-old boy falls from a swing onto his outstretched right hand. He has a dinner-fork deformity of the wrist, pain and loss of function, with normal distal neurovascular status. Which injury would you expect on X-ray?
options: Greenstick fracture of the ulnar shaft
items.why: A dinner-fork deformity with pain at the wrist after a fall on an outstretched hand in a child points to a distal radius injury, here a physeal injury (epiphyseal separation). An associated ulnar fracture is possible, but the main lesion is radial.
notes: Monteggia involves proximal ulna fracture with radial head dislocation at the elbow, not the wrist.
A radial head fracture causes elbow pain, not wrist deformity.
An ulnar shaft greenstick fracture would not explain the dinner-fork wrist deformity, which is a distal radius injury.

items.stem: A 65-year-old obese woman falls onto her outstretched hand with the elbow extended. She has arm pain and swelling, and cannot extend her wrist or fingers. Which injury is most likely?
options: Humeral shaft fracture with both-bone forearm fracture
Humeral shaft fracture with radial nerve injury
items.why: Arm pain and swelling with inability to extend the wrist and fingers (wrist drop) indicates a humeral shaft fracture with radial nerve injury. The radial nerve is involved in about 10–18% of these fractures.
notes: This would cause shoulder findings and does not explain the loss of wrist and finger extension.
An elbow dislocation would localise to the elbow and does not explain the radial nerve deficit.
Nothing suggests a forearm fracture, and the finger extension deficit is not explained by this.

items.stem: A 74-year-old patient has 2 months of low back pain radiating to both legs, neurogenic claudication and pain on extending the trunk. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Back and leg pain with neurogenic claudication in an older patient, eased by flexion and worsened by extension, is typical of lumbar spinal canal stenosis. Flexion widens the canal.
notes: Disc herniation causes unilateral radicular pain, usually in younger patients, and is not classically relieved by flexion with claudication.
A fracture would follow trauma or osteoporosis with acute focal pain, not progressive claudication.
Instability causes mechanical back pain; it does not typically cause claudication relieved by flexion.

items.stem: A 70-year-old diabetic, hypertensive woman had an open mid-distal tibial fracture treated with debridement and an intramedullary nail. At 11 months she has an atrophic nonunion with purulent discharge at the wound. What is the best immediate management?
options: Triple antibiotics and wound cleaning, removing distal locking screws to promote union
Expectant management with oral quinolone antibiotics
Autologous bone graft and growth factors (BMP-2/7) to stimulate union
Remove the nail, debride, apply an external fixator, and give culture-directed antibiotics
items.why: This is implant-associated infection with nonunion, managed like chronic osteomyelitis. Remove all hardware, debride aggressively, stabilise with an external fixator, and give prolonged culture-directed antibiotics. Reconstruction comes after infection is cured.
notes: Dynamisation has no proven benefit in established nonunion and leaves the infected nail in place.
Antibiotics alone are only for patients too comorbid for surgery; the infected implant must be removed.
Grafting and BMPs are considered only after infection is eradicated, not in the presence of active infection.

items.stem: A 46-year-old man with bipolar disorder presents after a lithium carbonate overdose with severe tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, myoclonus and fasciculations. Serum lithium is 4.1 mmol/L. Which treatment is most indicated?
items.why: Severe lithium toxicity with neurological signs and a very high level requires urgent haemodialysis, as lithium is small, water-soluble and not protein-bound.
notes: Aminophylline and cathartics have no role in removing lithium.
Activated charcoal does not bind lithium and is not indicated.
Forced diuresis is not effective or recommended; it risks fluid overload and electrolyte disturbance.

items.stem: A 58-year-old hypertensive man has exertional syncope while jogging. BP is 135/65 mmHg. There is a loud systolic murmur that decreases with Valsalva, and a soft second heart sound. ECG shows sinus rhythm, LV hypertrophy and anterior T-wave inversion. Which statement is correct?
options: This is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with severe LV outflow tract obstruction
Aortic dissection should be excluded with CT angiography
items.why: Exertional syncope, LV hypertrophy, a soft second sound and a systolic murmur that decreases with Valsalva indicate severe aortic stenosis. The HCM murmur increases with Valsalva.
notes: PE would not give a systolic murmur and LVH with strain; the ECG and murmur point to a valve lesion.
An HCM outflow murmur increases with Valsalva, whereas this one decreases.
Dissection would present with tearing pain and BP differences, none of which are described.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man is admitted with severe blunt chest trauma and multiple rib fractures. He initially improves with analgesia and oxygen, then develops severe hypoxaemia. What is the most likely cause of this deterioration?
options: Chest wall instability from multiple rib fractures
Impaired gas exchange from pulmonary contusion
items.why: Pulmonary contusion is the thoracic injury that causes hypoxaemia earliest and carries the worst prognosis. Blood–alveolar fluid fills the lung and causes V/Q mismatch and shunt.
notes: An unstable chest wall causes progressive hypoventilation and atelectasis, so hypercapnia and later hypoxaemia. It is less immediate than contusion.
Aspiration occurs later and only with reduced consciousness or airway events, not in all chest trauma.
Hypovolaemia (e.g. haemothorax) would appear early with haemodynamic instability, not primarily as isolated severe hypoxaemia.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man arrives after a motor vehicle crash. GCS 15, BP 140/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 35/min, heart rate 110/min, SpO2 91% on air. There is reduced air entry and hyperresonance to percussion over the right hemithorax. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Reduced breath sounds with hyperresonance to percussion indicates pneumothorax, here with marked respiratory distress. Dullness would instead suggest haemothorax.
notes: Tamponade presents with muffled heart sounds, raised JVP and hypotension, not unilateral hyperresonance.
Haemothorax gives reduced air entry with dullness to percussion, not hyperresonance.
Contusion does not cause hyperresonance and unilateral absent air entry.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man has had fever 38.7°C, cough, purulent sputum and dyspnoea for 48 hours. BP 85/60 mmHg, HR 100, RR 35, SpO2 80%, and he is confused. There are crackles at the left base, and chest X-ray shows left lingular and lower lobe pneumonia. What is the most appropriate place of care?
items.why: He scores at least 4 on CURB-65 (confusion, RR, low BP, age) even without urea, and has hypotension and severe hypoxaemia. This is severe pneumonia needing ICU care.
notes: Far too unsafe: he has multiple severe features.
An observation unit cannot provide the organ support he is likely to need.
A ward is suited to moderate severity, not hypotension with severe hypoxaemia.

items.stem: A 10-year-old boy vomited since yesterday and was given an antiemetic syrup (metoclopramide) at home. For 2 hours he has had painful involuntary turning of the neck to the right. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Delay treatment until an EEG is done in coming days
Delay treatment until CSF culture results are available
Start intravenous antibiotics after a throat swab
items.why: This is acute dystonia (torticollis) from metoclopramide, common in children. It is treated with an anticholinergic such as benztropine, given intravenously or intramuscularly.
notes: An EEG is irrelevant; this is a drug-induced movement disorder needing prompt treatment, not a seizure.
There is no suggestion of meningitis, and waiting days for culture would leave the dystonia untreated.
Nothing suggests bacterial infection such as pharyngitis; the dystonia follows a dopamine-antagonist antiemetic.

items.stem: A man is brought from an enclosed-space fire involving burning polyurethane foam. He is conscious but increasingly drowsy, with headache and severe dyspnoea. SpO2 is 92% and lactate is 8 mmol/L. Which specific treatment is most appropriate?
items.why: Burning polyurethane releases cyanide, suggested by altered mentation and marked lactic acidosis. Give high-flow oxygen plus the antidote hydroxocobalamin.
notes: Oxygen should be given at FiO2 1.0, not 50%, and it is not the specific antidote.
Hyperbaric therapy would be considered only for coexisting carbon monoxide poisoning.
This rate is inadequate; if shock were present, rapid fluid boluses would be used, and fluids are not the specific treatment.

items.stem: An 18-year-old cyclist hit by a car arrives at the emergency department. Heart rate is 115/min, blood pressure 110/75 mmHg, radial pulse palpable, capillary refill 2.5 seconds and respiratory rate 25/min. What do these findings indicate?
options: Loss of 15–30% of blood volume, requiring volume replacement
Loss of more than 30% of blood volume, requiring volume and blood replacement
Loss of more than 40% of blood volume, requiring surgical treatment
Loss of more than 50% of blood volume, requiring volume and blood replacement
items.why: Tachycardia, a preserved blood pressure, mildly delayed capillary refill and a raised respiratory rate fit ATLS class II haemorrhage (15–30%, about 750–1500 mL). Resuscitation is indicated.
notes: Loss above 30% (class III) would cause hypotension, marked tachycardia and confusion.
Loss above 40% (class IV) would cause profound shock with hypotension and depressed consciousness.
Loss above 50% would cause near-terminal shock, not a normal blood pressure and palpable radial pulse.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man taking carbamazepine for epilepsy develops fever (38.8°C), sore throat, conjunctivitis and widespread brownish target-like skin lesions. Over 30% of his body surface area has epidermal detachment with slight friction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Target lesions, a positive Nikolsky sign and epidermal detachment over 30% of body surface area after carbamazepine indicate toxic epidermal necrolysis. Admission to a burns or intensive care unit is needed.
notes: Urticaria causes transient itchy wheals, with no epidermal detachment or mucosal involvement.
Erythema multiforme minor has typical target lesions with minimal mucosal involvement and no extensive epidermal detachment.
Stevens-Johnson syndrome involves detachment of under 10% of body surface area; 10–30% is overlap.

items.stem: A 15-year-old girl has delayed puberty with primary amenorrhoea and short stature. She has no intellectual disability. Which genetic test is routinely used to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
items.why: Short stature with delayed puberty in a girl suggests Turner syndrome (45,X). Standard confirmation is a conventional karyotype.
notes: NGS panels are for unclear presentations or specific syndromes such as Noonan, not routine here.
FISH can detect a single X signal but is not the routine test.
Microarray is reserved for intellectual disability or suspected microdeletion syndromes.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman who carries an FMR1 premutation (fragile X syndrome) wishes to have children. Which statement about genetic counselling is correct?
options: All her sons will inherit the premutation and be affected
Genetic anticipation occurs, so her offspring may have earlier, more severe disease
Sex selection of embryos by FISH is the best way to ensure healthy offspring
Half her daughters will be carriers and none will have clinical features
items.why: Premutation alleles (55–200 CGG repeats) can expand to a full mutation (>200) during maternal transmission, causing earlier and more severe disease in sons and daughters. This is anticipation.
notes: Only about half of her children inherit the allele, and a premutation in a son is not the same as the full-mutation disease.
Sex selection does not ensure healthy offspring, as daughters can be affected and not all sons are.
Daughters inheriting the allele may have a full mutation and be affected, so 'no clinical features' is wrong.

items.stem: A 67-year-old has had progressive lymphocytosis over 6 months. Latest results: Hb 154 g/L, WCC 18.5 × 10^9/L with 82% mature lymphocytes expressing CD5/CD19/CD23, platelets 240 × 10^9/L. No symptoms are reported. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Test for TP53 mutation to establish prognosis
Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy to confirm diagnosis
Repeat clinical review and blood tests in 6 months
items.why: This is CLL phenotype without cytopenias or symptoms, so watch and wait is appropriate. TP53 testing is done when treatment is about to start, not at diagnosis.
notes: TP53 mutation affects prognosis but is tested when treatment is being started, not in asymptomatic early disease.
The diagnosis is established by blood flow cytometry; marrow biopsy is not required.
PET/CT is not needed for staging early CLL and does not guide observation.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man has had progressive lymphocytosis on two routine tests over 6 months. Haemoglobin is 154 g/L, white cell count 18.5 ×10⁹/L (82% mature lymphocytes, CD5+/CD19+/CD23+), and platelets 240 ×10⁹/L. He is asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: TP53 mutation testing to establish prognosis
Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy to confirm diagnosis
Clinical and blood count review in 6 months
items.why: This is asymptomatic early-stage (Binet A/Rai low-risk) CLL with no cytopenias, so watch and wait with periodic clinical and blood review is appropriate. Treatment is not yet needed.
notes: Prognostic testing is done when treatment is being considered, not at asymptomatic observation stage.
Marrow biopsy is not needed for diagnosis (flow cytometry suffices) and there are no unexplained cytopenias.
PET/CT is reserved for suspected Richter transformation, which is not suggested here.

items.stem: An 8-year-old boy has had an insidious limp for one month with no trauma or constitutional symptoms. Passive hip movement is restricted, especially abduction and internal rotation. Perthes disease is suspected. Which statement is FALSE?
options: In transient synovitis the onset is usually acute
In Perthes disease the prognosis is worse the younger the age at onset
The cause may be a hypercoagulable state
items.why: In Perthes disease, younger age at onset carries a better prognosis, and older children (over about 6 to 8 years) do worse. The statement that younger onset is worse is therefore false.
notes: This is true. A hip X-ray is the first investigation.
This is true. Transient synovitis presents acutely, unlike the insidious course here.
This is true. Thrombophilia has been implicated in Perthes disease.

items.stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with fever. Hb 114 g/L, WCC 0.86 ×10^9/L, platelets 48 ×10^9/L, fibrinogen 1.18 g/L, D-dimer markedly raised. Bone marrow shows acute leukaemia with t(15;17) in 60% of cells. Which is the correct management?
options: If asymptomatic, ATRA alone with day-hospital review
Arsenic trioxide plus ATRA with supportive care
Conventional chemotherapy plus heparin for DIC
Antibiotics first; start leukaemia treatment once fever settles
items.why: This is acute promyelocytic leukaemia with t(15;17) and coagulopathy. Treatment is urgent: arsenic trioxide plus ATRA with supportive care, without heparin or conventional chemotherapy.
notes: ATRA alone is incomplete treatment, and it should start promptly whether or not the patient is symptomatic.
Heparin and conventional chemotherapy are no longer used first-line; ATRA plus arsenic trioxide is standard, with blood product support for the coagulopathy.
The fever is attributable to the leukaemia itself, and delaying specific therapy risks fatal haemorrhage; treatment is not deferred.

items.stem: An 18-year-old, previously well, presents with several days of epistaxis and multiple ecchymoses. He is afebrile with no splenomegaly. Platelets are 6 ×10⁹/L with enlarged platelets on the smear; haemoglobin, white cell count, coagulation and biochemistry are normal. Most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Isolated severe thrombocytopenia with mucocutaneous bleeding, large platelets, normal coagulation and otherwise normal counts in a well patient indicates primary immune thrombocytopenia.
notes: TTP would show fever, haemolysis, neurological signs and schistocytes on the smear.
DIC requires abnormal coagulation tests and an underlying trigger, which are absent.
Infection-induced thrombocytopenia is unlikely in an afebrile patient with no infective features.

items.stem: An 18-year-old with no relevant history presents with several days of epistaxis. He is afebrile with multiple ecchymoses and no splenomegaly. WCC 7.2 ×10⁹/L, Hb 123 g/L, platelets 6 ×10⁹/L. The film confirms thrombocytopenia with enlarged platelets. Coagulation and biochemistry are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Isolated severe thrombocytopenia with large platelets, normal haemoglobin, normal coagulation and no systemic illness or splenomegaly is primary immune thrombocytopenia.
notes: TTP would show anaemia, schistocytes and usually fever, renal or neurological features.
DIC would have abnormal coagulation and a precipitating illness.
No infective features are present to suggest this.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has 3 weeks of worsening weakness, hand arthralgia and a photosensitive rash on the neckline. She is pale and tachycardic. Hb is 60 g/L, MCV 105 fL, LDH is raised, and WCC and platelets are near normal. Which test is most needed to guide immediate management?
items.why: The picture suggests lupus with probable autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (macrocytosis from reticulocytosis, high LDH, rapid onset). A direct Coombs test guides management: if positive, treat the autoimmune cause (steroids) and avoid transfusion except in extreme cases.
notes: B12 deficiency is more gradual in onset and does not fit the rapid fall with raised LDH.
ANA helps diagnose lupus but does not guide treatment of the anaemia right now.
Anti-dsDNA helps with lupus diagnosis and activity but does not decide the immediate anaemia management.

items.stem: A 65-year-old woman with no comorbidities has breast-conserving surgery and sentinel node biopsy. Histology shows an 11 mm grade 3 invasive ductal carcinoma, two negative sentinel nodes, ER 0%, PR 0%, HER2 negative, Ki-67 70%. Staging is negative. What is the most appropriate adjuvant treatment?
options: Anthracycline and taxane chemotherapy, radiotherapy and trastuzumab
Anthracycline and taxane chemotherapy, radiotherapy and tamoxifen
Anthracycline and taxane chemotherapy and radiotherapy
Anthracycline and taxane chemotherapy, radiotherapy and an aromatase inhibitor
items.why: This is triple-negative, high-grade breast cancer over 1 cm, so chemotherapy is indicated, and breast-conserving surgery requires adjuvant radiotherapy. Endocrine and HER2-directed therapy have no role without receptor expression.
notes: Trastuzumab requires HER2-positive disease; this tumour is HER2 negative.
Tamoxifen requires hormone receptor positivity; this tumour is ER and PR negative.
Aromatase inhibitors work only in hormone receptor-positive tumours, regardless of menopausal status.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man has a normal physical examination. CT shows a mediastinal mass and a hepatic nodule. Serum lactate dehydrogenase, beta-hCG and alpha-fetoprotein are all elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Metastatic extragonadal non-seminomatous germ cell tumour
items.why: Raised beta-hCG with alpha-fetoprotein and LDH in a young man with a mediastinal mass indicates a non-seminomatous germ cell tumour. Pure seminoma does not raise AFP.
notes: Hepatocellular carcinoma can raise AFP alone, but not beta-hCG.
Seminoma may raise LDH (and mildly hCG), but AFP is normal in pure seminoma.
Lymphoma can raise LDH but does not raise beta-hCG or AFP.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history has one month of pain along the ulnar border of the left arm and left ptosis. Chest imaging shows a left apical mass invading the second rib. What is the most appropriate treatment for the suspected diagnosis?
options: Chemotherapy alone, followed by radiotherapy without surgery
items.why: This is a Pancoast (superior sulcus) tumour with Horner syndrome. Induction concurrent chemoradiotherapy followed by surgical resection is the standard approach for resectable disease.
notes: Omitting surgery forgoes the curative resection achievable after induction therapy in resectable disease.
Upfront surgery is difficult with chest wall and rib invasion; induction chemoradiotherapy comes first.
Radiotherapy alone is the older approach; concurrent chemotherapy improves outcomes and is preferred.

items.stem: A 65-year-old man has two months of dysphagia to solids. Endoscopy shows a partially stenosing mid-oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Endoscopic ultrasound and PET-CT show no pathological lymph nodes. What is the most appropriate management?
items.why: Locally advanced resectable oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma is treated with preoperative chemoradiotherapy (e.g. CROSS regimen) followed by surgery, as guidelines recommend.
notes: Surgery alone gives poorer outcomes than multimodal therapy for locally advanced disease.
Surgery alone omits the neoadjuvant therapy that improves survival, whatever the operative technique.
Chemotherapy alone is inferior to combined chemoradiotherapy for squamous cell carcinoma.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man with abdominal pain and upper gastrointestinal bleeding has a tumour of the gastric wall. Histology shows a spindle cell tumour with few mitoses that is CD117 positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: GISTs are spindle cell tumours arising from the interstitial cells of Cajal and are characteristically CD117 (c-KIT) positive.
notes: Neurofibromas are S100 positive and are not typically CD117 positive.
Leiomyomas are smooth muscle tumours, positive for desmin and SMA and negative for CD117.
Granulocytic sarcoma is a myeloid tumour and not a spindle cell gastric tumour.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has had daily heartburn since youth, self-treated with antacids. Endoscopy shows mild erosive oesophagitis and a squamocolumnar junction 7 cm above the gastric folds. Distal oesophageal biopsies show intestinal-type columnar epithelium with low-grade dysplasia. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Continue antacids, as the oesophagitis is mild and the dysplasia low grade
Indefinite high-dose PPI, making endoscopic surveillance unnecessary
Periodic surveillance endoscopy and indefinite PPI therapy
items.why: This is Barrett's oesophagus with low-grade dysplasia. It needs endoscopic surveillance plus long-term PPI (or antireflux surgery) to limit progression.
notes: Antacids do not control acid adequately, and dysplasia needs surveillance.
PPIs do not remove the need for endoscopic surveillance.
Oesophagectomy is not indicated for low-grade dysplasia; it is reserved for invasive cancer not suitable for endoscopic therapy.

items.stem: A 15-year-old girl presents with delayed menarche and short stature, without intellectual disability. Which genetic test is routinely used to establish the likely diagnosis?
items.why: Delayed puberty with short stature in a girl suggests Turner syndrome (45,X), which is diagnosed by karyotype.
notes: NGS is for single-gene disorders and is not the routine test for suspected Turner syndrome.
FISH is targeted at specific loci and is not the routine diagnostic test here.
Microarray is for submicroscopic copy-number changes, not the routine first test for Turner syndrome.

items.stem: A 5-year-old boy with chronic kidney disease presents with vomiting, malaise and palpitations. ECG shows peaked T waves and serum potassium is 5.9 mmol/L. Intravenous calcium gluconate is given immediately. What is its purpose?
options: Shift potassium from plasma into cells
Bind circulating potassium to promote hepatic elimination
Bind circulating potassium to promote renal elimination
Antagonise the effect of potassium on the myocardial cell membrane
items.why: Calcium gluconate does not lower serum potassium. It stabilises the cardiac myocyte membrane, reducing excitability and the risk of arrhythmia.
notes: Shifting potassium into cells is the action of insulin with glucose or salbutamol, not calcium.
Calcium does not chelate potassium, and potassium is not eliminated by the liver.
Calcium does not chelate potassium or alter renal excretion; that requires diuretics, resins or dialysis.

items.stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with moderate respiratory distress, intercostal and subcostal recession, scattered expiratory wheeze, prolonged expiration and SpO2 95% in room air. He is afebrile and has no murmur. He is kept for observation. What is the most appropriate approach to investigations?
options: Venous blood gas, white cell count and acute phase reactants
Arterial blood gas and acute phase reactants
items.why: This is likely bronchiolitis, a clinical diagnosis. No investigations are needed unless the infant deteriorates.
notes: Blood tests and inflammatory markers are not routinely indicated in bronchiolitis.
Chest X-ray is not routine in typical bronchiolitis and is reserved for atypical or deteriorating cases.
Arterial gases and inflammatory markers are not indicated in a stable infant.

items.stem: An 8-year-old boy has had pubic hair at the base of the penis for 12 months. Testicular volume and penile size have not increased, growth velocity is unchanged, and bone age is one year ahead of chronological age. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Pubic hair without testicular enlargement (volume under 4 mL), penile growth or growth spurt indicates premature adrenarche, due to early adrenal androgen secretion.
notes: Central precocious puberty requires testicular enlargement (4 mL or more), which is absent here.
Peripheral precocious puberty would usually cause penile enlargement and more marked virilisation, not isolated pubic hair.
An androgen-secreting adrenal tumour would cause marked virilisation, rapid hair growth and penile enlargement, which he lacks.

items.stem: A 9-year-old boy has sudden-onset obsessive-compulsive disorder along with tics and chorea. Infection with which organism should be ruled out?
items.why: Abrupt OCD with tics or chorea in a child suggests PANDAS, a post-infectious autoimmune complication of group A beta-haemolytic streptococcal (Streptococcus pyogenes) infection.
notes: S. viridans is a cause of endocarditis and is not linked to PANDAS.
Alpha-haemolytic streptococci include viridans group and pneumococcus; they are not linked to PANDAS.
Enterococcus is not associated with post-infectious neuropsychiatric syndromes.

items.stem: A 79-year-old nursing home resident with no available history is brought to the ED. He is disoriented, has poor short-term memory and sees threatening people. He is agitated at times and drowsy and inattentive at others. Which feature best favours delirium over dementia?
items.why: Delirium is an acute disturbance of attention and awareness that fluctuates over the day. A fluctuating level of consciousness or alertness distinguishes it from dementia.
notes: Visual hallucinations occur in delirium but also in dementia, such as Lewy body dementia.
Cognitive impairment is present in both delirium and dementia.
Agitation can occur in both conditions and is not specific.

items.stem: A 9-year-old boy has sudden-onset obsessive-compulsive disorder together with tics and chorea. Which infection is most likely associated with this presentation?
items.why: Abrupt-onset OCD with tics or chorea in a child suggests a post-streptococcal autoimmune process (PANDAS/Sydenham chorea) following group A beta-haemolytic streptococcal infection.
notes: Viridans streptococci cause endocarditis, not post-streptococcal neuropsychiatric disorders.
Alpha-haemolytic streptococci are not linked to this autoimmune neuropsychiatric syndrome.
Enterococcus is not associated with post-infectious OCD, tics or chorea.

items.stem: A 46-year-old man with bipolar disorder presents after an intentional lithium carbonate overdose. He has severe tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, myoclonus and fasciculations. Serum lithium is 4.1 mmol/L (toxic >1.5). Which treatment is most appropriate?
items.why: Severe lithium toxicity with neurological signs and a very high level needs haemodialysis, as lithium is small, water-soluble and not protein bound. Dialysis is indicated for neurotoxicity or markedly raised levels.
notes: Aminophylline does not enhance lithium elimination in any useful way, and cathartics do not remove it.
Activated charcoal does not bind lithium, so it is ineffective.
Forced diuresis is not effective or safe for severe toxicity and risks fluid and electrolyte disturbance.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman has an incidental 2 cm polycystic lesion with central calcification in the pancreatic tail, not communicating with the main duct, and bilateral renal cysts. Fluid analysis is consistent with serous cystadenoma. What is the most appropriate management?
items.why: Serous cystadenoma is benign and usually asymptomatic. Surgery is reserved for symptomatic lesions or diagnostic doubt, so surveillance imaging is appropriate.
notes: Surgery is not needed for a benign, asymptomatic lesion.
Ablation is not indicated for a benign serous lesion.
Transplant has no role for benign cysts.

items.stem: A 37-week pregnant woman is HBsAg positive. She asks how her newborn should be managed and whether she can breastfeed. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Hepatitis B vaccine at birth only; formula feeding
Vaccine and immunoglobulin at birth; breastfeeding only from one month
Immunoglobulin at birth only; formula feeding
Vaccine and immunoglobulin within 12 hours of birth; breastfeeding is fine
items.why: Infants of HBsAg-positive mothers should receive hepatitis B vaccine and immunoglobulin at separate sites soon after birth (within 12 hours). Breastfeeding is not contraindicated as transmission risk via milk is very low.
notes: Immunoglobulin is also needed for immediate passive protection.
Delaying breastfeeding is unnecessary once the infant is immunised.
Vaccine is also needed for active immunity, and formula feeding is not required.

items.stem: A 79-year-old woman taking olmesartan has had 2 months of watery diarrhoea, 4 to 6 stools daily, after a 3-week NSAID course. Gastroscopy, colonoscopy and duodenal biopsies are normal. Colonic biopsies show chronic inflammation, a subepithelial collagen band over 10 µm thick and over 20 intraepithelial lymphocytes per 100 epithelial cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Chronic watery diarrhoea with a macroscopically normal colon and a thickened subepithelial collagen band with increased intraepithelial lymphocytes is microscopic (collagenous) colitis. Budesonide is the treatment.
notes: NSAID enteropathy affects the small bowel and does not give this colonic histology.
Olmesartan enteropathy causes duodenal villous atrophy, but the duodenal biopsies here are normal.
IBS has normal histology and no collagen band.

items.stem: A patient treated for acute diverticulitis with amoxicillin with clavulanic acid develops fever and diarrhoea on day 5. Clostridioides difficile colitis is diagnosed, the antibiotic is stopped and metronidazole started. After 4 days there is no response, but the patient is clinically stable. What is the next step?
options: Change to oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days
Change to piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 8 hours
Fashion a loop ileostomy with antegrade colonic lavage
items.why: Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days is the treatment for C. difficile infection that fails to respond to metronidazole. Fidaxomicin is an alternative.
notes: Another broad-spectrum antibiotic would worsen C. difficile infection and has no activity against it.
Colectomy is reserved for fulminant colitis with shock, ileus, megacolon or perforation; this patient is stable.
Diverting ileostomy with lavage is a surgical option for severe or fulminant disease, not for a stable patient.

items.stem: After a road crash, an injured man opens his eyes when spoken to and says only inappropriate words. He localises pain with his right limbs, but shows abnormal extension to pain in his left limbs. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale score?
items.why: Always score the best response in each domain. Eyes open to voice = E3, inappropriate words = V3, localising pain = M5, giving E3V3M5 (11/15).
notes: Verbal response is inappropriate words (V3), not incomprehensible sounds (V2), and the best motor response is M5, not M4.
Eye opening to voice is E3, not E2 (to pain), and the best motor response is M5, not M4.
Eye opening to voice is E3, not E2 (to pain), and inappropriate words score V3 rather than V4 (confused).

items.stem: A 15-year-old is ejected after being hit by a car. He is conscious with left chest pain and dyspnoea. BP 90/60 mmHg, HR 130, SpO2 90%, RR 35, with absent breath sounds and dullness on the left. X-ray shows left rib fractures and a massive effusion. A chest drain returns 1700 mL of blood. What is the next step?
options: Analgesia, oxygen, blood transfusion and urgent surgery
Intubation, transfusion and observation, operating only if he worsens
Intubation and urgent CT scan to assess injuries
items.why: Initial drainage over 1500 mL of blood is an indication for urgent thoracotomy per ATLS. Resuscitate with analgesia, oxygen and transfusion while arranging urgent surgery.
notes: Non-invasive ventilation does not secure the airway and does not control the bleeding.
Waiting for deterioration increases morbidity and mortality when immediate drainage is massive.
CT may be reasonable only if he stabilises, but with massive haemothorax haemorrhage control takes priority.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man is a pedestrian struck by a car. He is pale and sweaty with a thready pulse, BP 90/50 mmHg, HR 127/min, RR 28/min, SpO2 92%. After 1 L of crystalloid his vitals improve transiently, then deteriorate on arrival at hospital. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Immediate uncrossmatched group O blood (massive transfusion protocol)
Group-specific blood transfusion once typing is complete
Prepare crossmatched blood in case transfusion becomes necessary
Give a further 1 L crystalloid bolus
items.why: Transient response to fluids in a trauma patient indicates ongoing haemorrhagic shock. With vital compromise, blood must be given immediately as uncrossmatched group O (activate the massive transfusion protocol), alongside haemorrhage control.
notes: Group-specific blood requires typing time that this unstable, ongoing-bleeding patient does not have.
Crossmatching takes too long; transfusion is already indicated, not merely possible.
More crystalloid dilutes clotting factors and worsens acidosis, hypothermia and coagulopathy; blood products are needed.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman taking propranolol develops stridor, rash, vomiting and hypotension (90/40 mmHg) 30 minutes after a penicillin dose. Hypotension persists after repeated IM adrenaline and IV fluids. Which additional drug is most specifically indicated?
items.why: Beta-blockade can make anaphylaxis resistant to adrenaline, causing refractory hypotension and bradycardia. Glucagon (1–2 mg IV/IM, repeated or infused) bypasses the beta-receptor and is used in this setting.
notes: Corticosteroids have no proven role in acute resuscitation and do not address adrenaline resistance.
Antihistamines are adjuncts for skin symptoms only and do not treat refractory hypotension.
Salbutamol may help bronchospasm but does not reverse beta-blocker-related refractory hypotension.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man who migrated to Australia 4 years ago has had anxiety and low mood for 10 months, moderately affecting daily activities. He has no psychiatric history. Symptoms began after his older brother, to whom he was very close, died in a car accident. Which diagnosis is most appropriate?
items.why: Mild anxious-depressive symptoms after an identifiable stressor, with no previous psychiatric history, fit adjustment disorder. The stressor (bereavement) and its consequences are ongoing.
notes: The symptoms are relatively mild and do not seriously impair function, which argues against major depression.
There is no history of hypomanic episodes.
Requires symptoms for at least 2 years.

items.stem: A 7-year-old afebrile girl has had a red face since yesterday. Today she has a confluent maculopapular rash on both cheeks, sparing the perioral area, giving a 'slapped' look, and a reticular, lacy, non-itchy rash on the trunk. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Bilateral slapped cheeks followed by a lacy reticular truncal rash are typical of erythema infectiosum, caused by parvovirus B19.
notes: Varicella gives itchy vesicles in crops, not a slapped-cheek and lacy rash.
Rubella causes a rash spreading from the face with postauricular lymphadenopathy, not a lacy reticular pattern.
Roseola presents with high fever for several days, then a rash on the trunk as the fever settles.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes diagnosed 3 months ago has a BMI of 31 kg/m² and poor glycaemic control despite diet and exercise. Which of the following glucose-lowering drugs is associated with weight gain?
items.why: Pioglitazone (a thiazolidinedione) causes dose-dependent weight gain from fat accumulation and sometimes fluid retention.
notes: Metformin is weight neutral or causes modest weight loss.
SGLT2 inhibitors cause weight loss through glycosuria.
GLP-1 receptor agonists cause significant weight loss.

items.stem: A man with newly diagnosed HIV (CD4 45 cells/µL, viral load 500,000 copies/mL, negative tuberculin skin test) started an integrase inhibitor plus two NRTIs. At 3 months, viral load has fallen and CD4 is rising, but he develops fever and cervical lymphadenopathy. Node aspirate shows acid-fast bacilli and epithelioid granulomas. What is the best interpretation?
options: Lymph node tuberculosis caused by incomplete immunological recovery
Antiretroviral treatment failure with a new opportunistic infection
Opportunistic infection unmasked as part of immune reconstitution syndrome
A negative tuberculin skin test excludes tuberculosis in this patient
items.why: He is responding virologically and immunologically to ART, so the TB lymphadenitis has been unmasked by immune reconstitution (IRIS). It is not caused by incomplete recovery or treatment failure.
notes: The infection was unmasked during immune recovery; it is not a consequence of incomplete recovery.
Viral load has fallen and CD4 is rising, so this is the expected response, not treatment failure.
A negative tuberculin test does not exclude TB in severe immunosuppression because false negatives occur.

items.stem: An 86-year-old woman has non-valvular atrial fibrillation and a CHADS2 score of 3. Similar patients have a stroke risk of 2.2% on warfarin versus 5.2% without. What is the number needed to treat to prevent one stroke?
items.why: Absolute risk reduction is 5.2% − 2.2% = 3.0%. NNT = 1/0.03 = 33.3.
notes: 3 is the ARR in percentage points, not its reciprocal.
19.2 is the reciprocal of 5.2%, i.e. not the risk difference.
49.5 does not follow from the risk difference; NNT = 1/ARR.

items.stem: An 86-year-old woman has non-valvular atrial fibrillation and a CHADS2 score of 3. Stroke risk is 2.2% on warfarin versus 5.2% without it. What is the number needed to treat (NNT) with anticoagulation to prevent one stroke?
items.why: NNT = 1 / absolute risk reduction. ARR = 5.2% − 2.2% = 3% = 0.03, so NNT = 1/0.03 = 33.3.
notes: 3 is the absolute risk reduction in percentage points, not its reciprocal.
19.2 does not result from the correct calculation (1/0.03).
49.5 does not result from the correct calculation (1/0.03).

items.stem: A patient's arterial blood gas shows pH 7.40, PaCO2 60 mmHg and bicarbonate 36 mmol/L. What is the acid–base disturbance?
options: None, as the pH is normal
items.why: A normal pH can mask a mixed disorder. Raised PaCO2 indicates respiratory acidosis and raised bicarbonate indicates metabolic alkalosis (compensatory in chronic CO2 retention, as in COPD).
notes: A normal pH does not exclude a disorder; both PaCO2 and bicarbonate are abnormal.
Uncompensated respiratory acidosis would give a low pH and near-normal bicarbonate.
Metabolic alkalosis alone would not explain the raised PaCO2 of 60 mmHg.

items.stem: A 53-year-old obese woman with migraine has repeated clinic BP readings below 140/90 mmHg. She buys a validated home BP monitor and is taught to use it correctly. Over several weeks her home readings are consistently above 140/90 mmHg. What does she have?
items.why: Masked hypertension is normal clinic BP with elevated out-of-office BP on home or ambulatory monitoring. Her home readings stay raised over several weeks.
notes: No investigation has shown a secondary cause, so this label is unsupported.
White-coat hypertension is the reverse: raised clinic BP with normal home readings.
Resistant hypertension requires uncontrolled BP despite several drugs. She is untreated.

items.stem: An 18-year-old presents with oedema. Tests show proteinuria of 8 g/day without haematuria, hypoalbuminaemia, hypercholesterolaemia and normal renal function. After one month of empirical corticosteroids, he has fully recovered. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Nephrotic syndrome with normal renal function and complete response to corticosteroids indicates minimal change disease, which responds to steroids in about 85–90% of cases.
notes: Amyloidosis causes nephrotic syndrome but is rare at this age and does not remit with steroids.
IgA nephropathy usually presents with haematuria and does not typically give a full steroid response.
Alport syndrome presents with haematuria, hearing loss and progressive renal impairment, not steroid-responsive nephrosis.

items.stem: A man with CKD G4 (eGFR 20 mL/min/1.73 m²) presents with generalised weakness. His potassium is 7.0 mmol/L and the ECG shows hyperkalaemic changes. What is the first treatment to give?
options: Insertion of a dialysis catheter to start haemodialysis
items.why: In severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, IV calcium gluconate is given first to stabilise the cardiac myocyte membrane and protect against arrhythmia. It does not lower potassium, but it buys time for shifting and removal measures.
notes: Resins remove potassium slowly and do not protect the heart, so they are not first-line in an emergency.
Dialysis may be needed if the response is poor, but it takes time to set up and is not the first step.
Oral furosemide acts too slowly and is unreliable at eGFR 20. Cardiac membrane stabilisation comes first.

items.stem: A patient has had an ulcerovegetating lesion of the mandibular gingiva in the molar region for 5 months. He now develops numbness of the chin. What should be ruled out as the cause?
options: Herpes virus infection in an immunosuppressed patient.
items.why: Chin numbness (mental nerve neuropathy, numb chin syndrome) here indicates direct infiltration of the inferior alveolar nerve in the mandibular canal by the local oral carcinoma, not a paraneoplastic effect.
notes: Numb chin from a local tumour is direct infiltration, not paraneoplastic.
Sarcoidosis causes facial palsy, not mental nerve numbness, and does not fit a gingival tumour.
Herpes infection does not fit a chronic ulcerovegetating lesion with no immunosuppression.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with MEN-2A and a RET mutation has a 6 mm hypoechoic calcified thyroid nodule on ultrasound. Total thyroidectomy and neck dissection show three small nodules of uniform round cells in solid sheets with calcification and amyloid, no nuclear clearing or pseudoinclusions, synaptophysin positive, and nodal metastases. What is the diagnosis?
items.why: Multifocal medullary carcinoma arises from C cells in RET-mediated MEN-2A. Solid sheets of uniform cells with amyloid and neuroendocrine marker positivity are typical, and nodal metastases exclude simple hyperplasia.
notes: Papillary carcinoma shows optically clear nuclei, grooves and pseudoinclusions, and lacks amyloid; these are explicitly absent here.
Follicular carcinoma shows follicular architecture with capsular or vascular invasion, not amyloid or neuroendocrine staining.
C-cell hyperplasia is a precursor lesion and does not form invasive nodules or nodal metastases.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with reflux, Raynaud phenomenon and skin induration of the hands and arms was recently started on prednisolone 20 mg daily. She now has headache and malaise, BP 200/110 mmHg and creatinine 220 µmol/L. Which autoantibody is most associated with this complication?
items.why: This is systemic sclerosis with scleroderma renal crisis, precipitated by corticosteroids. Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies are most associated with diffuse disease and renal crisis.
notes: Anti-centromere is linked to limited disease and pulmonary hypertension, with renal crisis rare.
Anti-proteinase 3 is associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis, not scleroderma.
Anti-PM-Scl is linked to scleroderma–myositis overlap, not renal crisis.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman has leg oedema, reduced urine output, fever and a malar rash for 20 days. Creatinine is 265 µmol/L, Hb 105 g/L (normocytic), leukopenia, CRP 90 mg/L, ESR 60 mm/h. Which statement about her likely condition is correct?
options: Anti-Sm antibodies are not specific for this condition
Anti-centromere antibodies are present in 90% of cases
ANA are present in only 50% of cases
Anti-dsDNA antibodies correlate with the risk of nephritis
items.why: This is SLE with renal involvement. Anti-dsDNA antibodies correlate with disease activity and the risk of lupus nephritis.
notes: Anti-Sm antibodies are highly specific for SLE, though not sensitive.
Anti-centromere antibodies are typical of limited systemic sclerosis, not SLE.
ANA are positive in over 90% of SLE cases, so it is a sensitive screening test.

items.stem: A 75-year-old man has 3 weeks of malaise, bitemporal headache and jaw claudication, then amaurosis fugax of the left eye. The left temporal artery is thickened and pulseless. ESR is 92 mm/h and CRP is raised. Which statement about treatment of the likely diagnosis is correct?
options: Rituximab is first-line, as glucocorticoids are now second-line
Tocilizumab reduces relapses and cumulative prednisolone dose
With ischaemic symptoms, glucocorticoid doses above 30 mg/day should be avoided
Infliximab with 1 g glucocorticoid boluses is first-line for induction
items.why: This is giant cell arteritis. Glucocorticoids remain first-line (pulse doses if visual involvement), and tocilizumab is the steroid-sparing agent shown to reduce relapses and cumulative steroid dose.
notes: Glucocorticoids remain first-line in giant cell arteritis; rituximab is not standard therapy.
Visual or ischaemic involvement needs high-dose glucocorticoids (often IV pulses), not restriction to under 30 mg/day.
Infliximab has not been shown to be effective in giant cell arteritis and is not first-line.

items.stem: After reduction of an anterior shoulder dislocation and 3 weeks in a sling, a woman has numbness over the lateral shoulder and can abduct only to 15 degrees. MRI shows an intact rotator cuff. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Lateral shoulder sensory loss (regimental badge area) and deltoid weakness, with abduction beyond 15 degrees lost, indicate axillary nerve injury, a common complication of anterior dislocation.
notes: The rotator cuff is intact on MRI, and this would not cause sensory loss.
Adhesive capsulitis causes pain and stiffness, especially on external rotation, not focal sensory loss.
The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus (first 15 degrees of abduction, preserved here) and has no cutaneous territory.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has had a first episode of low back pain for 3 weeks that limits her daily activities. There was no trauma, she has no known underlying disease, and neurological examination is normal. Which imaging is indicated?
options: Plain X-ray of the lumbar spine
items.why: Acute low back pain (under 6 weeks) without red flags such as fracture, infection or malignancy does not need imaging. Management is reassurance, analgesia and staying active.
notes: Plain films add radiation and rarely change management without red flags.
MRI is reserved for red flags or persistent radicular symptoms; incidental findings are common and can mislead.
CT gives high radiation and is not indicated without suspected fracture or other red flags.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman taking the oral contraceptive pill has 2–3 days of weight loss, polyuria, polydipsia, nausea and deep rapid breathing (RR 28). BP 100/60, dry mucosa, afebrile, alert. Glucose 23 mmol/L, Na 131, pH 7.08, HCO3 8 mmol/L, ketonuria +++. What is the best management?
options: New type 2 diabetes; dyspnoea likely from pneumonia or pulmonary embolism
Diabetic ketoacidosis: IV insulin, IV fluids, supportive care and search for a precipitant
Type 1 diabetes: give bicarbonate first, then add IV insulin once acidosis corrected
Likely alcoholic ketoacidosis: measure blood alcohol before starting insulin
items.why: This is DKA at presentation of diabetes. Priorities are IV insulin and IV fluids, with bicarbonate only for severe acidosis; insulin should never be delayed.
notes: Ketoacidosis with Kussmaul breathing explains the dyspnoea; this is not type 2 diabetes with pneumonia or PE.
Bicarbonate is not first-line and insulin must not be delayed until acidosis is corrected.
Waiting for an alcohol level would delay insulin, which must not be delayed.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man develops right buttock pain after a long car trip and cannot tolerate prolonged sitting. He has intermittent right leg numbness relieved by standing. MRI, hip X-ray, sensation and reflexes are normal. Resisted abduction and external rotation with the hip flexed to 90° reproduces the pain. Most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Piriformis syndrome is sciatic nerve irritation by the piriformis muscle, causing gluteal pain and paraesthesia after prolonged sitting. Pain on resisted abduction and external rotation in 90° flexion (PACE manoeuvre) with normal imaging and neurology supports it.
notes: Causes groin pain and reduced internal rotation, with abnormal hip imaging or positive FADIR; not buttock pain on sitting with normal X-ray.
Causes lateral hip or iliotibial band pain, not sciatic-type buttock pain with leg numbness.
Radiculopathy would typically give reflex or sensory changes and MRI findings, which are normal here.

items.stem: A haemodynamically stable 25-year-old man has a motorcycle crash with negative FAST, mild head injury (GCS 14) and a displaced intracapsular right hip fracture. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Early reduction and internal fixation, within 24–36 hours
Elective total hip arthroplasty the following Monday
Delay until the head injury improves, then elective reduction and fixation next week
Emergency bipolar hemiarthroplasty because of the risk of non-union
items.why: In a young patient a displaced intracapsular fracture needs early anatomical reduction and fixation, preserving the native hip, to reduce the risk of avascular necrosis. He is stable, so surgery need not be delayed.
notes: Arthroplasty is avoided in a young patient. Delay also raises the risk of avascular necrosis.
Surgery should not be postponed in a stable patient, as delay increases the risk of avascular necrosis.
Replacement is avoided in a young patient. Fixation with reduction is preferred.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman with asthma and atopic dermatitis develops hypotension, tachycardia, urticaria and bronchospasm after eating peanuts. Which is the first drug to give and a blood test useful for later evaluation?
options: Intramuscular promethazine first; eosinophil cationic protein
items.why: This is anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline (0.01 mg/kg, max 0.5 mg in adults) is first-line. Serum tryptase, taken early and again at 4–6 hours, supports the diagnosis.
notes: Bronchodilators and other agents are adjuncts only; adrenaline must not be delayed.
Antihistamines are adjuncts and must not precede adrenaline; ECP is not the marker used.
Adrenaline is right, but eosinophil cationic protein is not the useful marker; tryptase is.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with prior gastrointestinal anisakiasis after eating fish has specific IgE to Anisakis simplex of 10 kU/L. Which dietary advice is most appropriate?
options: Avoid all fish, crustaceans, molluscs and cephalopods.
Fresh fish is safe if cooked on the grill.
Commercially deep-frozen fish is safe if thoroughly cooked.
Fresh marinated or cold-smoked fish is safe.
items.why: Anisakis larvae are killed by freezing (-20°C for at least 5 days) and by cooking above 60°C. Fresh raw, marinated, smoked or lightly grilled fish should be avoided.
notes: Unnecessary restriction; sensitisation is to the parasite, not to fish or other seafood.
Grilling may not heat the flesh sufficiently to kill larvae in fresh, unfrozen fish.
Marinating and cold smoking do not reliably kill larvae.

items.stem: A 16-year-old with grass pollen allergic rhinoconjunctivitis has inadequate seasonal control despite oral antihistamines and intranasal corticosteroids. Which disease-modifying treatment is indicated?
options: Allergen immunotherapy (sublingual or subcutaneous) for at least 3 years
Allergen immunotherapy (sublingual or subcutaneous) for a maximum of 1 year
Omalizumab every 4 weeks for up to 1 year
Omalizumab every 4 weeks for at least 6 months
items.why: Allergen immunotherapy is the only treatment that modifies the natural course of allergic rhinitis and should be given for at least 3 consecutive years.
notes: One year is too short to achieve a lasting disease-modifying effect.
Omalizumab is reserved for severe allergic asthma or urticaria, not isolated rhinitis.
Omalizumab is not indicated for rhinoconjunctivitis alone.

items.stem: A 78-year-old man has 3 months of fatigue and dyspnoea, now present at rest, plus exertional angina. BP is 110/80 mmHg, HR 85/min. There is a harsh systolic murmur at the right second intercostal space and bibasal crackles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Angina, heart failure symptoms and a harsh systolic murmur at the aortic area in an elderly patient indicate aortic stenosis; symptom onset marks a poor prognosis and need for valve replacement.
notes: Mitral regurgitation gives an apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla, not a right upper sternal border murmur.
Aortic regurgitation causes an early diastolic murmur and wide pulse pressure, not a harsh systolic murmur with narrow-ish pulse pressure.
Ischaemic cardiomyopathy would not explain a harsh aortic-area systolic murmur; the triad of angina, dyspnoea and murmur fits aortic stenosis.

items.stem: An 82-year-old woman with permanent atrial fibrillation for 10 years and preserved biventricular systolic function has episodes of symptomatic complete atrioventricular block. Which permanent pacing system is most appropriate?
items.why: In permanent AF there is no effective atrial activity to sense or pace, so a single-chamber ventricular (VVI) pacemaker is indicated for AV block. Preserved systolic function means no CRT is needed.
notes: Atrial sensing and tracking are useless in permanent AF, so a second lead adds no benefit.
An atrial lead cannot correct AV block, and the atria are fibrillating.
CRT is for reduced LVEF with LBBB or expected high ventricular pacing burden with heart failure; function is preserved here.

items.stem: A 23-year-old man with known Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome presents with palpitations. ECG shows an irregular wide-complex tachycardia at 205 bpm consistent with pre-excited atrial fibrillation. Which drug is appropriate to terminate it?
items.why: In pre-excited AF, drugs prolonging the accessory pathway refractory period (procainamide, or amiodarone) are used if cardioversion is not possible. DC cardioversion is the treatment of choice if unstable.
notes: AV nodal blockers like verapamil can increase conduction down the accessory pathway and cause VF.
Digoxin is contraindicated as it may increase ventricular rate and precipitate VF.
