Adenosine blocks the AV node and is ineffective or dangerous in pre-excited AF.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with resistant hypertension on an ACE inhibitor, a diuretic and a calcium channel blocker has BP 149/100 mmHg, K+ 2.2 mmol/L, metabolic alkalosis and creatinine 106 µmol/L. Which statement about his likely condition is correct?
options: It is caused by autonomous aldosterone secretion from the adrenal medulla
Plasma renin activity is typically raised
Adrenal CT is part of the work-up once biochemical confirmation is obtained
Spironolactone is contraindicated in its management
items.why: This is primary hyperaldosteronism. After biochemical screening (aldosterone:renin ratio) and confirmation, adrenal CT is used for subtype assessment, followed by adrenal vein sampling if surgery is considered.
notes: Aldosterone is made in the adrenal cortex (zona glomerulosa), not the medulla.
Renin is suppressed in primary hyperaldosteronism because of volume expansion.
Spironolactone (a mineralocorticoid antagonist) is a mainstay of medical treatment, not contraindicated.

items.stem: A 75-year-old woman with heart failure (LVEF 25%) and an ICD is stable in NYHA class III on maximum tolerated lisinopril, carvedilol and spironolactone. BP is 118/74 mmHg, HR 78/min, with a third heart sound and no congestion. What is the most appropriate next step?
items.why: In symptomatic HFrEF despite optimal ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker and MRA therapy, the ACE inhibitor should be replaced by sacubitril/valsartan. A 36-hour washout is needed because of angioedema risk.
notes: Combining it with an ACE inhibitor is contraindicated because of the risk of angioedema.
Ivabradine is a later option, and the ACE inhibitor should be changed to an ARNI first.
The beta-blocker has proven mortality benefit and should not be stopped.

items.stem: Ten days after hemithyroidectomy for a 1.5 cm thyroid nodule, histology shows a very cellular follicular neoplasm with invasion of adjacent blood vessels and nerves. Which statement is correct?
options: A follicular pattern is an indication for prophylactic central neck dissection
This is follicular carcinoma and completion thyroidectomy is required
Serum calcitonin distinguishes papillary from follicular carcinoma
items.why: Invasion of vessels and nerves means follicular carcinoma with adverse features, so completion thyroidectomy followed by radioiodine assessment is appropriate. Avoiding it is reserved for low-risk tumours such as microcarcinomas under 1 cm.
notes: Omitting further surgery is reserved for low-risk disease, not tumours with vascular or nerve invasion.
Prophylactic neck dissection is associated with medullary carcinoma, not a follicular pattern.
Calcitonin is a marker of medullary carcinoma and does not separate papillary from follicular carcinoma.

items.stem: A 65-year-old smoker with hypertension and dyslipidaemia has cyanotic mottled toes bilaterally. CT angiography shows a 7 cm descending thoracic aortic aneurysm distal to the left subclavian artery, with mural thrombus. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Statin therapy alone to stabilise the thrombus.
Open replacement with a tubular graft and reimplantation of the supra-aortic trunks.
items.why: A 7 cm symptomatic aneurysm with thrombus embolising to the feet needs repair. Thoracic endovascular repair is preferred for a descending aneurysm with suitable anatomy.
notes: Statins do not stabilise thrombus or prevent embolisation, and a 7 cm aneurysm needs repair.
CT angiography has already defined the anatomy; invasive aortography adds risk and delay.
Supra-aortic trunk reimplantation applies to arch disease; this aneurysm lies distal to the left subclavian artery.

items.stem: An 85-year-old man with permanent atrial fibrillation has 6 hours of sudden pain and coldness in the right foot. There is plantar cyanosis with partial sensory and motor deficit. The femoral pulse is palpable; popliteal and distal pulses are absent. What is the best management?
options: Avoid revascularisation because of the ischaemia time
Apply heat and wait for vascular review
items.why: This is acute limb ischaemia from an embolus (AF) with a threatened limb (sensory and motor deficit), needing urgent revascularisation by embolectomy, alongside heparin.
notes: At 6 hours the limb is still salvageable, so revascularisation is indicated.
Heat worsens ischaemic injury, and this threatened limb needs urgent intervention, not delay.
Prostaglandins are not adequate treatment for an acute embolic occlusion.

items.stem: A 4-year-old girl has had fever for 6 days. She has a maculopapular rash on the trunk and groin that is confluent but not scarlatiniform, non-purulent conjunctival injection, red lips, strawberry tongue, oedema and erythema of the hands and feet, and a 2 cm unilateral cervical node. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Fever for 5 or more days plus rash, non-exudative conjunctivitis, oral changes, acral oedema/erythema and cervical lymphadenopathy fulfils the criteria for Kawasaki disease.
notes: Measles has cough, coryza and exudate-free conjunctivitis with Koplik spots; it lacks acral oedema, red lips and a single large node.
Rubella is a milder illness with posterior auricular/occipital nodes and not prolonged high fever.
Scarlet fever has a sandpaper scarlatiniform rash and exudative pharyngitis, and the rash here is not scarlatiniform.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 6 years, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, ischaemic heart disease and prior biliary pancreatitis takes metformin, lisinopril, metoprolol, aspirin and atorvastatin. BP 151/93 mmHg, BMI 27.1 kg/m², HbA1c 8.3% (67 mmol/mol). Which add-on agent is most appropriate?
items.why: Empagliflozin, an SGLT2 inhibitor, lowers HbA1c, blood pressure and weight, and reduces cardiovascular events in people with established cardiovascular disease, so it suits this patient.
notes: Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycaemia and weight gain and have no cardiovascular benefit; they are not preferred in ischaemic heart disease.
Acarbose has modest HbA1c effect, causes GI side effects, and gives no cardiovascular benefit.
Sitagliptin lowers HbA1c but has no cardiovascular or BP/weight benefit, and DPP-4 inhibitors carry a pancreatitis concern given his history.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes since age 15 has nausea and abdominal distension, worse after meals. Evaluation is consistent with diabetic gastroparesis. Which medication is most appropriate to improve her symptoms?
items.why: Metoclopramide is the first-line prokinetic for gastroparesis. It antagonises D2 receptors and stimulates 5-HT4 receptors, increasing gastric contractions and antropyloroduodenal coordination, and it is also antiemetic.
notes: A proton pump inhibitor reduces acid but does not improve gastric emptying.
An antiemetic may ease nausea but is not a prokinetic and does not treat the underlying dysmotility.
Loperamide slows gut motility and would worsen gastroparesis.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has his GP request a serum vitamin B12 level because of his antidiabetic medication. Which drug is he most likely taking?
items.why: Long-term metformin is associated with reduced vitamin B12 absorption and lower serum levels, which is reversible on stopping. Monitoring B12 is recommended, especially with neuropathy or anaemia.
notes: Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycaemia and weight gain, not B12 deficiency.
Repaglinide is an insulin secretagogue and is not linked to B12 deficiency.
Pioglitazone causes fluid retention, weight gain and fractures, not B12 deficiency.

items.stem: An obese, asymptomatic 58-year-old man drinks alcohol moderately. Fasting plasma glucose is 8.5 mmol/L with negative urine glucose. On two later occasions weeks apart, fasting glucose is 6.6 and 7.5 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate step to confirm diabetes?
options: Perform a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test
He already meets the diagnostic criteria for diabetes
Measure HbA1c before making the diagnosis
items.why: Diabetes is diagnosed when fasting plasma glucose is ≥7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) on two separate occasions in an asymptomatic patient. Two of his three readings (8.5 and 7.5) meet this, so no further testing is needed.
notes: Not needed. An OGTT is reserved for equivocal results, and the fasting criteria are already met twice.
Insulin or C-peptide helps classify diabetes type. It is not a diagnostic test for diabetes.
HbA1c ≥6.5% is an alternative criterion, but it is not required when two fasting glucose results are already diagnostic.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman on the oral contraceptive pill presents with fever and left hemibody paraesthesias. Hb 75 g/L, platelets 7 ×10⁹/L, LDH 1200 U/L, reticulocytes 10%, haptoglobin undetectable, direct Coombs negative, schistocytes on film, normal PT and APTT. Which diagnosis is most likely?
items.why: The picture of neurological disturbance, fever, Coombs-negative microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia fits TTP.
notes: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia has a positive direct Coombs test and no schistocytes.
Evans syndrome combines Coombs-positive haemolysis with immune thrombocytopenia, and schistocytes are absent.
Immune thrombocytopenia has no haemolysis or schistocytes, and does not explain fever or neurological symptoms.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman on the oral contraceptive pill presents with fever and left hemibody paraesthesias. Hb 75 g/L, platelets 7 ×10⁹/L, LDH 1200 U/L, reticulocytes 10%, haptoglobin undetectable, direct Coombs negative, schistocytes on film, normal PT and APTT. Most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Fever, neurological symptoms, Coombs-negative microangiopathic haemolysis with schistocytes, severe thrombocytopenia and normal coagulation indicate TTP. Start urgent plasma exchange; ADAMTS13 confirms it later.
notes: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia has a positive direct Coombs test and no schistocytes. It does not cause this severe thrombocytopenia.
Evans syndrome is autoimmune haemolysis plus immune thrombocytopenia, so the Coombs test would be positive and schistocytes absent.
Immune thrombocytopenia is isolated thrombocytopenia. It does not cause haemolysis, schistocytes or neurological features.

items.stem: A 14-year-old girl has 2–3 years of slowed growth, delayed puberty (no menarche, little breast and pubic development), headaches and a left temporal partial hemianopia. Height is −2.1 SD, bone age is delayed 2 years, and FSH, LH and oestradiol are low. What is the best interpretation?
options: Hormone deficiency with optic chiasm involvement from a sellar or suprasellar lesion
Constitutional delay with a refractive error causing the visual symptoms
Isolated growth hormone deficiency, with an optometry review for glasses
items.why: Short stature, delayed puberty with low gonadotrophins, headache and visual field defect indicate a hypothalamic–pituitary lesion (e.g. craniopharyngioma) compressing the optic chiasm. Imaging is needed.
notes: Turner syndrome causes high gonadotrophins and low oestradiol (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism).
Refractive errors do not cause hemianopia, and the absence of polyuria does not exclude a sellar tumour.
Growth hormone deficiency alone does not explain low gonadotrophins, and refractive error does not cause hemianopia.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus on hydroxychloroquine has 15 days of progressive weakness and pallor. FBC shows Hb 74 g/L and MCV 108 fL. Which test is most useful in deciding management?
items.why: Subacute anaemia with macrocytosis (reticulocytosis) in SLE suggests autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, which is confirmed by a positive direct antiglobulin test and determines treatment.
notes: Haptoglobin supports haemolysis but does not show it is autoimmune, so it will not direct treatment.
B12 deficiency is a less likely cause of rapid anaemia in a young woman with SLE.
ANA is already known to be positive in SLE and does not explain the anaemia.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus on hydroxychloroquine has 15 days of progressive generalised weakness. She is pale. FBC shows Hb 74 g/L, Hct 0.31 and MCV 108 fL. Which test will be most useful in deciding management?
items.why: Rapid-onset anaemia in a patient with lupus suggests autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, and the direct Coombs test confirms the autoimmune mechanism. Reticulocytosis explains the mildly raised MCV.
notes: Low haptoglobin would suggest haemolysis but not its autoimmune cause, so it is less useful in deciding management.
B12 deficiency would give a higher MCV and a much slower onset than 15 days.
ANA adds nothing to the anaemia work-up as lupus is already diagnosed.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has had dyspnoea for 4 days. She has a regular tachycardia, no murmurs and normal chest auscultation. Arterial blood gas: pO2 9.3 kPa, pCO2 4.3 kPa. Blood count, renal and liver function are normal. PT 90%, APTT ratio 2.0 (normal <1.2). Which is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Dyspnoea, tachycardia, hypoxaemia and hypocapnia suggest pulmonary embolism. A prolonged APTT with thrombosis points to lupus anticoagulant, so antiphospholipid syndrome is the most likely cause.
notes: Factor V Leiden causes thrombosis but does not prolong the APTT, so it does not explain the coagulation result.
Haemophilia would not present with thrombosis and is very unlikely in a woman.
Acute pericarditis does not explain the hypoxaemia and does not prolong the APTT.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with 6 years of hypertension has poor control (BP 149/100 mmHg) despite an ACE inhibitor, a diuretic and a calcium channel blocker. Creatinine is 106 µmol/L, potassium 2.2 mmol/L with metabolic alkalosis; urinalysis is normal. Which statement is correct?
options: Aldosterone excess results from autonomous adrenal medullary overactivity
Bilateral adrenocortical hyperplasia is the usual cause
CT of the adrenals is part of the work-up once biochemically confirmed
items.why: This is probable primary aldosteronism (resistant hypertension with hypokalaemic alkalosis). After biochemical confirmation, adrenal CT defines the subtype and excludes carcinoma.
notes: Aldosterone is produced by the adrenal cortex (zona glomerulosa), not the medulla.
The most frequent cause is an aldosterone-producing adenoma, with bilateral hyperplasia the other main cause.
Spironolactone is the medical treatment of choice.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman has chronic kidney disease from diabetic nephropathy. Her creatinine is 283 µmol/L and eGFR (CKD-EPI) is 14 mL/min/1.73 m². Which statement is correct?
options: She has stage 3 CKD and should start phosphate binders
She has stage 5 CKD and kidney replacement therapy should be considered
Good glycaemic control can reverse her kidney failure
Proteinuria above 500 mg/24 h is unlikely
items.why: An eGFR below 15 mL/min/1.73 m² is stage 5 (G5) CKD, where kidney replacement therapy (or conservative care) should be discussed.
notes: Stage 3 is an eGFR of 30–59; her eGFR of 14 is stage 5.
Glycaemic control may slow progression but will not reverse established advanced damage.
Diabetic nephropathy usually has albuminuria above 300 mg/24 h, sometimes nephrotic range.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman is treated with ciprofloxacin for 5 days for uncomplicated cystitis. A week later she has malaise, arthralgia and a rash. Her eGFR is 45 mL/min/1.73 m² (100 six months ago). Urine microscopy shows leukocytes; nitrites are negative. What is the most likely cause of her renal impairment?
items.why: Malaise, arthralgia, rash, acute kidney injury and sterile pyuria after a drug exposure suggest drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis. Antibiotics, including ciprofloxacin, are among the commonest causes.
notes: Post-infectious GN typically follows streptococcal infection and presents with haematuria, mainly in children and older adults.
Direct tubular toxicity (crystal formation) from ciprofloxacin is very rare.
Pyelonephritis would present with fever and loin pain, and usually positive urine culture.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man presents with 12 hours of dark brown urine, 4–5 days after an upper respiratory tract infection. BP 150/95 mmHg, afebrile. Creatinine 71 µmol/L, urea 4.2 mmol/L, normal platelets and complement/autoimmune screen. Proteinuria 0.75 g/24 h; urine has 90% dysmorphic red cells, no white cells. Most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Macroscopic haematuria coinciding with an upper respiratory infection, mild proteinuria and normal renal function is typical of IgA nephropathy.
notes: Minimal change disease causes nephrotic-range proteinuria, not haematuria.
Post-infectious GN follows a latent period of 1–3 weeks and usually has low complement.
Interstitial nephritis shows pyuria and white cell casts, with renal impairment, and no dysmorphic red cells.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has dysmorphic haematuria, proteinuria of 3 g/24 h, eGFR 85 mL/min/1.73 m² and sensorineural hearing loss. His maternal grandmother needed dialysis at 70, and his mother and younger sister have isolated microscopic haematuria. Which diagnosis is most likely?
items.why: Haematuria, proteinuria and sensorineural deafness in a young man, with haematuria in female relatives, indicates Alport syndrome (usually X-linked, COL4A5 mutation).
notes: IgA nephropathy does not cause sensorineural deafness and is not typically inherited in an X-linked pattern with affected female relatives.
Fabry disease is X-linked and can cause proteinuria, but features are acroparaesthesias, angiokeratomas and corneal opacities rather than haematuria with deafness.
ADPKD causes large cystic kidneys, hypertension and usually little proteinuria; it is not associated with deafness.

items.stem: A 42-year-old obese woman has elevated serum, urinary and salivary cortisol. Cortisol remains elevated after an overnight dexamethasone suppression test, and ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome is suspected. Which test would best localise the cause?
items.why: ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome is caused by an adrenal adenoma, carcinoma or hyperplasia, so adrenal CT is the imaging of choice. In practice, confirm a suppressed ACTH first.
notes: Petrosal sinus sampling is used to separate pituitary from ectopic ACTH-dependent disease, not adrenal causes.
Octreotide scanning is used to find ectopic ACTH-secreting neuroendocrine tumours, which are ACTH-dependent.
Ultrasound has poor sensitivity for small adrenal lesions and is not the imaging of choice.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man develops malaise, oliguria and headache after a respiratory infection. BP is 210/120 mmHg with grade III hypertensive retinopathy. Hb 74 g/L, platelets 85 ×10⁹/L, schistocytes on film, LDH raised, creatinine 773 µmol/L, haematuria and proteinuria. ADAMTS-13 activity is normal. No diarrhoea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury indicate thrombotic microangiopathy. Normal ADAMTS-13 excludes TTP, no diarrhoea argues against STEC-HUS, and no coagulopathy argues against DIC, leaving atypical HUS.
notes: Normal ADAMTS-13 activity rules out TTP, which is characterised by severely reduced activity.
DIC would show deranged coagulation (prolonged PT/APTT, low fibrinogen) and bleeding, not described here.
Typical HUS follows a Shiga toxin-producing E. coli diarrhoeal illness, which is absent here.

items.stem: A 75-year-old woman on sertraline presents with confusion. She is euvolaemic with no oedema, BP 130/70. Na is 126 mmol/L, K 4 mmol/L, urine sodium 45 mmol/L; diuretics are excluded. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Treat as Addison disease with immediate corticosteroids
Give hypertonic saline to normalise sodium rapidly
Restrict fluids and review the sertraline
Order a brain MRI for presumed diabetes insipidus
items.why: This is euvolaemic hyponatraemia from SIADH, probably drug-induced. With moderate symptoms and Na above 125 mmol/L, fluid restriction is first-line; rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination.
notes: Adrenal insufficiency usually causes hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, not a euvolaemic picture.
Hypertonic saline is for severe neurological symptoms, and rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination.
Diabetes insipidus causes hypernatraemia, the opposite of this picture.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has chronic kidney disease classified as G3a/A1. Which eGFR and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) values correspond to this stage?
options: eGFR 45–59 mL/min/1.73 m² and ACR <3 mg/mmol
eGFR 30–44 mL/min/1.73 m² and ACR <3 mg/mmol
eGFR 45–59 mL/min/1.73 m² and ACR 3–30 mg/mmol
eGFR 15–29 mL/min/1.73 m² and ACR <3 mg/mmol
items.why: G3a is an eGFR of 45–59 mL/min/1.73 m², and A1 is a normal to mildly increased ACR (<3 mg/mmol).
notes: This eGFR range is G3b, not G3a.
ACR 3–30 mg/mmol is A2 (moderately increased albuminuria), not A1.
This eGFR range is G4, not G3a.

items.stem: A 75-year-old woman is brought by her family because of months of low mood and memory lapses. She herself feels well. Which sequence best describes the usual progression of symptoms in Alzheimer's disease?
options: Mood changes, behavioural symptoms, cognitive deficits.
Behavioural symptoms, motor symptoms, loss of functional independence.
Mood changes, cognitive deficits, loss of functional independence.
Behavioural symptoms, mood changes, motor symptoms.
items.why: Alzheimer's disease typically begins with mood change and memory/cognitive deficits, followed by progressive loss of functional independence. Early prominent behavioural or motor symptoms should prompt consideration of other dementias.
notes: Prominent behavioural symptoms are not typically the second step before cognitive deficits; cognitive decline is the core feature.
Early behavioural and motor symptoms suggest other dementias (e.g. frontotemporal, Lewy body), not typical Alzheimer's.
Early behavioural symptoms suggest other dementias, and motor symptoms occur late in Alzheimer's disease.

items.stem: An 80-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetes suddenly develops language impairment. Newly detected atrial fibrillation is found. She has fluent speech, poor comprehension, inability to repeat and difficulty naming. Which aphasia is this?
items.why: Wernicke's aphasia is fluent with impaired comprehension, repetition and naming. Here it is likely from an embolic stroke in the dominant temporal lobe in the setting of atrial fibrillation.
notes: Broca's aphasia is non-fluent with preserved comprehension.
Conduction aphasia has preserved comprehension, with impaired repetition.
Transcortical sensory aphasia resembles Wernicke's but repetition is preserved.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman, a heavy smoker with childhood febrile seizures, has stereotyped episodes of an ascending epigastric sensation and unpleasant smell, then unresponsiveness with lip-smacking and repeated left-hand opening and closing. Episodes last 2 minutes, followed by confusion. Most likely diagnosis?
options: Focal impaired awareness seizures of temporal lobe origin
Transient ischaemic attacks in the right carotid territory
items.why: An epigastric rising aura with olfactory hallucination, then impaired awareness with oral and manual automatisms and postictal confusion, is classic mesial temporal lobe epilepsy. Febrile seizures in childhood are a risk factor. Formerly called complex partial seizures.
notes: TIAs cause sudden negative symptoms (weakness, numbness), not stereotyped aura, automatisms and postictal confusion.
Focal aware motor seizures preserve awareness and involve clonic motor activity; here awareness is lost.
Transient global amnesia is a single episode of isolated anterograde amnesia without automatisms or aura, in older patients.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man has unilateral periocular headaches that rapidly become very intense. Attacks last 30–60 minutes, occur 2–3 times daily, and come with ipsilateral tearing and rhinorrhoea. What is the most appropriate preventive treatment?
options: Oral prednisolone weaned over one month, plus verapamil 80–180 mg every 8 hours
Indomethacin 50 mg every 8 hours for one month
items.why: This is cluster headache. Verapamil is the main preventive, usually started with a short tapering course of corticosteroid to cover the delay before it takes effect.
notes: Steroid alone is only a short bridge and is not adequate preventive therapy; verapamil is needed.
Carbamazepine is used for trigeminal neuralgia, not cluster headache.
Indomethacin is for paroxysmal hemicrania and hemicrania continua, which have shorter, more frequent attacks.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has a one-year history of progressive memory loss now requiring help with daily activities. He has migraines and past self-limited focal neurological episodes. Neuropsychology shows early dementia and MRI shows severe leukoencephalopathy. Which test should be ordered?
options: Lumbar puncture for CSF amyloid and tau
items.why: This is CADASIL, an autosomal dominant NOTCH3 small-vessel arteriopathy. It presents with migraine, recurrent strokes or TIAs, early cognitive decline and severe leukoencephalopathy.
notes: CSF amyloid and tau support Alzheimer disease, which does not explain migraine, focal episodes and marked leukoencephalopathy.
PSEN1 causes early-onset familial Alzheimer disease, not this vascular picture.
Progranulin mutations cause frontotemporal dementia, which presents with behavioural or language change.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man had a ruptured middle cerebral artery aneurysm causing subarachnoid haemorrhage, treated surgically. He recovered and walked, but one month later becomes progressively drowsy and struggles to follow commands. Which statement is correct?
options: He is at the stage when vasospasm is most frequent
The deterioration is most likely due to aneurysm rebleeding
Subacute deterioration is most likely due to hydrocephalus
Cerebral angiography is the diagnostic test of choice
items.why: Progressive decline in consciousness weeks after SAH suggests (communicating) hydrocephalus. Vasospasm occurs within the first 1–2 weeks, and non-contrast CT brain is the investigation of choice.
notes: Vasospasm typically occurs in the first week or two after the bleed (peak days 4–14), not at one month.
Rebleeding is most likely in the first 24 hours and would present abruptly, not as a progressive decline after the aneurysm was treated.
The first-line test is non-contrast CT brain to show ventricular enlargement; angiography is not the test of choice here.

items.stem: A 49-year-old man with severe traumatic brain injury and intraparenchymal haemorrhage is in ICU with an intracranial pressure monitor. Before intubation he did not open his eyes, made no sounds and extended to pain. Which statement is correct?
options: His Glasgow Coma Scale score on arrival was 7.
Cerebral perfusion pressure equals mean arterial pressure plus intracranial pressure.
Vasogenic oedema results from cell swelling, membrane rupture and cell death.
Cerebral blood flow increases with hypercapnia and acidosis.
items.why: Hypercapnia and acidosis cause cerebral vasodilatation, raising cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure.
notes: His GCS was 4 (E1 V1 M2): extension is M2.
CPP is mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure.
Cell swelling and death describe cytotoxic oedema; vasogenic oedema follows blood–brain barrier disruption.

items.stem: An asymptomatic 31-year-old woman is 10 weeks pregnant. Her brother, aged 26, has ataxia and a confirmed expanded CAG repeat (70 repeats) in the SCA3 gene. She is considering chorionic villus sampling. What is the appropriate approach?
options: Test her genotype first; fetal testing only if she carries the mutation
No testing, as the disease is fully penetrant and she is asymptomatic so not a carrier
Test the first child after birth and offer prenatal testing in a later pregnancy
Offer fetal testing regardless of her genotype, as inheritance is maternal
items.why: SCA3 is autosomal dominant, so she has a 50% prior risk. Test her first; if she is negative the fetus cannot inherit it, and if positive chorionic villus sampling can be offered.
notes: Being asymptomatic at 31 does not exclude carrying the mutation, as onset is variable and often later.
Waiting until after birth does not address the current pregnancy and is not the appropriate pathway.
Inheritance is autosomal dominant, not exclusively maternal, so unnecessary invasive testing would be avoided.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents after falling off an e-scooter with a closed head injury. She had no loss of consciousness or amnesia, has a mild headache without vomiting, a normal neurological examination and a GCS of 15. She takes no anticoagulants. What imaging is indicated?
items.why: A minor head injury with GCS 15, no anticoagulant or antiplatelet use and no red flags needs no imaging, as validated decision rules (for example the Canadian CT Head Rule) show.
notes: Non-contrast CT is for patients with red flags (such as GCS below 15, vomiting, anticoagulation or suspected skull fracture), none of which are present.
Contrast CT has no role in the acute assessment of head trauma.
Plain skull X-ray is not recommended, as it is poor at excluding intracranial injury.

items.stem: A 61-year-old smoker with hypertension presents with 15 minutes of sudden right-hand weakness and tingling, now almost fully resolved. ECG shows sinus rhythm at 93 bpm. Regarding the most likely diagnosis, which statement is FALSE?
options: A probable cause is artery-to-artery embolism from a detached carotid plaque.
Carotid duplex ultrasound of the supra-aortic vessels is of little diagnostic use.
Brain imaging is needed to assess for infarction of the parenchyma.
Revascularisation is indicated if imaging shows symptomatic carotid stenosis >70%.
items.why: This is a TIA. The basic aetiological work-up includes duplex ultrasound of the supra-aortic (carotid) vessels, echocardiography and targeted bloods, so calling duplex of little use is false.
notes: True: carotid plaque embolism is a common cause of TIA in a vascular-risk patient.
True: CT or MRI brain is needed to exclude haemorrhage and detect infarction.
True: symptomatic stenosis of 70% or more is an indication for carotid endarterectomy.

items.stem: A 53-year-old man develops low back pain after lifting weights at the gym. Hours later it radiates down the back of the right leg to the lateral border of the foot. He has a positive straight leg raise at 40°, an absent ankle reflex and cannot stand on tiptoe. What is the most likely cause?
items.why: Pain to the lateral foot, absent ankle reflex and inability to tiptoe (plantarflexion weakness) indicate S1 radiculopathy. An L5-S1 disc herniation compresses the traversing S1 root.
notes: L2-L3 herniation affects the L3 root, causing anterior thigh pain and a reduced knee reflex, not S1 signs.
L3-L4 herniation affects the L4 root, causing anterior thigh and medial leg pain, quadriceps weakness and a reduced knee reflex.
L4-L5 herniation affects the L5 root: dorsum of foot pain, weak dorsiflexion and hallux extension, with an intact ankle reflex.

items.stem: A 43-year-old woman with a levonorgestrel intrauterine device has poor sleep, hot flushes and palpitations. Free T4 and TSH are normal; FSH is 95.6 IU/L, LH 21 IU/L and estradiol is below 0.07 nmol/L. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Oral oestrogen plus progestogen, continuous regimen
items.why: Her hormone profile is menopausal (early menopause/premature ovarian insufficiency) with systemic vasomotor symptoms, so systemic oestrogen is indicated. The levonorgestrel IUD already provides endometrial protection.
notes: Benzodiazepines do not treat the cause and are not appropriate for vasomotor symptoms.
Vaginal oestrogen acts locally and does not control systemic vasomotor symptoms.
Added oral progestogen is redundant with the levonorgestrel IUD, and oral oestrogen carries a higher thrombotic risk.

items.stem: A primigravida at 34 weeks has BP 165/95 mmHg and a 2-day headache. Platelets 98 ×10⁹/L, AST 356 U/L, ALT 234 U/L, LDH 878 U/L, and schistocytes on blood film. Antenatal corticosteroids were completed 24 hours ago. Fetal weight is below the 1st centile with absent end-diastolic umbilical flow. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Expectant management with antihypertensives and magnesium sulfate until platelets improve
Home antihypertensive treatment with review every 48 hours
Delay delivery until fetal lung maturity is confirmed
items.why: This is HELLP syndrome with severe features and a growth-restricted fetus with absent end-diastolic flow at 34 weeks. Corticosteroids are complete, so immediate delivery is indicated.
notes: Expectant management is not appropriate for HELLP at 34 weeks with fetal compromise.
Home management is unsafe in severe HELLP syndrome.
Fetal lung maturation has already been achieved with the completed corticosteroids, so there is no reason to delay.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman wants contraception. She had an emergency caesarean section 7 months ago and is exclusively breastfeeding. Which statement is correct?
options: If amenorrhoeic, she needs no other contraception while breastfeeding
A levonorgestrel IUD is contraindicated within a year of caesarean section
A progestogen-only hormonal method is suitable
Combined hormonal contraception is the preferred option
items.why: Progestogen-only methods are suitable and preferred while breastfeeding. Oestrogen-containing methods are best avoided because they may reduce milk supply.
notes: Lactational amenorrhoea is only reliable within 6 months postpartum; at 7 months she needs another method.
A levonorgestrel IUD is not contraindicated after caesarean section.
Oestrogen-containing contraception may reduce milk supply, so it is not preferred while breastfeeding.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man presents with conjunctival hyperaemia, foreign body sensation and tender preauricular lymphadenopathy. Which of the following conditions is the LEAST likely cause of this presentation?
items.why: Preauricular lymphadenopathy is typical of infective conjunctivitis. Allergic conjunctivitis is not infectious and does not cause lymphadenopathy.
notes: Adenoviral conjunctivitis classically causes preauricular lymphadenopathy, so it fits.
Parinaud syndrome (e.g. Bartonella, tularaemia) is an infective conjunctivitis with regional nodes, so it fits.
Chlamydial conjunctivitis causes follicles and a lymphoid response with adenopathy, so it fits.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a sudden transient loss of consciousness. Which of the following has the highest diagnostic yield in determining the cause?
items.why: History, with a witness account, examination and orthostatic vital signs, is the most useful step in sorting out the cause of loss of consciousness. It guides which tests, if any, are needed.
notes: ECG is an important screening test but yields a diagnosis in a minority and is guided by the history.
EEG has low yield unless seizure is suspected from the history.
CT brain has low yield without focal signs or head trauma.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman wears +4.00 D distance glasses in both eyes. For some weeks she has had eye pain, headache and blurred vision at night while watching television in dim light. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Hyperopia and age over 50 give a shallow anterior chamber and thickened lens. Pupil dilation in dim light can close the angle, causing eye pain, headache, and blurred vision from corneal oedema.
notes: Migraine is not tied to dim light, and eye pain with blurred vision is not typical.
Actinic keratitis follows ultraviolet exposure and is unrelated to hyperopia or dim light.
Dry eye causes burning, grittiness and foreign-body sensation, not this picture.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman who wears +4.00 D glasses for distance has had several weeks of eye pain, headache and blurred vision at night while watching television in dim light. Which condition is she most likely to have?
items.why: A hyperopic eye is short with a crowded anterior segment, and an ageing lens thickens. Dim light causes mydriasis, which can intermittently close the angle and cause pain, headache and blurred vision.
notes: Migraine is usually in younger patients with a history, and is worsened by bright light and noise, not dim light.
Actinic keratitis follows intense UV exposure (for example welding or snow), not dim light.
Dry eye does not usually cause headache or this dim-light pattern.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman has several days of profuse watery diarrhoea, 10 kg weight loss, facial flushing, presyncope and colicky abdominal pain. Bloods show hypokalaemia. Ultrasound shows a 1.5 cm mass in the pancreatic tail. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Profuse watery diarrhoea with hypokalaemia and flushing, plus a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, indicates a VIPoma (Verner–Morrison syndrome).
notes: Causes hypoglycaemic symptoms, not secretory diarrhoea.
Usually clinically silent or causes mild symptoms; it does not produce this syndrome.
Causes necrolytic migratory erythema, diabetes and weight loss rather than watery diarrhoea.

items.stem: A 2-month-old has had a 3-day coryzal illness and now has moderate respiratory distress and expiratory wheeze. SpO2 is 89% in room air and RSV is isolated from a nasopharyngeal aspirate. Which treatment is most appropriate?
items.why: This is RSV bronchiolitis, which is managed with supportive care. Supplemental oxygen is indicated for hypoxaemia (SpO2 persistently below about 90–92%).
notes: Ribavirin has no role in routine bronchiolitis management and is not given orally.
Bronchodilators do not improve outcomes in bronchiolitis and are not recommended.
Corticosteroids have no proven benefit in bronchiolitis.

items.stem: A 79-year-old woman is admitted with an osteoporotic hip fracture. Regarding secondary prevention of fragility fractures, which one of the following statements is INCORRECT?
options: Low adherence to treatment is associated with an increased risk of fracture.
Bone turnover markers may help with early monitoring of response to treatment.
Vitamin D monotherapy effectively reduces fractures in community-dwelling older adults.
Increasing dietary calcium or taking calcium alone does not protect against fractures.
items.why: Vitamin D alone is not shown to reduce fractures in community-dwelling older adults. Calcium and vitamin D are given alongside antiresorptive or anabolic drugs, whose trials included them, but not as monotherapy.
notes: This is true: poor adherence to osteoporosis treatment is a major factor in increased fracture risk.
This is true: bone turnover markers can help with early monitoring of adherence and response to treatment.
This is true: neither increased dietary calcium nor calcium supplements alone protect against fractures.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man has 3 months of fatigue and fever, then nasal obstruction with bloody crusting and clots, and painful right proptosis. ESR is 65 mm/h; urinalysis shows microscopic haematuria and proteinuria of 520 mg/24 h. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Upper airway disease (crusting nasal mucosa, orbital mass causing proptosis) with glomerulonephritis is the classic presentation of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener's).
notes: EGPA features asthma, eosinophilia and neuropathy; destructive nasal and orbital disease with glomerulonephritis is less typical.
Microscopic polyangiitis causes glomerulonephritis and pulmonary capillaritis, but not granulomatous nasal or orbital disease.
Polyarteritis nodosa spares the lungs and glomeruli and does not cause nasal or orbital granulomas.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has 4 days of dyspnoea and tachycardia, with clear lungs, pO2 70 mmHg and pCO2 32 mmHg. Blood count, renal and liver function are normal. PT is normal, but the APTT ratio is 2 (normal <1.2). Which diagnosis is most likely?
items.why: Hypoxaemia with likely pulmonary embolism plus an isolated prolonged APTT suggests antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant), which prolong phospholipid-dependent tests in vitro yet cause thrombosis.
notes: Factor V Leiden causes thrombosis but does not prolong clotting times.
Haemophilia prolongs the APTT but is not a typical cause of thromboembolism.
Pericarditis would not explain the hypoxaemia or the prolonged APTT, and lacks typical features.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man's father died of colon cancer at 38. Colonoscopy shows hundreds of adenomas throughout the colon. Which statement about this patient is incorrect?
options: Annual colonoscopy surveillance with colectomy at age 40 is the best management.
Without colectomy he will almost certainly develop colorectal cancer.
Each of his children has a 50% risk of inheriting the condition.
items.why: In familial adenomatous polyposis, prophylactic colectomy is advised once polyposis is established, usually in early adulthood. Waiting until 40 is too late, as cancer typically develops around that age.
notes: This is correct: hundreds of colonic adenomas with a family history indicate FAP.
This is correct: untreated, the cancer risk approaches 100%.
This is correct: it is autosomal dominant (APC mutation), so each child has a 50% risk.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman has had 1 month of shoulder and pelvic girdle pain and stiffness, worst on rising and easing with movement. She has no fever, headache or systemic upset. Examination shows painful, stiff shoulders and hips. ESR and CRP are raised. What is the most likely diagnosis and initial treatment?
items.why: Age over 50, bilateral shoulder pain, morning stiffness, hip involvement and raised inflammatory markers indicate polymyalgia rheumatica, treated initially with moderate-dose corticosteroids.
notes: RA causes small-joint synovitis rather than isolated girdle stiffness at this age.
Fibromyalgia does not raise inflammatory markers.
Ankylosing spondylitis begins in young adults with inflammatory back pain, not in a 70-year-old woman.

items.stem: A 61-year-old woman with obesity, hypertension and metabolic syndrome has pain in both buttocks, the left lateral thigh to the knee and the left leg to mid-calf. It is reproduced by lifting the leg with the knee extended and relieved by flexing the knee. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Gouty arthritis of the left hip
items.why: Pain reproduced by the straight-leg raise and relieved by knee flexion is a positive Lasègue sign, indicating lumbosacral nerve root irritation (lumbar radiculopathy).
notes: Gout causes an acute, red, hot joint and would not follow a root distribution or change with knee flexion.
Hip osteoarthritis gives groin pain worsened by weight-bearing and reduced hip rotation, not pain below the knee with a straight-leg raise.
Neurogenic claudication is provoked by walking or standing and relieved by sitting or lumbar flexion, not by a straight-leg raise.

items.stem: A 61-year-old woman has pain in both buttocks, the left lateral thigh to the knee and the leg to mid-calf. Pain is reproduced by raising the left leg with the knee extended and eases when the knee is flexed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Gouty arthritis of the left hip
Neurogenic claudication from spinal canal stenosis
items.why: Pain provoked by the straight leg raise (Lasègue) test stretches the sciatic nerve root and indicates lumbar radiculopathy (sciatica).
notes: Hip joint disease does not give a positive straight leg raise test.
Hip osteoarthritis does not give a positive straight leg raise test.
Claudication from stenosis is brought on by walking or extension and does not give a positive straight leg raise.

items.stem: A 61-year-old woman with obesity, hypertension and metabolic syndrome has pain in both buttocks, the left trochanteric region, lateral thigh to the knee and leg to mid-calf. Pain is provoked by raising the leg with the knee extended and relieved by knee flexion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Gouty arthritis of the left hip
Neurogenic claudication from spinal canal stenosis
items.why: Pain reproduced by straight leg raise (Lasegue) and relieved by knee flexion indicates radicular irritation in the lumbosacral region, i.e. lumbosciatica.
notes: Nothing suggests an acute gouty joint, and hip pathology would not give a positive straight leg raise.
Hip osteoarthritis gives pain limiting walking, stiffness and a negative Lasegue test.
Stenosis pain worsens with trunk extension (walking, standing) and eases with flexion/sitting, not with leg raise.

items.stem: A 35-year-old postal worker has had 24 hours of neck pain without trauma, radiating down the left arm to the hand, with paraesthesia of the radial forearm. There is no weakness, neck movement is preserved but painful, and paravertebral muscle spasm is present. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Conservative treatment with analgesia/NSAIDs, local heat and relative rest
Urgent MRI and nerve conduction studies/EMG
Urgent referral to an orthopaedic outpatient clinic
items.why: This is acute cervical radiculopathy without red flags or motor deficit. Most cases settle with conservative care (about 75-90%).
notes: Surgery is reserved for progressive deficit, myelopathy or failed prolonged conservative care. None applies here.
Imaging and EMG are not needed without red flags or persistent symptoms after conservative treatment.
Urgent referral is not needed in the absence of red flags or neurological deficit.

items.stem: A 35-year-old postal worker has 24 hours of neck pain without trauma, radiating down the left arm to the hand with paraesthesia along the radial forearm. There is no weakness, neck movement is preserved but painful, and paravertebral spasm is present. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Conservative treatment with NSAIDs, local heat and relative rest
Urgent neurosurgical review for surgical assessment
Urgent MRI and nerve conduction studies/EMG
Urgent referral to an orthopaedic outpatient clinic
items.why: This is cervical radiculopathy (cervicobrachialgia) without red flags, so initial management is conservative with analgesia, heat and relative rest.
notes: There are no red flags such as progressive deficit, so this is not urgent surgical.
Investigations may be reasonable later, but pain control should come first when there are no alarm signs.
There are no alarm signs requiring urgent specialist referral; conservative treatment comes first.

items.stem: A 35-year-old postal worker presents with 24 hours of neck pain without trauma, radiating down the left arm to the hand with paraesthesia along the radial forearm. There is no weakness, neck movement is painful but preserved, and paravertebral spasm is present. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Conservative treatment with simple analgesia/NSAIDs, heat and relative rest
Urgent neurosurgical referral for surgical assessment
Urgent MRI of the cervical spine and nerve conduction studies/EMG
Routine referral to an orthopaedic outpatient clinic
items.why: This is an acute cervical radiculopathy (C6 pattern) without red flags. About 75% improve with non-surgical treatment, which is first line in the initial stages.
notes: Surgery is reserved for progressive neurological deficit, myelopathy or failure of conservative care; none is present here.
MRI is indicated for red flags (fever, weight loss, night pain, weakness) or persistent symptoms despite conservative treatment, not at first presentation.
Referral is not the first step; initial management is conservative and can be started immediately in primary care or the ED.

items.stem: A 27-year-old regular runner has calf pain during prolonged running that settles within hours of rest. Physiotherapy for presumed calf muscle overload has not helped over several months. Which investigation is most useful to confirm the likely diagnosis?
options: Posterior compartment pressure measurement immediately after exercise
Doppler ultrasound to exclude lower limb arterial disease
items.why: Recurrent exertional leg pain that resolves with rest and fails to respond to physiotherapy suggests chronic exertional compartment syndrome. Diagnosis is confirmed by measuring compartment pressures at rest and after exercise.
notes: PET is not used for diagnosing exertional compartment syndrome.
Doppler can exclude arterial causes (e.g. popliteal entrapment), but the picture fits compartment syndrome, which needs pressure measurement.
Magnetic resonance spectroscopy is not a standard diagnostic test for this condition.

items.stem: A 27-year-old male runner has had months of right calf pain that comes on with running and eases over hours of rest. Physiotherapy for 'calf overload' has failed. Which investigation would best help confirm the diagnosis?
options: Compartment pressure measurement of the posterior leg at rest and after exercise
Doppler ultrasound to exclude lower limb arterial disease
items.why: This is chronic exertional compartment syndrome. Diagnosis is confirmed by measuring intracompartmental pressures at rest and after exertion.
notes: PET has no role in diagnosing exertional leg pain of this kind.
Doppler may exclude vascular causes such as popliteal entrapment, but the history fits compartment syndrome and pressure measurement is the confirmatory test.
MR spectroscopy is a research tool and is not used to diagnose compartment syndrome.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man fell 2 m. He has a swollen left heel, tingling over the right anterior thigh and scrotum, and dysaesthesia in both feet. He moves both arms normally with no arm symptoms. Leg rotation and pelvic compression are painless. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Palpate the abdomen and log-roll him to examine the thoracolumbar spine
Apply a cervical collar and send for cervical spine and lower limb imaging
items.why: The sensory symptoms suggest a lumbar and sacral root injury, so the spine examination must be completed before imaging. He should be moved en bloc (log-roll) to palpate the thoracolumbar spine. The cervical spine appears clinically unaffected.
notes: Imaging the limb alone would miss a probable lumbar spine injury; the full secondary survey including the back comes first.
Arm function and sensation are normal, so the cervical spine is not the likely site of injury. The symptoms localise to the lumbosacral region.
An abdominal ultrasound does not address the neurological findings pointing to the lumbar spine.

items.stem: A 95-year-old woman in a residential aged care facility, independent in basic activities of daily living and walking in the garden, has mild cognitive impairment. She falls at night and X-ray shows a displaced subcapital fracture of the right hip. What is the most appropriate treatment?
items.why: A displaced subcapital (Garden III–IV) fracture in an elderly, mobile patient is treated surgically, usually with hemiarthroplasty, because of the high risk of avascular necrosis and non-union.
notes: Intramedullary nails are used for pertrochanteric (extracapsular) fractures.
Cannulated screws are for undisplaced fractures, and fail often when the fracture is displaced.
Non-operative care suits non-ambulatory patients with minimal pain or prohibitive surgical risk. She is mobile.

items.stem: A 95-year-old woman in residential aged care, independent in basic activities of daily living with mild cognitive impairment, falls at night. X-ray shows a displaced subcapital fracture of the right hip. What is the recommended treatment?
items.why: Displaced intracapsular fractures in elderly patients are treated with arthroplasty; hemiarthroplasty suits an older, low-demand patient.
notes: Intramedullary nails are for extracapsular (trochanteric) fractures.
Cannulated screws are reserved for undisplaced intracapsular fractures.
Conservative care is for very low functional demand or surgical contraindication; this patient is independent.

items.stem: A 95-year-old nursing home resident, independent in basic activities of daily living and with mild cognitive impairment, falls at night. X-ray shows a displaced subcapital fracture of the right neck of femur. What is the recommended treatment?
items.why: Displaced intracapsular fractures in the elderly carry a high risk of femoral head avascular necrosis, so arthroplasty is preferred. Hemiarthroplasty is shorter and less aggressive than total hip replacement.
notes: Intramedullary nails suit extracapsular (trochanteric) fractures, not subcapital ones.
Screw fixation is for undisplaced subcapital fractures, typically in younger patients.
Non-operative care is reserved for patients with very poor baseline status and limited life expectancy.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man presents with several days of knee pain. On examination, the Thessaly test (pain with internal and external rotation of the flexed knee, weight-bearing) is positive. Which injury is most likely?
items.why: The Thessaly test is a provocation test for meniscal injury: pain or catching on rotation of the flexed knee suggests a meniscal tear.
notes: ACL rupture is assessed with Lachman, anterior drawer and pivot shift tests, not the Thessaly test.
PCL rupture is assessed with the posterior drawer and posterior sag signs.
Osteoarthritis causes gradual pain, stiffness and crepitus; the Thessaly test is not used to diagnose it.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man has had knee pain for several days. The Thessaly test (pain on internal and external rotation with the knee slightly flexed, weight-bearing on one leg) is positive. What is the most likely lesion?
items.why: The Thessaly test is used to diagnose meniscal tears, with high sensitivity and specificity.
notes: ACL rupture is assessed with the Lachman and anterior drawer tests.
PCL rupture is assessed with the posterior drawer and sag signs.
Degenerative arthropathy is not diagnosed by the Thessaly test.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man presents with several days of knee pain. On examination, the Thessaly test (pain with internal and external rotation of the flexed, weight-bearing knee) is positive. Which injury is most likely?
items.why: The Thessaly test is a meniscal provocation manoeuvre. Joint-line pain, locking or catching on loaded rotation of the slightly flexed knee suggests a meniscal tear.
notes: ACL assessment uses the Lachman and anterior drawer tests, and no trauma is described.
PCL assessment uses the posterior drawer test and sag sign, and no trauma is described.
Possible, but unlikely in a 41-year-old with an acute presentation, and the test points to a meniscus.

items.stem: A 13-year-old girl, 3 months post-menarche, has progressive idiopathic scoliosis. Standing X-ray shows a thoracolumbar curve of 35° (Cobb angle) and Risser grade 0. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Swimming and review in three months
Review in 6 months with repeat X-ray
items.why: A Cobb angle of 25–45° in a skeletally immature patient (Risser 0) with remaining growth is an indication for bracing to prevent progression.
notes: Exercise alone does not prevent progression of a curve of this size.
Physiotherapy does not halt curve progression in a growing adolescent.
Observation alone risks progression during rapid growth.

items.stem: A 13-year-old girl, menarche 3 months ago, has idiopathic scoliosis followed since age 10 and now progressing. Examination shows a 7° rib hump on Adams test. X-ray: T4–L1 curve of 35° (Cobb), Risser 0. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Recommend swimming and review in 3 months
Refer to physiotherapy for spinal stretching
Review in 6 months with a repeat X-ray
items.why: Curves below about 50° are managed conservatively. With a progressing 35° curve and substantial growth remaining (Risser 0, recent menarche), bracing is indicated to slow progression.
notes: Swimming does not prevent curve progression and review is too late for a progressing curve.
Physiotherapy alone does not halt progression of a significant growing curve.
Simple observation is inadequate for a progressing 35° curve in a skeletally immature patient.

items.stem: A 79-year-old woman is admitted with an osteoporotic hip fracture. Regarding secondary prevention of fragility fractures, which statement is INCORRECT?
options: Low adherence to treatment is associated with increased fracture risk
Bone turnover markers may help monitor early response to treatment
Vitamin D monotherapy reliably reduces fractures in community-dwelling older people
Calcium alone, from diet or supplements, does not protect against fractures
items.why: Vitamin D alone has not been shown to reduce fractures in community-dwelling older people. Calcium plus vitamin D may modestly reduce non-vertebral fractures, mainly in deficient or institutionalised people.
notes: This is true; poor adherence to antiresorptives is associated with more fractures.
This is true; turnover markers such as CTX and P1NP can show early response.
This statement is true; calcium alone has not been shown to prevent fractures.

items.stem: A 79-year-old woman is admitted with an osteoporotic hip fracture. Regarding secondary prevention of fragility fractures, which statement is INCORRECT?
options: Low adherence to treatment is associated with increased fracture risk
Bone turnover markers may help in early monitoring of treatment response
Vitamin D monotherapy reduces fractures in community-dwelling older people
Calcium alone, from diet or supplements, does not protect against fractures
items.why: Vitamin D alone is not effective for fracture prevention in community-dwelling older people. Calcium and vitamin D are used alongside antiosteoporotic drugs, not as monotherapy.
notes: This is true; poor adherence raises fracture risk.
This is true; turnover markers can help monitor adherence and response.
This is true; calcium alone does not prevent fractures.

items.stem: A 20-year-old man presents after a bicycle crash with facial trauma. CT shows a midface fracture involving the orbitozygomatic region, including the orbital floor. Which of the following is a common complication of this type of fracture?
items.why: Orbitozygomatic fractures often involve the orbital floor, increasing orbital volume and causing enophthalmos, as well as diplopia from inferior rectus displacement or entrapment.
notes: The TMJ is close to but not part of the orbitozygomatic complex.
Malocclusion occurs with fractures lower in the midface involving the maxilla, not typically an orbitozygomatic one.
Nasoethmoidal injuries involve the nasal bones, which lie anterior to the medial orbital rim, outside the orbit.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman with breast cancer has metastases at the intervertebral foramina between C4 and C5 and between T4 and T5. Which spinal nerves are at risk?
items.why: There are 8 cervical nerves but 7 cervical vertebrae: C1–C7 exit above their vertebra, and C8 exits between C7 and T1. So C5 exits between C4 and C5. Thoracic nerves exit below their vertebra, so T4 exits between T4 and T5.
notes: C4 exits between C3 and C4, not C4 and C5.
T5 exits between T5 and T6, and C4 exits between C3 and C4.
T5 exits between T5 and T6, not between T4 and T5.

items.stem: A 56-year-old overweight man with type 2 diabetes has mild hepatomegaly and drinks alcohol only rarely. Liver biopsy shows macrovesicular fat in 50% of hepatocytes, neutrophilic inflammatory foci, Mallory hyaline and pericentral fibrosis. Which statement is correct?
options: The diagnosis is hepatic glycogenosis associated with diabetes.
The changes are irreversible and will inevitably progress to cirrhosis.
The injury is clearly alcohol-related despite the patient's denial.
Weight loss and good diabetes control may prevent progression to cirrhosis.
items.why: This is steatohepatitis (NASH), which diabetes and obesity can cause just as alcohol does. In the early stage it is reversible if the cause is removed, so weight reduction and glycaemic control are key.
notes: The vacuoles are intracellular fat, not glycogen.
In the early phase the changes are reversible when the cause is removed; cirrhosis is not inevitable.
Diabetes causes similar changes, so there is no reason to disbelieve the patient.

items.stem: An elderly woman is drowsy with faecal soiling. BP 100/60 (sitting 70/30), HR 100, Kussmaul respiration, weight 50 kg. pH 7.25, pCO2 14 mmHg, HCO3 5 mmol/L, Na 133, K 2.5, Cl 118 mmol/L, creatinine 300 µmol/L, urea 21 mmol/L. Which statement is correct?
options: Respiratory compensation for the acidosis is inadequate
Bicarbonate should never be given in any circumstances
She has acute kidney injury of prerenal cause
items.why: This is a normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis with hypokalaemia, consistent with diarrhoeal losses. Postural hypotension and raised urea and creatinine indicate volume depletion and prerenal AKI.
notes: Expected pCO2 is about 1.5 × 5 + 8 = 15.5 (±2), so a pCO2 of 14 is appropriate compensation.
Postural hypotension and tachycardia point to volume depletion, so dehydration is not excluded.
Bicarbonate is generally avoided unless pH falls below about 7.10, but 'never in any circumstances' is too absolute.
items.origin: ANESTHESIOLOGY, CRITICAL CARE AND EMERGENCY MEDICINE

items.stem: A 64-year-old man with hypertension and ischaemic heart disease presents to the emergency department with oppressive chest pain that began at rest. At triage, BP is 155/95 mmHg and SpO2 is 95% on room air. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Ask him to wait in the waiting room until tests are arranged
Transfer him directly to the resuscitation bay
Obtain a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival
Refer him directly from triage to the coronary care unit
items.why: Suspected acute coronary syndrome needs a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival. Management (resuscitation bay, cardiology review, CCU) then depends on the ECG findings.
notes: Chest pain of possible cardiac origin should not wait; he is haemodynamically stable but needs an urgent ECG.
He is stable, so resuscitation bay transfer is not needed before the ECG shows ischaemic changes.
Admission to CCU depends on ECG and troponin results; it is not decided at triage.
items.origin: ANESTHESIOLOGY, CRITICAL CARE AND EMERGENCY MEDICINE

items.stem: An 82-year-old woman with moderate Alzheimer's disease, AF, depression and osteoarthritis has become more confused. She takes digoxin and warfarin (stable for 3 years), fluoxetine (4 months) and ibuprofen (1 month). BP 130/80 mmHg, HR 48/min, RR 10/min. What is the most likely cause?
items.why: Acute confusion with bradycardia in a patient on digoxin suggests digoxin toxicity, likely precipitated by reduced renal clearance after starting an NSAID (ibuprofen).
notes: Progression is gradual; a sudden change with bradycardia points to a precipitant such as a drug effect.
Depression has been treated and would not explain the bradycardia.
Ibuprofen may contribute by impairing renal function, but it does not itself explain the bradycardia and confusion as well as digoxin toxicity.
items.origin: ANESTHESIOLOGY, CRITICAL CARE AND EMERGENCY MEDICINE

items.stem: A 48-year-old man has a 5 cm right colon tumour on colonoscopy. His maternal grandmother had colon cancer. Superficial biopsies show a poorly differentiated medullary carcinoma with abundant stromal inflammatory cells. Which statement is correct?
options: Chemotherapy is the treatment of choice
Prognosis depends mainly on its high degree of anaplasia
It is unlikely this tumour arose from a previous adenoma
Microsatellite instability and mismatch repair genes should be tested
items.why: Medullary carcinoma almost always shows microsatellite instability (Lynch syndrome or sporadic MLH1 methylation) and has a better prognosis than other poorly differentiated tumours, so mismatch repair testing is indicated.
notes: Colon cancer is treated primarily surgically, with adjuvant chemotherapy depending on stage.
Despite poor differentiation, medullary tumours have a relatively favourable prognosis.
Most colorectal cancers arise from adenomas, including those with microsatellite instability.

items.stem: A patient with recent fever and chest pain presents with dyspnoea and tachypnoea. Examination shows hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure with a preserved X descent and pulsus paradoxus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Hypotension with raised JVP and pulsus paradoxus indicates tamponade. Fever and chest pain suggest an inflammatory pericardial effusion.
notes: Ischaemia does not explain the raised JVP, hypotension and pulsus paradoxus triad.
Dilated cardiomyopathy causes heart failure but not pulsus paradoxus.
Aortic stenosis would present with a systolic murmur, syncope or angina, not this picture.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man presents to a regional hospital 2 hours after onset of severe chest pain. He is cold and sweaty with BP 80 mmHg systolic. ECG shows marked ST elevation in V1–V6, I and aVL. He had a stroke 4 months ago. Which reperfusion strategy is most appropriate?
options: Immediate fibrinolysis at the regional hospital
Immediate transfer to a tertiary centre for fibrinolysis
Immediate transfer to a tertiary centre for primary percutaneous coronary intervention
Haemodynamic stabilisation followed by deferred revascularisation
items.why: An extensive anterior STEMI with cardiogenic shock needs urgent primary PCI regardless of delay. A stroke 4 months ago is also a relative contraindication to fibrinolysis.
notes: Shock favours PCI, and the recent stroke is a relative contraindication to fibrinolysis.
Transferring a patient for fibrinolysis wastes time. If fibrinolysis were chosen, it would be given where he is.
Urgent reperfusion is indicated in STEMI with shock, so deferring it is inappropriate.

items.stem: A 37-year-old man presents with syncope after 2 days of exertional dyspnoea. BP 75/50 mmHg, HR 130 sinus, SpO2 89%, troponin 1.2 µg/L, T-wave inversion V1–V4. CT pulmonary angiogram shows filling defects in both main pulmonary arteries. BP stays 70/55 mmHg an hour later. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: Unfractionated heparin bolus, then systemic thrombolysis with alteplase
Enoxaparin 80 mg subcutaneously 12-hourly, started on clinical suspicion
Enoxaparin 80 mg subcutaneously 12-hourly, started once diagnosis confirmed
items.why: Persistent hypotension defines high-risk (massive) PE, for which systemic thrombolysis is the accepted treatment, with unfractionated heparin anticoagulation.
notes: Enoxaparin alone would suit haemodynamically stable PE, not persistent hypotension.
Same error, and anticoagulation should not wait for confirmation when suspicion is high.
Surgical embolectomy is considered only if thrombolysis is contraindicated or fails; thromboendarterectomy is for chronic disease.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman with heart failure (on ramipril and furosemide) and insulin-treated type 2 diabetes presents with dyspnoea. Arterial blood gas on room air: pH 7.45, PaO2 56 mmHg, PaCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3 26 mmol/L. What does this show?
options: Hypoxaemic respiratory failure with compensated respiratory alkalosis
Acute metabolic alkalosis with hypoxaemic, hypocapnic respiratory failure
Chronic normocapnic respiratory failure with normal acid-base balance
Chronic hypoxaemic respiratory failure with compensated metabolic acidosis
items.why: Low PaO2 with low PaCO2 and a high-normal pH indicates hyperventilation, a primary respiratory alkalosis. Renal bicarbonate handling is beginning to compensate and keep pH near normal.
notes: Bicarbonate is not raised, so there is no metabolic alkalosis.
PaCO2 is low, not normal, and the pH is at the alkalotic end of normal.
Bicarbonate would be low in metabolic acidosis, and the primary disturbance is respiratory.

items.stem: A patient admitted with acute pancreatitis develops tachypnoea, tachycardia, sweating and progressive cyanosis. PaO2 is 55 mmHg (PaO2/FiO2 <200), CXR shows bilateral alveolar infiltrates, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is normal and oxygen does not help. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Bilateral infiltrates, severe hypoxaemia (PaO2/FiO2 <200) refractory to oxygen and a normal wedge pressure (non-cardiogenic) define ARDS, a recognised complication of acute pancreatitis.
notes: Pneumonia would usually give focal consolidation, not diffuse bilateral infiltrates with this picture after pancreatitis.
Cardiac failure would show raised wedge pressure; here it is normal, so the oedema is non-cardiogenic.
PE does not typically cause bilateral alveolar infiltrates; the criteria described fit ARDS.

items.stem: A 76-year-old obese woman with type 2 diabetes on metformin has had 3 days of fever, polyuria, dysuria, thirst and falling consciousness. She is dehydrated, BP 95/54 mm Hg, no focal neurology. Glucose is 47 mmol/L, creatinine 159 µmol/L, with leukocytosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: An older type 2 diabetic with infection (likely urinary), severe hyperglycaemia, dehydration, prerenal AKI and reduced consciousness has hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state.
notes: A subdural haematoma does not fit the picture and would usually cause focal neurological signs.
Obstructive renal failure would not explain polyuria, dysuria, and the hyperglycaemic picture.
DKA is more typical of type 1 diabetes and is less likely in an older type 2 patient with this picture.

items.stem: A 17-year-old with colonic Crohn's disease on azathioprine presents with 5 days of bilateral, tender, warm, purplish-red pretibial subcutaneous nodules, with increased stool frequency and abdominal pain. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Rest, warm compresses to both legs and add an antidepressant
Biopsy skin away from the lesions and start opioid analgesia
Suspect drug-induced bilateral lower limb ischaemia
Adjust treatment of the underlying Crohn's disease
items.why: These are erythema nodosum lesions accompanying a Crohn's flare. Treating and controlling the bowel disease usually improves the skin lesions; biopsy is not needed.
notes: Antidepressants and warm compresses do not address the flare driving the erythema nodosum.
Biopsy is unnecessary for typical erythema nodosum, and opioids are not indicated.
The picture is typical of erythema nodosum, not ischaemia from azathioprine.

items.stem: A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman has fatigue and exertional dyspnoea. Hb 60 g/L, MCV 69 fL, ferritin 4 µg/L, iron 2.3 µmol/L. She has mild epigastric pain and heartburn, no vaginal bleeding. Gastroscopy shows only a small hiatus hernia without oesophagitis. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Oral iron and monitor the anaemia
Proton pump inhibitor and review at three months
items.why: Iron deficiency anaemia in a postmenopausal woman is occult gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise. With a non-explanatory gastroscopy, colonoscopy is next, as colonic lesions are more common than small bowel ones.
notes: Iron alone treats the result without finding the source of bleeding, which may be a colorectal cancer.
A small hiatus hernia without oesophagitis does not explain severe iron deficiency; PPI alone would delay the work-up.
Capsule endoscopy is reserved for when bidirectional endoscopy is negative, as small bowel lesions are less common.

items.stem: A patient has had diarrhoea for over 4 weeks. Which feature in the history can occur in people without organic disease, such as in irritable bowel syndrome?
options: Weight loss with or without rectal bleeding
Extraintestinal features such as dermatitis or arthritis
Passage of mucus with more than 25% of bowel motions
items.why: Passage of mucus is compatible with irritable bowel syndrome. Weight loss, nocturnal diarrhoea, bleeding and extraintestinal features are alarm features suggesting organic disease.
notes: Weight loss and bleeding are alarm features of organic disease.
Nocturnal diarrhoea suggests an organic cause.
Dermatitis or arthritis suggests inflammatory bowel disease or coeliac disease.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has had a year of generalised pruritus, fatigue, dry mouth and dry eyes, and now has jaundice. She has no hepatitis risk factors and does not drink alcohol. Examination shows excoriations and non-tender hepatomegaly. Bilirubin is 51 µmol/L, ALP 400 U/L, ESR 40 mm/h. Which test best establishes the diagnosis?
items.why: This is classic primary biliary cholangitis: middle-aged woman, pruritus, sicca symptoms and a cholestatic picture. Anti-mitochondrial antibodies make the diagnosis.
notes: Iron studies screen for haemochromatosis, which does not give this cholestatic picture with sicca symptoms.
Imaging would exclude rare biliary malformations or Caroli disease, but is not the diagnostic test for this picture.
Serology would exclude viral hepatitis, which is unlikely without risk factors and with a cholestatic pattern.

items.stem: A 52-year-old asymptomatic man has had raised transaminases for two years. His father died of cirrhosis. He has bronze skin pigmentation and mild hepatomegaly; glucose is 8.3 mmol/L, ferritin 950 microgram/L, transferrin saturation >45%, viral serology negative. HFE testing shows C282Y homozygosity. What is the best next step?
items.why: C282Y homozygosity with raised transferrin saturation and ferritin confirms hereditary haemochromatosis, so no biopsy is needed. Venesection is the treatment of choice.
notes: Biopsy is reserved for uncertain diagnosis or suspected advanced fibrosis (e.g. ferritin >1000 or markedly abnormal liver tests); the diagnosis here is already established.
MRI can quantify iron but is not required when genetics and iron indices confirm the diagnosis; it would not change management.
Chelation is second-line, used only when venesection is not possible (e.g. anaemia or poor venous access).

items.stem: A 78-year-old man has idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy with mildly reduced left ventricular function (ejection fraction 48%) and chronic atrial fibrillation. Which one of the following drugs should be avoided in his treatment?
items.why: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen inhibit renal prostaglandin synthesis, raising vascular resistance and causing sodium and water retention with reduced renal perfusion. This can precipitate decompensated heart failure.
notes: Digoxin gives symptomatic benefit in heart failure and helps with rate control in AF, though it doesn't improve survival.
Anticoagulation is indicated in chronic AF to prevent thromboembolism.
ACE inhibitors block neurohormonal activation in heart failure and improve survival in systolic dysfunction.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man has exertional angina. Coronary angiography shows significant proximal stenoses in all three major coronary vessels with good distal run-off. His left ventricular ejection fraction is below 30%. What is the best management?
items.why: Three-vessel disease with severe LV dysfunction is best treated with surgical revascularisation (CABG), which improves outcomes over PCI or medical therapy when the distal vessels are suitable.
notes: PCI is a reasonable option for three-vessel disease with preserved LV function, but not the best choice with severe LV dysfunction.
Medical therapy alone gives poorer outcomes than surgery in multivessel disease with depressed LV function.
Transplantation is reserved for end-stage heart failure with no revascularisation option; here the targets are graftable with good distal beds.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man has idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, LBBB, LVEF 26% and mild-to-moderate mitral regurgitation. He remains NYHA class III despite furosemide, spironolactone, enalapril and bisoprolol. Which intervention is most appropriate?
options: Implantation of a ventricular assist device.
Implantation of a cardiac resynchronisation system.
items.why: Cardiac resynchronisation therapy is indicated for LVEF below 35%, wide QRS (typically LBBB) and NYHA class III-IV despite optimal medical therapy. Biventricular pacing restores synchronous contraction.
notes: Revascularisation is of little benefit here; the cardiomyopathy is idiopathic and there is no ischaemic target.
The mitral regurgitation is mild-to-moderate and likely secondary to annular dilatation, so valve replacement is not the answer.
A VAD is reserved for end-stage refractory heart failure as a bridge to transplant or destination therapy, not for this patient yet.

items.stem: A 75-year-old hypertensive, dyslipidaemic man with heart failure (EF <30%) has worsening dyspnoea over weeks. BP is 160/95 mmHg, HR 65 bpm, chest clear, JVP normal. Creatinine is 3.7 mg/dL (about 330 µmol/L) with normal electrolytes. Which drug is most appropriate to improve his prognosis?
items.why: With severe renal impairment, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and potassium-sparing MRAs risk worsening renal function and hyperkalaemia. A beta-blocker such as bisoprolol improves prognosis without these risks.
notes: ACE inhibitors can worsen renal function and raise potassium in severe renal impairment.
ARBs carry the same risk of renal deterioration and hyperkalaemia.
Spironolactone is potassium-sparing and risks dangerous hyperkalaemia with this degree of renal failure.

items.stem: A patient with a recent febrile illness and chest pain presents with dyspnoea and tachypnoea. BP is low, JVP is elevated with a prominent x descent, and there is pulsus paradoxus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Hypotension, raised JVP with a preserved prominent x descent and pulsus paradoxus indicate cardiac tamponade, here after probable pericarditis. Constrictive pericarditis instead shows a deep y descent.
notes: Dilated cardiomyopathy does not cause pulsus paradoxus or a prominent x descent.
Aortic stenosis gives an ejection systolic murmur and a slow-rising pulse, not pulsus paradoxus.
Constrictive pericarditis has a prominent y descent and is typically chronic.

items.stem: A 26-year-old asymptomatic man has a mid-systolic murmur at the aortic area and left sternal border that increases with the Valsalva manoeuvre. BP and pulses are normal. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy and deep T-wave inversion in V3–V6. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: A young man with a systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva, left ventricular hypertrophy and deep lateral T-wave inversion is the classic picture of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Valsalva reduces preload and worsens outflow obstruction.
notes: Aortic stenosis murmurs usually decrease with Valsalva, and pulses are typically reduced at that age only with severe disease.
Aortic regurgitation causes an early diastolic murmur with a wide pulse pressure.
A VSD gives a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge that does not increase with Valsalva.

items.stem: A 78-year-old woman with hypertension was admitted 3 months ago with heart failure and atrial fibrillation (moderate LV dysfunction), and is now on furosemide and enalapril. She feels better but BP is 150/90 mmHg and AF rate is 110–120 bpm. Which treatment best improves symptoms and reduces cardiovascular mortality?
items.why: She has AF needing anticoagulation (warfarin) and heart failure with reduced EF needing a rate-controlling beta-blocker with proven survival benefit, such as carvedilol.
notes: Digoxin controls rate but does not reduce mortality, and aspirin is inadequate stroke prevention in AF.
