Aspirin is inadequate for stroke prevention in AF, and atenolol lacks the proven survival benefit of carvedilol in heart failure.
Verapamil is contraindicated in systolic heart failure and should not be combined with beta-blockers because of the risk of conduction block.

items.stem: A 64-year-old smoker with diabetes and hypertension has right calf pain on climbing hills and prolonged walking, relieved within minutes by standing still. The right foot is well perfused but the pedal pulse is reduced. Which initial test best confirms the diagnosis and assesses severity?
items.why: This is typical intermittent claudication from peripheral arterial disease. The ankle-brachial index is the first-line, non-invasive test to confirm the diagnosis and gauge severity.
notes: Imaging is reserved for planning revascularisation, not as the initial test.
Invasive angiography is used when revascularisation is being considered, not initially.
Imaging such as MR angiography is used to plan revascularisation, not initially.

items.stem: An 87-year-old man with chronic bronchitis and heart failure has acute calculous cholecystitis. After four days of fasting, IV fluids and piperacillin/tazobactam he still has fever, abdominal pain and leukocytosis. What is the most appropriate next step?
items.why: Cholecystectomy is definitive but this frail patient has very high operative risk (ASA IV). Failure of medical therapy is managed with percutaneous cholecystostomy drainage, with elective surgery reconsidered after recovery.
notes: Urgent surgery carries prohibitive risk given his age, lung disease and heart failure.
Piperacillin/tazobactam already gives adequate cover; the problem is an undrained inflamed gallbladder, not antibiotic choice.
Changing antibiotics does not drain the source, and aminoglycosides add toxicity in the elderly.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has a hepatic flexure colon cancer. Her mother, an aunt (diagnosed at 45) and a grandfather also had colon cancer, suggesting Lynch syndrome. Which operation is most appropriate to reduce the risk of metachronous cancer?
items.why: The family history suggests Lynch syndrome, and conventional right hemicolectomy carries over 30% recurrence risk. Total colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis is preferred; prophylactic rectal excision is unnecessary.
notes: Segmental resection leaves colon at high risk of metachronous cancer in Lynch syndrome.
Extended resection still leaves much of the at-risk colon behind.
Removing the rectum is not needed prophylactically; it is used for FAP or rectal disease.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer (bone metastases) has good pain control on a weak opioid and NSAIDs. She now has headache unresponsive to this analgesia, and CT brain shows brain metastases. Which management is most appropriate for this pain?
options: Give extra opioid doses as needed
Add a corticosteroid such as dexamethasone
Switch to a strong opioid and continue NSAIDs
items.why: Headache from brain metastases is due to raised intracranial pressure and vasogenic oedema, which responds to corticosteroids (e.g. dexamethasone 4–16 mg daily).
notes: Opioids do not treat the oedema causing this headache.
Extra opioid doses do not address raised intracranial pressure from vasogenic oedema.
Changing opioid and continuing NSAIDs still does not treat the cerebral oedema.

items.stem: A 17-year-old boy with colonic Crohn's disease on maintenance azathioprine has 5 days of tender, warm, red-purple bilateral pretibial subcutaneous nodules, with more frequent stools and abdominal pain. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Biopsy skin away from the lesions and prescribe opioid analgesia.
Suspect a malignant intestinal tumour as the trigger of the skin lesions.
Suspect drug-induced bilateral lower limb ischaemia.
Adjust the treatment of the bowel disease.
items.why: The nodules are erythema nodosum, which here accompanies a Crohn's flare. Treating the underlying bowel disease is the correct approach.
notes: Biopsy and opioids are not needed for typical erythema nodosum.
A malignant tumour is a very rare cause in a 17-year-old; Crohn's is far more likely.
Painful pretibial nodules with a flare are erythema nodosum, not ischaemia.

items.stem: A 17-year-old boy with colonic Crohn's disease on azathioprine maintenance has had 5 days of bilateral, tender, warm, red-purple pretibial subcutaneous nodules, with increased stool frequency and abdominal pain. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Relative rest and warm compresses to both legs, plus an antidepressant
Biopsy skin away from the lesions and prescribe opioid analgesia
Suspect a malignant intestinal tumour as the trigger of the skin lesions
Adjust treatment of the bowel disease
items.why: This is erythema nodosum associated with a Crohn's flare. It usually resolves with treatment of the intestinal flare and recurs with relapses.
notes: Rest and leg elevation are supportive, but antidepressants have no described role and the underlying flare needs treating.
Erythema nodosum is a clinical diagnosis and self-limiting; biopsy and opioids are unnecessary.
Malignancy is an unlikely trigger in a 17-year-old; the nodules reflect the Crohn's flare.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man developed blisters on the dorsum of his hands 10 days ago after sun exposure, with skin fragility. Histology shows a subepidermal blister with PAS-positive deposits in and around superficial dermal vessels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Photodistributed blistering with skin fragility and a subepidermal blister with PAS-positive perivascular hyaline deposits is typical of porphyria cutanea tarda.
notes: Hailey–Hailey is a suprabasal acantholytic disorder of flexures, not photo-induced.
Bullous pemphigoid causes tense blisters in older patients but is not photodistributed and lacks PAS-positive vessel deposits.
Pemphigus vulgaris is an intraepidermal (suprabasal) blister with mucosal involvement, not photo-induced.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man reports blistering lesions on the dorsum of his hands appearing 10 days ago after sun exposure, with skin fragility. Histology shows a subepidermal blister with PAS-positive deposits in and around superficial dermal vessels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Porphyria cutanea tarda causes skin fragility with erosions and blisters on photoexposed sites such as the dorsum of the hands. Histology shows a subepidermal blister with PAS-positive perivascular hyaline deposits.
notes: Hailey-Hailey disease is an intraepidermal acantholytic disorder affecting flexures, not photoexposed subepidermal blisters.
Pemphigoid causes tense blisters without photodistribution or perivascular PAS-positive hyaline deposits.
Pemphigus vulgaris is intraepidermal (suprabasal acantholysis) and is not related to sun exposure.

items.stem: A woman has had a 2-week itchy eruption of multiple flat-topped, polygonal, violaceous papules on the volar wrists, shins and lower back. She also has white reticulated lesions on the buccal mucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Pruritic purple polygonal flat-topped papules on flexor wrists and shins with oral Wickham striae are typical of lichen planus.
notes: Mycosis fungoides gives patches or plaques with a chronic course, not violaceous papules with oral reticulation.
Guttate psoriasis causes small scaly pink papules after streptococcal infection, without oral lesions.
Pityriasis rosea has a herald patch and oval scaly lesions in a Christmas-tree pattern, without mucosal lesions.

items.stem: A woman has a 2-week pruritic eruption of multiple flat-topped, polygonal, violaceous papules on the anterior wrists, shins and lower back, plus whitish reticulated lesions on the buccal mucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Pruritic, violaceous, polygonal flat-topped papules on the flexor wrists and ankles with oral whitish reticulation (Wickham striae) are classic for lichen planus.
notes: Mycosis fungoides gives chronic patches or plaques, not acute polygonal papules with oral reticulation.
Guttate psoriasis gives small scaly erythematous papules after streptococcal infection, without mucosal lesions.
Pityriasis rosea has a herald patch then oval scaly lesions in a Christmas-tree pattern, with no oral involvement.
